cases.title: Union of India v. OmniSearch Inc.
cases.facts:
OmniSearch Inc. is a private multinational technology conglomerate that
enjoys a 98% market share in internet search and social networking within
India. The platform has become the de facto public square for civic
debate, political campaigning, and government announcements. In 2025,
OmniSearch updated its algorithmic content moderation policy. Relying on
an opaque AI system, OmniSearch permanently banned the accounts of
several prominent Indian investigative journalists and a minority
political party, classifying their criticism of certain government
policies as "coordinated inauthentic behavior."

The banned entities filed a writ petition under Article 32 directly in
the Supreme Court of India against OmniSearch Inc. They alleged a gross
violation of their fundamental right to Freedom of Speech and Expression
under Article 19(1)(a). OmniSearch moved to dismiss the writ, arguing
that they are a purely private corporate entity governed by contract law
(Terms of Service) and cannot be subjected to writ jurisdiction, as they
do not fall under the definition of "State" under Article 12 of the
Constitution.
cases.issues:
Has a private multinational technology corporation possessing a near-
absolute monopoly over the digital public square become an
instrumentality or agency of the "State" under Article 12 of the
Constitution?

Can a writ petition under Article 32 or 226 be maintained against a
private social media platform for the violation of Fundamental Rights?

Does the algorithmic moderation of civic and political speech on a
monopolistic platform constitute the discharge of a "public duty" or a
sovereign function?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Banned Entities)
The Plaintiffs relied on the evolving jurisprudence of Article 12, citing
cases like Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib and Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of
India. They argued the "Public Function" test. OmniSearch is not merely
selling shoes; it controls the modern infrastructure of democratic
discourse. Because the government itself relies on OmniSearch for
critical public broadcasts, the platform has stepped into the shoes of
the State. The Plaintiffs argued that when a private entity achieves such
absolute monopolistic control over a fundamental right (speech), it
assumes a public duty. Allowing a private, unaccountable algorithm to
censor journalists without due process effectively outsources state
censorship to a corporation, bypassing the Constitution entirely.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (OmniSearch Inc.)
OmniSearch firmly defended its private corporate status. They argued that
holding a massive market share does not magically transform a corporation
into the Government of India. They receive no state funding, possess no
sovereign powers of coercion or taxation, and have no government
directors on their board. They argued the relationship is purely
contractual: users agree to the Terms of Service, which grant the company
the absolute right to curate its own platform. Subjecting private tech
companies to Article 12 would mean every moderation decision is subject
to judicial review, paralyzing the tech industry and forcing private
property to act as an unmoderated government utility.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court delivered a split verdict but ultimately ruled in favor
of the Plaintiffs. The Court held that OmniSearch Inc., in the specific
context of moderating political and journalistic speech, discharges a
public function and is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226,
though not fully classified as "State" under Article 12. The Plaintiff
partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court fundamentally modernized constitutional jurisprudence for the
digital age. The judge acknowledged that OmniSearch fails the traditional
financial and administrative tests for being an "instrumentality of the
State" under Article 12. However, the Court expanded upon the "Public
Function" doctrine.

The Court ruled that the physical public square has been entirely
subsumed by the digital public square. When a private entity holds a 98%
monopoly over the primary conduit of information and democratic
participation, it effectively controls the realization of Article
19(1)(a). The Court held that while OmniSearch is not the "State" for all
purposes (e.g., employment disputes), its specific action of regulating
and censoring public, journalistic, and political speech constitutes the
discharge of a profound public duty. Therefore, an aggrieved citizen can
invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts (Article 226) against the
corporation to enforce their fundamental rights, stripping the tech giant
of its absolute contractual immunity when it comes to arbitrary
censorship.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case significantly expands the doctrine of Public Function and Writ
Jurisdiction. It establishes the legal principle that monopolistic
private tech platforms controlling the digital public square, while not
strictly "State" under Article 12, discharge a public duty and are
amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226 when their actions
violate fundamental constitutional rights like Freedom of Speech.

cases.title: State of Kerala v. The Synapse Project
cases.facts:
The State Government initiated a mandatory welfare program requiring all
citizens applying for subsidized food rations to register with "The
Synapse Project." Unlike traditional biometric systems (fingerprints/iris
scans), Synapse required beneficiaries to wear an EEG-enabled headband
for five minutes while viewing a screen. The device recorded their
brainwave patterns (neural data) to create an absolutely unforgeable,
unique neuro-biometric signature.

An alliance of privacy activists filed a writ petition in the Supreme
Court, seeking to strike down the project. They argued that collecting
raw brainwave data represents the ultimate breach of human privacy, as
neural data can inadvertently reveal underlying psychological conditions,
emotional states, and subconscious responses. The State defended the
project, citing the elimination of widespread welfare fraud and arguing
that the data was heavily encrypted and used solely for authentication,
not psychological profiling.
cases.issues:
Does the mandatory collection of neural data (brainwaves) for welfare
authentication violate the fundamental Right to Privacy embedded in
Article 21 of the Constitution?

Does the "Synapse Project" satisfy the three-fold proportionality test
established in the K.S. Puttaswamy judgment for restricting fundamental
rights?

Does the Constitution recognize a specific subset of "Cognitive Privacy"
or "Mental Integrity" as an absolute right?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Privacy Activists)
The Plaintiffs relied heavily on the K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
(Right to Privacy) and Selvi v. State of Karnataka (Narcoanalysis)
judgments. They argued that the brain is the final sanctuary of human
dignity. Unlike a fingerprint, an EEG reads internal biological thoughts
and states. Forcing impoverished citizens to surrender their neural data
to eat is a grotesque violation of cognitive liberty and bodily autonomy.
They argued the project fails the proportionality test: the goal
(stopping ration fraud) can be achieved by less intrusive means (standard
biometrics). The risk of a state database containing the neural profiles
of millions of citizens creates an unprecedented architecture for
Orwellian mass surveillance and psychological manipulation.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Kerala)
The State argued that the right to privacy is not absolute and must be
balanced against the State's compelling interest in ensuring scarce
public resources reach the truly destitute (Article 47 - Directive
Principles). They argued that traditional biometrics were failing due to
advanced spoofing techniques, causing massive leakages in the exchequer.
The State presented expert testimony asserting the EEG data collected was
a mere mathematical hash used for matching, and the algorithm was
physically incapable of "reading thoughts" or diagnosing conditions. They
argued the intrusion was minimal, statutory safeguards were in place, and
the socio-economic benefit overwhelmingly justified the technological
upgrade.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in favor of the Privacy Activists.
The Court struck down "The Synapse Project" as unconstitutional, ordering
the immediate destruction of all collected neural data. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling establishing the frontiers of
neuro-rights. The judge strictly applied the Puttaswamy proportionality
test: Legality, Legitimate State Aim, and Proportionality. While saving
public funds is a legitimate aim, the Court ruled the means were
devastatingly disproportionate.

The Court formally recognized "Cognitive Privacy" and "Mental Integrity"
as the highest, most impenetrable tiers of Article 21. The judge reasoned
that neural data is fundamentally different from a fingerprint; it
emanates from the organ of human consciousness. Even if the State
currently only uses it for hashing, the centralized storage of raw
brainwave data creates an irreversible vulnerability. The State cannot
demand access to the biological source of human thought as a toll-gate
for basic survival (food rations). The Court held that forcing citizens
to choose between starvation and surrendering their cognitive privacy is
coercive, unconscionable, and completely destroys the dignity guaranteed
by the Constitution.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the constitutional doctrine of Cognitive Privacy
and Mental Integrity under Article 21. It sets the absolute legal
principle that the mandatory collection of neural or brainwave data by
the State for civilian administrative purposes fails the proportionality
test and constitutes an unconstitutional invasion of the deepest sanctum
of human privacy.

cases.title: Republic Party v. Election Commission of India
cases.facts:
In 2026, the Parliament passed the 107th Constitutional Amendment Act.
This amendment completely overhauled the Delimitation Commission (which
redraws electoral constituency boundaries). The amendment removed human
judges from the commission and mandated that all future electoral
boundaries be drawn autonomously by "Delim-AI," an advanced algorithm
managed by the executive branch. The amendment explicitly ousted the
jurisdiction of all courts, including the Supreme Court, to review or
challenge the boundaries generated by Delim-AI, adding a clause to
Article 329.

The opposition Republic Party filed a writ petition challenging the 107th
Amendment. They provided evidence that Delim-AI's hidden training data
was fundamentally flawed, resulting in "digital gerrymandering" that
systematically diluted the voting power of minority demographics. The
Government argued that the amendment was validly passed with a two-thirds
majority and that algorithms provide purely objective, mathematical
boundaries free from human political bias.
cases.issues:
Does the 107th Constitutional Amendment, which entrusts electoral
delimitation entirely to an executive-controlled AI and ousts judicial
review, violate the Basic Structure Doctrine?

Is the power of Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 a part of the
basic structure that cannot be amended away by Parliament?

Does algorithmic gerrymandering violate the foundational constitutional
principle of free and fair elections and equal representation (Article
14)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Republic Party)
The Plaintiffs anchored their case in the bedrock of Kesavananda Bharati
v. State of Kerala and Minerva Mills v. Union of India. They argued that
Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is not absolute; it cannot
destroy the Constitution's "Basic Structure." They argued that (1) Free
and Fair Elections, (2) Democracy, and (3) Judicial Review are undeniable
pillars of the basic structure. By delegating the architecture of
democracy to an opaque, executive-controlled black-box algorithm and
explicitly stripping the Supreme Court of its power to review the
algorithm's output for constitutional bias, the amendment completely
destroys the separation of powers and guarantees an authoritarian
electoral advantage.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued parliamentary supremacy in legislative matters.
They asserted that Article 329(a) already protects delimitation laws from
judicial interference to prevent the endless stalling of elections. The
107th Amendment merely updated this for the AI era. They argued that
humans gerrymander; mathematics does not. The AI was programmed to
optimize for population parity and geographic contiguity. Subjecting
millions of lines of code to judicial review by judges untrained in
computer science would paralyze the democratic process. They maintained
the amendment was a valid exercise of constituent power to modernize
elections.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of the Republic Party. The
Court struck down the 107th Constitutional Amendment Act as ultra vires
the Constitution and violative of the Basic Structure. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of judicial independence and
democratic integrity. The judge unequivocally reaffirmed that Judicial
Review is a core feature of the Basic Structure. Any constitutional
amendment that attempts to create an absolute "no-go zone" for the
Supreme Court, especially regarding the foundational mechanics of
democracy, is inherently unconstitutional.

The Court scrutinized the deployment of AI in sovereign functions. The
judge ruled that algorithms are not inherently objective; they encode the
biases of their programmers and training data. Handing the power to shape
electoral constituencies to an opaque algorithm controlled entirely by
the executive branch destroys the democratic level playing field. The
Court held that while technology can assist the Delimitation Commission,
the final sovereign authority must rest with human constitutional
functionaries subject to judicial oversight. Stripping the judiciary of
the power to audit algorithmic outputs for Article 14 (Equality)
violations effectively replaces constitutional supremacy with algorithmic
supremacy, which the Court flatly rejected.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case aggressively reasserts the Basic Structure Doctrine (Article
368) in the face of technological delegation. It establishes the absolute
principle that Judicial Review and Free and Fair Elections are
unamendable basic features. Parliament cannot use constitutional
amendments to delegate sovereign democratic functions to opaque
algorithms while ousting the jurisdiction of constitutional courts.

cases.title: The Sabarimala Trust v. Aditi Sharma
cases.facts:
The ancient "Shakti Peeth" temple in the mountains of Uttarakhand
worshipped a unique manifestation of a warrior goddess. For over five
hundred years, the temple possessed a rigid, unbroken tradition: men
between the ages of 15 and 50 (the "warrior age") were strictly
prohibited from entering the inner sanctum. The temple trust claimed this
exclusion was rooted in a foundational scripture stating the goddess was
in a state of eternal, fierce penance and the presence of men of fighting
age disturbed her martial focus.

Aditi Sharma, a prominent constitutional lawyer, filed a PIL challenging
this ban. While acknowledging the irony of women fighting to let men into
a temple, she argued the ban violated Article 14 (Equality) and Article
15 (Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex). The Temple Trust
invoked Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) and Article 26 (Freedom to
manage religious affairs), arguing that the exclusion was an "Essential
Religious Practice" unique to their specific denomination, and the courts
could not dictate theology.
cases.issues:
Does a centuries-old religious tradition banning a specific gender and
age demographic from a public place of worship violate the fundamental
rights to Equality (Article 14) and Non-Discrimination (Article 15)?

Does the exclusion of men of a certain age constitute an "Essential
Religious Practice" protected under Article 25 and Article 26 of the
Constitution?

In the clash between Constitutional Morality (equality) and Religious
Freedom, which principle holds paramount supremacy?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Aditi Sharma)
The Plaintiff relied heavily on the transformative jurisprudence of the
Sabarimala (Indian Young Lawyers Association) judgment. She argued that
Article 25(2)(b) specifically empowers the State to throw open Hindu
religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections.
She argued that discrimination based purely on biological sex and age is
inherently exclusionary and violates "Constitutional Morality." She
asserted that untouchability and exclusionary practices cannot be
shielded under the guise of religious freedom. The deity is public, and
the temple receives state infrastructure support; therefore, it cannot
operate as a private exclusionary club violating the fundamental dignity
of male devotees.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Sabarimala Trust)
The Temple Trust fiercely defended its denominational autonomy under
Article 26. They relied on the Shirur Mutt case, arguing that what
constitutes an "essential religious practice" must be decided with
reference to the doctrines of that specific religion. They argued the ban
was not based on "pollution" or "misandry," but on the specific agamic
(scriptural) celibate, martial nature of this particular deity. They
argued that forcing the temple to admit men destroys the very essence of
the deity's manifestation. Furthermore, they argued that Article 15(1)
applies to the State, and a religious trust exercising its core theology
is not bound by secular notions of equality that obliterate theological
diversity.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court, in a 4-1 majority, ruled in favor of Aditi Sharma. The
Court struck down the temple's rule banning men aged 15-50, declaring it
unconstitutional and ordering the temple open to all genders and ages.
The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound judgment cementing the supremacy of
Constitutional Morality over exclusionary religious dogma. The majority
applied the "Essential Religious Practices" test. The Court found that
while the practice was old, there was insufficient scriptural evidence to
prove that the very survival of the religion depended on the exclusion of
men.

More critically, the Court ruled that Article 25 (Freedom of Religion) is
explicitly subject to "public order, morality, and health," as well as
the other fundamental rights in Part III (including Articles 14 and 15).
The judge declared that in a modern, transformative Constitution,
"morality" means Constitutional Morality-the principles of equality,
liberty, and dignity. Any religious practice, no matter how ancient, that
systematically discriminates against a class of citizens based purely on
biological attributes (sex/age) violates human dignity. The Court held
that religious freedom cannot be weaponized to maintain exclusionary
fortresses in public spaces, affirming that the Constitution emancipates
the individual from the oppressive dictates of orthodox tradition.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case aggressively expands the application of Constitutional Morality
against Exclusionary Religious Practices (Articles 14, 15, 25, 26). It
establishes the legal principle that religious traditions discriminating
on the basis of gender or biological attributes, even if claimed as
essential, are unconstitutional, as the freedom of religion is strictly
subordinate to the fundamental rights of equality and human dignity.

cases.title: State of UP v. The Algorithm Audit Commission
cases.facts:
The State Government implemented a highly advanced AI system, "Merit-AI,"
to conduct the preliminary screening and shortlisting of all candidates
for State Civil Service examinations. Merit-AI evaluated candidates based
on test scores, socioeconomic background, geographic isolation, and
educational history to dynamically allocate "equity points" to
marginalized candidates.

However, a statistical audit by the independent "Algorithm Audit
Commission" revealed a glaring flaw: Merit-AI treated the broad category
of "Scheduled Castes" (SC) as a single, homogenous monolith.
Consequently, 90% of the AI's equity points and subsequent job placements
were captured by one specific, relatively affluent sub-caste within the
SC category, completely starving the most profoundly marginalized,
"invisible" sub-castes of any representation. The State refused to alter
the code, arguing that creating sub-quotas or differential weighting
within the SC category violated the Presidential list under Article 341.
The Commission filed a writ petition demanding the algorithm be rewritten
to ensure sub-classification for true equity.
cases.issues:
Under Article 14 and Article 16(4) of the Constitution, does the State
have the power (or duty) to sub-classify Scheduled Castes to ensure the
equitable distribution of reservation benefits?

Does treating a highly unequal group as a homogenous monolith for the
purpose of affirmative action violate the constitutional mandate of
substantive equality?

Can the State rely on an AI algorithm that structurally perpetuates the
monopolization of welfare benefits by the "creamy layer" of a
marginalized group?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Algorithm Audit Commission)
The Commission relied on the evolving jurisprudence leading up to the
Supreme Court's recent reconsideration of E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of A.P.
They argued that the fundamental goal of Article 16(4) is substantive,
not formal, equality. The SC category is not a homogenous class; it is
riddled with internal hierarchies and varying degrees of historical
trauma. By programming the AI to treat them equally, the State treated
unequals equally-a classic violation of Article 14. The Commission argued
that allowing one dominant sub-caste to siphon 90% of the benefits
defeats the entire purpose of affirmative action, leaving the most
wretchedly deprived citizens completely unrepresented.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of UP)
The State argued a strict, formalist constitutional defense. They relied
on Article 341, arguing that only the President of India has the power to
designate the list of Scheduled Castes. The State argued that any attempt
by a State government (or an algorithm coded by the state) to sub-divide,
prioritize, or create quotas within that Presidential list amounts to
unconstitutionally tinkering with it. They argued the AI was objective
and race-neutral in its execution of the existing law, and addressing
internal inequalities within the SC category requires a constitutional
amendment by Parliament, not judicial or algorithmic intervention.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Algorithm Audit Commission. The
Court directed the State to reprogram Merit-AI to incorporate evidence-
based sub-classification within the SC category to ensure equitable
distribution. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment recognizing the nuances of
systemic deprivation. Overruling rigid past precedents, the
Constitutional Bench held that the power to provide reservations under
Article 16(4) inherently includes the power to ensure those reservations
actually reach the intended beneficiaries.

The Court ruled that the Presidential list under Article 341 is merely a
mechanism for identification, not a mandate for homogenous treatment.
Recognizing the harsh reality that reservations are often monopolized by
the relatively advanced groups within a backward class, the judge stated
that treating highly unequal sub-castes as equals perpetuates historical
injustice. The Court ruled that substantive equality (Article 14) demands
the State to proactively identify and uplift the weakest of the weak.
Therefore, coding an AI to ignore intra-group disparities is a
constitutional failure. The State has the legislative and technological
competence to create sub-classifications to ensure the "trickle-down" of
affirmative action, and must redesign its algorithms to reflect this
constitutional equity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the constitutional validity of Sub-Classification
within Scheduled Castes (Articles 14, 16(4), and 341). It establishes the
legal principle that the State has the power and duty to rationally sub-
classify marginalized groups to ensure that affirmative action benefits
are not monopolized by a dominant sub-group, enforcing the doctrine of
substantive equality in the digital allocation of state resources.

cases.title: Union of India v. EcoDefenders NGO
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Central Government, aiming for rapid energy independence,
approved the "Black Gold Initiative," sanctioning the immediate opening
of 50 new massive open-cast coal mines across ecologically sensitive
dense forest regions. The government bypassed standard environmental
impact assessments using emergency executive powers.

EcoDefenders, a prominent environmental NGO, filed a massive Public
Interest Litigation (PIL) under Article 32 directly in the Supreme Court.
They presented peer-reviewed climate data proving that the carbon
emissions from these specific 50 mines would catastrophically accelerate
India's climate vulnerability, leading to extreme heatwaves and
devastating coastal flooding within a decade. The NGO argued that this
specific government action actively threatened the lives and livelihoods
of millions of coastal and agricultural citizens, violating their
fundamental Right to Life under Article 21.
cases.issues:
Is the "Right to be free from the adverse effects of Climate Change" a
recognized, enforceable fundamental right under Article 21 of the
Constitution?

Can the Supreme Court strike down sovereign macroeconomic and energy
policies on the grounds of future climate catastrophe?

Does the Government's duty to provide immediate energy security and
economic development override the long-term environmental rights of
future generations?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (EcoDefenders NGO)
EcoDefenders relied heavily on the Supreme Court's progressive expansion
of Article 21 (e.g., M.C. Mehta cases and the recent M.K. Ranjitsinh
judgment recognizing climate rights). They argued that the right to a
clean environment is meaningless if the State actively executes policies
guaranteeing climate collapse. They asserted that extreme heatwaves and
flooding are direct threats to the Right to Life, Health, and Livelihood.
Furthermore, they invoked Article 14 (Equality) and the Doctrine of
Intergenerational Equity, arguing that the government cannot irrevocably
destroy the ecological survival of future generations for short-term
political and economic gains today.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued for the absolute separation of powers. They
contended that energy policy, macroeconomic development, and poverty
alleviation are sovereign executive functions. India requires cheap,
immediate energy to lift hundreds of millions out of poverty, which is
also a mandate under Article 21. The State argued that climate change is
a global, cumulative phenomenon, and the Court cannot directly trace
future heatwaves specifically to these 50 mines. They asserted that
allowing courts to veto national infrastructure projects based on
predictive climate models would paralyze the government and violate the
basic structure by transferring executive policy-making to unelected
judges.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of EcoDefenders NGO. The Court issued a
writ of Mandamus, staying the "Black Gold Initiative" and ordering the
government to establish an independent, expert climate-impact committee
before any mining could commence. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a historic, globally significant environmental
judgment. The judge unequivocally articulated that the "Right to be free
from the adverse impacts of climate change" is a distinct, fundamental
right explicitly embedded within Article 21 and Article 14 of the
Constitution.

The Court acknowledged the separation of powers but ruled that the
judiciary cannot remain a mute spectator when executive action threatens
the existential survival of the populace. While energy security is vital,
the Court applied the doctrine of Sustainable Development and the
Precautionary Principle. The judge reasoned that the devastating impacts
of climate change-droughts, floods, and lethal heat-disproportionately
violate the fundamental rights of the poorest and most marginalized
citizens.

The Court held that the government cannot bypass mandatory environmental
scrutiny under the guise of an "emergency." The right to life includes
the right to a stable climate system capable of sustaining human
habitation. Therefore, massive, carbon-intensive state projects must
undergo rigorous, climate-specific impact assessments to balance
immediate developmental needs against the constitutional rights of
present and future generations.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case formally enshrines the Right against Adverse Climate Change as
a Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Article 14. It establishes the
legal principle that sovereign energy and development policies are
subject to judicial review if they pose an existential, scientifically
demonstrable threat to the climate stability necessary to sustain human
life, enforcing the doctrine of intergenerational equity.

cases.title: Republic of India v. MegaCorp Logistics
cases.facts:
MegaCorp Logistics operated a massive fleet of heavy diesel transport
trucks moving essential industrial goods between Maharashtra and Gujarat.
In 2025, the State of Maharashtra, facing a catastrophic air quality
crisis in its border districts, enacted the "Clean Air Transport Act."
This state legislation unilaterally banned the entry of all commercial
diesel trucks older than 5 years from crossing the border into
Maharashtra from any other state, while allowing older diesel trucks
already registered within Maharashtra a 2-year grace period to upgrade.

MegaCorp Logistics filed a writ petition, arguing this state law crippled
their supply chain and blatantly violated Article 301 of the
Constitution, which guarantees that trade, commerce, and intercourse
throughout the territory of India shall be free. The State of Maharashtra
argued the ban was a valid public health measure protected under Article
304(b), regulating health and environment.
cases.issues:
Does a state law banning the entry of specific inter-state commercial
vehicles for environmental reasons violate the freedom of trade and
commerce under Article 301 of the Constitution?

Can a state government invoke Article 304(b) (reasonable restrictions in
the public interest) if the law seemingly discriminates in favor of
intra-state vehicles over inter-state vehicles?

How does the Constitution balance the economic unity of India against the
sovereign right of a State to combat a localized ecological and public
health emergency?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MegaCorp Logistics)
MegaCorp anchored its argument in Article 301 and Article 304(a). They
argued that the fundamental purpose of Part XIII of the Constitution is
to maintain the economic unity of India as a single, unfragmented market.
By abruptly blocking thousands of inter-state trucks, Maharashtra
severely restricted the free flow of commerce. Furthermore, they pointed
out the blatant discrimination: older trucks from Gujarat were banned
instantly, while older trucks owned by Maharashtra residents were given a
2-year grace period. This violates the anti-discrimination mandate of
Article 304(a), proving the law was an unconstitutional protectionist
measure disguised as environmental policy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Maharashtra)
The State argued the defense of paramount public health under Article
304(b). They presented irrefutable medical data showing skyrocketing
respiratory mortality rates in the border districts caused primarily by
heavy interstate diesel traffic. They argued that Article 301 is not
absolute; it is subject to "reasonable restrictions" in the public
interest. The State contended that the 2-year grace period for local
trucks was an administrative necessity to prevent the total collapse of
local logistics, not malicious discrimination. They asserted that the
right to life and clean air (Article 21) of their citizens must override
the commercial profits of an interstate logistics conglomerate.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled partially in favor of MegaCorp Logistics. The
Court upheld the State's right to ban older polluting vehicles but struck
down the discriminatory 2-year grace period granted exclusively to intra-
state vehicles, ordering the ban to be applied uniformly. The Plaintiff
partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a precise judgment balancing federal economic unity
with state police powers. The judge affirmed that under Article 301, the
economic borders of the nation must remain porous. However, the Court
validated Maharashtra's invocation of Article 304(b). Combating a severe,
statistically proven public health crisis (air pollution) is an
overwhelmingly valid "public interest" that justifies placing reasonable
restrictions on the freedom of trade. The State has the constitutional
power to regulate and ban polluting vehicles to protect Article 21.

However, the Court came down heavily on the discriminatory
implementation. Applying Article 304(a), the judge ruled that a State
cannot levy restrictions on imported goods or services that it does not
equally apply to its own. The 2-year grace period for local trucks
destroyed the environmental defense; if old diesel trucks are lethal,
they are lethal regardless of which state they are registered in. The
Court held that environmental laws cannot be used as a cloak for economic
protectionism. The State must enforce the environmental standard equally,
maintaining the constitutional requirement of a non-discriminatory
national market.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case clarifies the boundaries of Freedom of Trade and Commerce
(Article 301) vs. State Regulatory Power (Article 304). It establishes
the legal principle that while States can impose reasonable restrictions
on inter-state commerce for severe environmental or public health
reasons, such restrictions are unconstitutional if they discriminate in
favor of intra-state commerce, enforcing the doctrine of a unified, non-
protectionist national economy.

cases.title: Chief Minister of Vindhya v. The Governor of Vindhya
cases.facts:
The State of Vindhya was governed by a coalition government led by the
regional "Vindhya Vikas Party" (VVP), fiercely opposed to the ruling
party at the Center. In 2026, a series of violent, localized riots broke
out in three districts of Vindhya over a controversial land-acquisition
policy. The Chief Minister deployed the state police, imposed curfews,
and controlled the riots within four days.

However, the Governor of Vindhya (appointed by the Central Government)
sent a secret, highly critical report to the President. The Governor
alleged that the Chief Minister was complicit in the riots and that the
state police had entirely lost control, declaring a "complete breakdown
of constitutional machinery." Based solely on this report, the Central
Government immediately invoked Article 356, dismissed the democratically
elected State Government, and imposed President's Rule. The ousted Chief
Minister filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court, challenging the
imposition of Article 356 as a mala fide, unconstitutional assassination
of federalism.
cases.issues:
Is the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 subject to
judicial review, and can the Supreme Court scrutinize the material facts
(the Governor's report) upon which the President's satisfaction was
based?

Does a localized law-and-order disturbance, which the state government
successfully controlled, constitute a "failure of constitutional
machinery" justifying the dismissal of an elected government?

How does the Constitution safeguard the federal structure against the
partisan, political misuse of emergency powers by the Central Government?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Chief Minister of Vindhya)
The Chief Minister relied entirely on the landmark Constitutional Bench
judgment in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India. He argued that federalism is a
basic feature of the Constitution, and state governments are not mere
vassals of the Center. He asserted that the imposition of Article 356 was
politically motivated and legally void. A four-day, localized riot is a
"law and order" problem, not a complete breakdown of the Constitution.
The Chief Minister provided data proving the police effectively restored
peace. He argued the Governor's report was a fabricated, partisan
document designed to subvert democracy and install the Center's rule
through the backdoor, demanding the immediate restoration of his
government.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Central Government argued that the satisfaction of the President
under Article 356 is highly subjective and immune from deep judicial
scrutiny. They contended that the Governor is the eyes and ears of the
President, and the Court cannot sit as an appellate body over the
Governor's assessment of state security. They argued that the riots were
organized and state-sponsored, presenting a grave threat to national
internal security. The Center asserted that Article 356 is a necessary
constitutional safety valve to prevent rogue state governments from
plunging their states into anarchy, and the executive's decision must be
respected.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Chief Minister of Vindhya. The
Court struck down the Presidential Proclamation, declared the imposition
of Article 356 unconstitutional, and ordered the immediate restoration of
the VVP State Government. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a crushing reaffirmation of federalism and the S.R.
Bommai principles. The judge ruled that the power under Article 356 is a
drastic, exceptional power, not an everyday political tool. The Court
categorically affirmed that the Presidential Proclamation is fully
subject to judicial review. While the Court will not judge the adequacy
of the material, it will heavily scrutinize whether the material was
relevant or tainted by mala fides.

The Court examined the Governor's report and found it shockingly
deficient. The judge drew a sharp constitutional distinction between a
"law and order situation" (which states handle daily) and a "breakdown of
constitutional machinery" (where the state is fundamentally paralyzed and
cannot govern). Controlling a riot in four days proves the state
machinery was functioning, not failing. The Court held that utilizing
Article 356 to dismiss a majority government over manageable local unrest
is a blatant, unconstitutional assault on the federal structure and
democratic mandate. The Governor's report was deemed legally perverse and
politically motivated, rendering the President's satisfaction invalid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case vigorously enforces the limits on President's Rule (Article
356) and protects the Federal Structure of the Constitution. It re-
establishes the absolute legal principle that Article 356 is subject to
strict judicial review; localized law-and-order problems do not
constitute a breakdown of constitutional machinery, and the Center cannot
use emergency powers for partisan dismissal of democratically elected
State governments.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Cryptography Alliance (Article 19(1)(a) - Free Speech and End-to-End Encryption)
cases.facts:
In 2025, to combat the rapid spread of terrorist recruitment and child
exploitation material, the Central Government passed the "Digital
Intermediary Security Rules." Clause 4 of these rules mandated that all
messaging applications operating in India (e.g., WhatsApp, Signal) must
implement "Traceability." This required the platforms to fundamentally
break their End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) architecture so that the
government could trace the "first originator" of any flagged message.

The Cryptography Alliance, a coalition of privacy advocates and
journalists, filed a writ petition challenging the rules. They argued
that breaking E2EE destroys the fundamental Right to Privacy (Article 21)
and severely chills the Freedom of Speech and Expression (Article
19(1)(a)), as citizens, journalists, and whistleblowers can no longer
communicate securely. The Government argued that anonymity is not a
fundamental right, and absolute encryption creates a dark, ungovernable
space for criminals, threatening national security (Article 19(2)).
cases.issues:
Does the fundamental Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression (Article
19(1)(a)) and the Right to Privacy (Article 21) implicitly include the
right to communicate securely and anonymously via End-to-End Encryption?

Does mandating "Traceability," which effectively breaks E2EE for all
users, satisfy the doctrine of proportionality when combating national
security threats?

Can the State mandate the systemic weakening of digital infrastructure,
rendering all citizens vulnerable to surveillance, to catch specific
criminals?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Cryptography Alliance)
The Alliance anchored their case in the K.S. Puttaswamy (Privacy) and
Anuradha Bhasin (Internet rights) judgments. They argued that privacy is
the bedrock of free speech; without the assurance of confidential
communication, journalists cannot protect sources, and citizens will
self-censor for fear of state surveillance (the "Chilling Effect"). They
argued from a technical standpoint: "Traceability" is a myth; to trace
one message, platforms must weaken the encryption for every single user,
creating a permanent backdoor. They argued this fails the proportionality
test miserably-it is the equivalent of installing a CCTV camera in every
citizen's bedroom to catch a few thieves, grossly violating Article 21.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that fundamental rights are not absolute. Under
Article 19(2), the State has a paramount duty to protect the sovereignty,
integrity, and security of India. They presented evidence that terrorists
coordinate attacks entirely via encrypted apps, operating completely
beyond the reach of law enforcement. The State argued they are not asking
to read every message, only to trace the specific originators of illegal,
lethal content. They contended that a private corporation's mathematical
protocol (Encryption) cannot be allowed to legally override the sovereign
investigative powers of the State and the safety of its citizens.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of The Cryptography Alliance. The Court
struck down Clause 4 (Traceability mandate) of the Digital Intermediary
Security Rules as unconstitutional, protecting the integrity of End-to-
End Encryption. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly technical, landmark judgment protecting
digital privacy. The judge applied the strict three-fold proportionality
test from Puttaswamy. While stopping terrorism is an undeniably
legitimate state aim, the Court ruled that breaking E2EE is a
devastatingly disproportionate means to achieve it.

The Court accepted expert cryptographic testimony confirming that it is
mathematically impossible to build a "backdoor" only for the "good guys."
Mandating traceability requires structurally compromising the encryption
architecture for all 500 million law-abiding citizens, leaving them
vulnerable to state overreach, corporate data breaches, and hostile
foreign hackers. The Court ruled that the Right to Privacy (Article 21)
and Free Speech (Article 19(1)(a)) are inextricably linked; the ability
to communicate without the chilling fear of absolute state surveillance
is essential to democracy. The State cannot burn down the entire forest
of digital privacy to catch a few hidden criminals. The government must
rely on traditional, targeted intelligence gathering rather than
mandating the systemic destruction of secure communications.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a monumental global precedent regarding Digital Privacy,
Free Speech, and Encryption (Articles 19(1)(a) & 21). It establishes the
legal principle that the State cannot mandate "Traceability" or systemic
backdoors that break End-to-End Encryption, as compromising the secure
digital infrastructure of all citizens to target specific criminals is
grossly disproportionate and unconstitutional.

cases.title: State of Haryana v. Apex Developers
cases.facts:
To rapidly accelerate urban development, the State Legislature of Haryana
passed the "Mega-City Development Act, 2025." Section 12 of this Act
granted the newly formed "State Urban Authority" (an unelected executive
body) the absolute, unguided power to acquire any private agricultural
land, rezone it for commercial use, and define the compensation rates "as
the Authority may deem fit and proper for the acceleration of the
economy." The Act contained no guidelines, limits, or principles
detailing how this power should be exercised.

Apex Developers, whose 100-acre agricultural land was seized by the
Authority at a fraction of the market rate to build a luxury mall, filed
a writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of Section 12.
They argued it was a blatant violation of Article 14 (Equality) and the
doctrine of Excessive Delegation. The State argued that modern economic
legislation requires administrative flexibility, and the legislature
validly delegated execution to experts.
cases.issues:
Does granting absolute, unguided, and uncanalized discretionary power to
an executive authority violate the fundamental right to Equality (Article
14)?

Did the State Legislature commit an "Unconstitutional Delegation of
Legislative Power" by failing to lay down the underlying policy or
guidelines in the Act?

Where is the boundary between permissible administrative delegation and
the unconstitutional abdication of legislative duty?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Developers)
The Plaintiff relied heavily on the landmark judgments in In re Delhi
Laws Act and A.N. Parasuraman v. State of Haryana. They argued that while
the legislature can delegate the "execution" of a law, it cannot delegate
its essential legislative function-which is to lay down the policy, the
principles, and the boundaries of the law. Section 12 provided absolutely
no guidelines on which land to acquire or how to calculate compensation.
This gave the executive body dictatorial, arbitrary power to pick and
choose targets, favoring political allies and destroying rivals. Because
unguided discretionary power is the very antithesis of the Rule of Law,
it inherently violates Article 14 (Equality before Law).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Haryana)
The State argued the necessity of administrative pragmatism. The
legislature cannot foresee every dynamic economic scenario required to
build a mega-city. Therefore, broad delegation to an expert urban body is
necessary. They argued that the preamble of the Act ("acceleration of the
economy") provided sufficient implicit guidance. Furthermore, they argued
that if the Authority acts arbitrarily in a specific instance, that
specific administrative order can be challenged, but the entire enabling
statute should not be struck down as unconstitutional simply because the
power might be abused.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled decisively in favor of Apex Developers. The Court
struck down Section 12 of the Mega-City Development Act, 2025, as
unconstitutional, declaring it an invalid delegation of legislative power
and violative of Article 14. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic defense of the Separation of Powers and the
Rule of Law. The judge ruled that the legislature cannot abdicate its
constitutional duty. The essential legislative function consists of
determining the legislative policy and formulating it as a binding rule
of conduct.

The Court scrutinized Section 12 and found a total legislative vacuum.
The Act gave the executive a blank check to seize land and set prices
without any statutory formula, caps, or appeals process. The judge firmly
ruled that Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness in State action.
Conferring naked, uncanalized, and unguided discretionary power upon any
executive authority is inherently arbitrary and discriminatory, as it
allows the executive to act as a sovereign law unto itself. The
preamble's vague goal of "economic acceleration" does not constitute a
legal guideline. Because the legislature failed to establish the
boundaries of the power, the delegation was excessive, unconstitutional,
and void ab initio.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Doctrine of Excessive Delegation and
Article 14 (Equality). It establishes the absolute legal principle that a
legislature cannot delegate absolute, unguided, and uncanalized
discretionary power to the executive branch. A statute must lay down
clear policies and guidelines; failing to do so violates the Rule of Law
and the protection against arbitrary state action.

cases.title: The Street Vendors Collective v. State of Maharashtra (Article 19(1)(g) vs. Urban Planning)
cases.facts:
In 2025, the State of Maharashtra initiated the "Smart Mumbai Vision," an
aggressive urban overhaul project. To beautify commercial districts and
ease traffic congestion, the Municipal Corporation issued a blanket
notification permanently banning all unlicensed and licensed street
vendors from operating within a 2-kilometer radius of any major transit
hub or commercial high street. Over 50,000 vendors, many of whom had
operated in these exact zones for generations, were abruptly evicted,
resulting in massive loss of livelihood. The Street Vendors Collective
filed a writ petition under Article 32, challenging the notification as a
draconian violation of their fundamental right to carry on any
occupation, trade, or business under Article 19(1)(g) and their Right to
Livelihood under Article 21.
cases.issues:
Does a blanket municipal ban on street vending in prime urban zones
violate the fundamental right to trade and profession under Article
19(1)(g)?

Does the State's restriction satisfy the test of "reasonable
restrictions" in the "interest of the general public" under Article
19(6)?

How does the Court balance the Right to Livelihood (Article 21) of
informal workers against the collective public right to unhindered urban
mobility and clean city infrastructure?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Street Vendors Collective)
The Plaintiffs relied on the landmark judgments of Sodan Singh v. New
Delhi Municipal Committee and the Street Vendors (Protection of
Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014. They argued that
street vending is not a nuisance; it is a constitutionally protected
trade and a vital part of the urban micro-economy. A blanket 2-kilometer
ban effectively outlaws vending in all profitable areas of the city,
rendering the right under Article 19(1)(g) illusory. Furthermore,
destroying their sole source of income violates the Right to Livelihood
embedded in Article 21. They argued that "regulation" under Article 19(6)
means organizing and creating dedicated vending zones, not absolute
prohibition and eviction without rehabilitation.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Maharashtra)
The State argued that the right under Article 19(1)(g) is not absolute.
Under Article 19(6), the State has the sovereign power to impose
reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public. Pavements
and transit hubs are public properties dedicated to the smooth transit of
citizens, not private commercial exploitation. The State presented data
showing that unchecked street vending caused severe traffic bottlenecks,
delayed emergency vehicles, and created massive sanitation hazards. They
argued that the public's collective right to safe, clean, and efficient
urban infrastructure heavily outweighs the individual commercial
interests of informal vendors.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Street Vendors Collective. The
blanket ban was struck down as unconstitutional, and the Municipal
Corporation was ordered to implement the Street Vendors Act, 2014, by
conducting proper surveys and establishing designated vending zones
before any evictions. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a powerful defense of the informal economy. The
judge ruled that the Constitution does not prioritize the aesthetics of a
"Smart City" over the survival of its poorest citizens. The Court
affirmed that the right to hawk on streets is a fundamental right under
Article 19(1)(g), subject only to reasonable restrictions.

Applying the doctrine of proportionality, the Court ruled that a blanket
ban is the antithesis of "regulation." While the State has a legitimate
interest in traffic management, completely extinguishing the livelihood
of 50,000 citizens is a grossly disproportionate measure. The State
cannot solve urban planning failures by simply erasing the poor. The
Court held that the Street Vendors Act of 2014 mandates a participatory
approach-town vending committees must identify specific zones and issue
certificates. Until the State fulfills its statutory duty to provide
alternative, viable vending zones, it cannot arbitrarily wield Article
19(6) to evict vendors into destitution, as doing so constitutes a direct
violation of their Right to Life (Article 21).
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Right to Livelihood and Trade (Articles
19(1)(g) & 21). It establishes the legal principle that a blanket ban on
street vending is unconstitutional as an unreasonable restriction under
Article 19(6). The State must balance urban planning with economic
survival by implementing statutory regulations (vending zones) rather
than utilizing arbitrary, absolute evictions.

cases.title: Union of India v. Foundation for Digital Equity
cases.facts:
Following a severe, prolonged resurgence of an airborne pandemic in 2026,
the Central Government mandated the absolute closure of all physical
schools indefinitely. The Ministry of Education shifted the entire
national curriculum to an exclusive online portal. However, over 40% of
children in rural and economically weaker sections lacked access to high-
speed internet or capable digital devices. The Foundation for Digital
Equity filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) under Article 32. They
argued that by mandating exclusive digital education without providing
the necessary digital infrastructure to marginalized children, the State
was effectively denying millions their fundamental Right to Free and
Compulsory Education under Article 21A.
cases.issues:
In a mandatory digital learning environment, does the fundamental Right
to Education (Article 21A) implicitly include the right to access digital
infrastructure (devices and internet)?

Can the State claim financial impossibility or lack of resources as a
valid defense for failing to deliver fundamental rights?

Does the systemic exclusion of rural students from the digital curriculum
violate the guarantee of Equality before Law under Article 14?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Foundation for Digital Equity)
The Plaintiffs argued a purposive interpretation of Article 21A. The
right to education is meaningless if the medium of education is locked
behind a financial and geographical wall. By migrating the entire state
apparatus to the internet without bridging the digital divide, the
government created an unconstitutional, two-tiered education system: one
for the digital haves, and a void for the have-nots. This constitutes
systemic discrimination under Article 14. They argued the State holds an
absolute, non-derogable positive obligation to provide the necessary
tools (tablets, subsidized data) to ensure the fundamental right is
actively realized, not merely theoretically available.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Article 21A mandates the provision of free
education, which they fulfilled by providing the digital portal and
broadcasting lessons on state television. They argued that providing free
laptops and high-speed internet to 100 million children is an impossible
fiscal burden that would bankrupt the national exchequer. The State
contended that the Constitution does not mandate the government to
provide the instruments of learning (like transport to a physical school
or a digital device for an online one), only the educational content
itself.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Foundation for Digital Equity.
The Court issued a writ of mandamus directing the Central and State
governments to immediately allocate funds to provision digital devices
and subsidized internet access to students from economically weaker
sections. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment recognizing internet access as an
indispensable facet of modern education. The judge rejected the State's
narrow interpretation of Article 21A. Education is not merely the
uploading of content to a server; it is the actual, effective
transmission of knowledge to the child. If the State mandates a digital
ecosystem, the digital medium becomes the "school."

The Court ruled that denying access to the medium is functionally
identical to locking the school gates. Under Article 14, the State cannot
ignore structural inequalities. Furthermore, the Court dismissed the
"financial impossibility" defense. The judge ruled that fundamental
rights (Part III) are not contingent upon budgetary convenience. The
State cannot abdicate its constitutional duty to children by citing
costs. The Court ordered that emergency funds must be diverted to bridge
the digital divide, declaring that in the 21st century, the Right to
Education under Article 21A is inextricably bound to digital inclusion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case expands the horizon of the Right to Free and Compulsory
Education (Article 21A). It establishes the constitutional principle that
when education is migrated to a digital platform, the State has a
positive, non-derogable obligation to provide the necessary digital
infrastructure (internet/devices) to marginalized students, and financial
constraints cannot excuse the violation of this fundamental right.

cases.title: Sharma v. GlobalTech Industries
cases.facts:
GlobalTech Industries, India's largest private IT conglomerate,
implemented a strict internal HR policy. The policy explicitly stated:
"To maintain a traditional corporate culture, the company shall not hire,
promote, or retain individuals identifying as LGBTQ+." Mr. Sharma, a
brilliant software engineer, was abruptly terminated after his same-sex
marriage was publicized on social media. Because GlobalTech is a purely
private entity, Sharma could not directly invoke Article 15 (which
generally prohibits the State from discrimination). Instead, Sharma filed
a writ petition against the Union of India, demanding the Court issue a
writ of Mandamus compelling the State to enact legislation banning
horizontal discrimination (discrimination between private
citizens/corporations) based on sexual orientation, arguing the State's
failure to protect him violated his rights under Articles 14 and 21.
cases.issues:
Do Fundamental Rights, specifically the prohibition of discrimination
(Article 15) and equality (Article 14), apply "horizontally" against
private corporations, or only "vertically" against the State?

Does the State have a positive constitutional obligation under Article 21
to enact laws protecting vulnerable minorities from systemic
discrimination in the private sector?

Can a private corporation enforce discriminatory employment policies
under the guise of freedom of trade and association?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Sharma)
Sharma anchored his case in the transformative jurisprudence of Navtej
Singh Johar (decriminalization of homosexuality) and K.S. Puttaswamy
(Privacy and Dignity). He argued that the Constitution guarantees dignity
and equality to all citizens. In a capitalist economy where the private
sector provides the vast majority of livelihoods, restricting anti-
discrimination laws only to government jobs renders the constitutional
guarantee of equality functionally meaningless. He argued the State has a
positive duty under Article 21 to protect his livelihood and dignity from
private tyranny. He urged the Court to recognize "Horizontal Application"
of fundamental rights, forcing private giants to adhere to constitutional
morality.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (GlobalTech & Union of India)
GlobalTech argued that Part III of the Constitution (Fundamental Rights)
is a social contract between the Citizen and the State (Article 12).
Private companies are not the State. Imposing constitutional equality
mandates on private businesses would destroy the freedom to contract, the
right to association, and the right to carry on a business (Article
19(1)(g)). The Union of India argued that enacting anti-discrimination
legislation is purely a legislative function. The Court cannot issue a
writ of mandamus compelling Parliament to pass a specific law, as that
violates the Separation of Powers.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled partially in favor of Mr. Sharma. While the Court
refused to directly issue a writ of mandamus compelling Parliament to
legislate, it utilized its powers under Article 142 to issue binding,
interim anti-discrimination guidelines applicable to major private sector
employers until formal legislation is enacted. The Plaintiff prevailed in
equity.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a watershed judgment on the horizontal application of
rights. The judge acknowledged the traditional "vertical" nature of Part
III but declared that Constitutional Morality cannot be quarantined to
the public sector.

The Court heavily emphasized the Navtej Singh Johar ruling, stating that
identity and sexual orientation are inextricable from human dignity
(Article 21). When a private entity achieves massive economic dominance,
systematic discrimination by such entities effectively exiles citizens
from the economy, choking their Right to Life. The Court ruled that while
it cannot force Parliament to pass a law, the State's passive silence in
the face of blatant, systemic corporate discrimination violates its
positive obligation to protect citizens' dignity. To fill this
legislative vacuum, the Court issued interim guidelines, holding that
large private corporations possess a "societal duty" to adhere to basic
constitutional non-discrimination metrics, thereby preventing the private
sector from becoming a sanctuary for bigotry.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case bridges the gap toward the Horizontal Application of
Fundamental Rights (Articles 14, 15, & 21). It establishes that the Right
to Life and Dignity compels protection against systemic discrimination
even within the private sector, and empowers constitutional courts to
issue interim guidelines checking private corporate discrimination when a
legislative vacuum actively harms vulnerable minorities.

cases.title: State of UP v. Azad
cases.facts:
Azad, a prominent civil rights activist, had been organizing peaceful
protests against a controversial state land-acquisition policy. Fearing
the protests would embarrass the government during an upcoming
international investment summit, the District Magistrate, acting under
the National Security Act (NSA), issued a preventive detention order.
Azad was detained without trial for three months.

The grounds of detention supplied to Azad stated only: "Your activities
are prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and the security of
the State." He was denied access to specific evidence or witness
statements against him, claiming "state privilege." Azad filed a writ of
Habeas Corpus under Article 32. He argued the detention was mala fide,
lacked objective satisfaction, and violated the strict procedural
safeguards of Article 22(5) by failing to communicate the actual grounds
of detention, rendering his constitutional right to make a representation
impossible.
cases.issues:
Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, what constitutes a legally
sufficient "communication of the grounds of detention" to a detenu?

Can the executive use vague, boilerplate language (e.g., "threat to
public order") to justify preventive detention without disclosing
specific factual incidents?

What is the scope of judicial review over the "subjective satisfaction"
of the detaining authority under the National Security Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Azad)
Azad argued that preventive detention is a draconian exception to
personal liberty and must be subjected to the strictest judicial
scrutiny. He relied on Khudiram Das v. State of West Bengal, arguing that
the constitutional right under Article 22(5) has two prongs: the right to
be informed of the grounds, and the right to make an effective
representation against the order. Azad argued that boilerplate, copy-
pasted grounds without specific dates, times, or acts are "vague and
illusory." A person cannot defend themselves against abstract
accusations. Furthermore, he argued the detention was a mala fide abuse
of power designed to stifle legitimate democratic dissent, not to prevent
actual threats to state security.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of UP)
The State defended the detention on the grounds of executive necessity.
They argued that preventive detention relies on the "subjective
satisfaction" of the detaining authority regarding future threats. The
Court cannot sit as an appellate body to review the sufficiency of the
evidence. The State invoked Article 22(6), arguing they have the
sovereign right to withhold facts whose disclosure they consider to be
"against the public interest." They maintained that intelligence reports
indicated Azad was planning violent sabotage, and preemptive action was
necessary.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of Azad. The Court issued a
writ of Habeas Corpus, quashed the detention order, and ordered his
immediate release. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of personal liberty against
executive tyranny. The judge ruled that the power of preventive
detention is repugnant to democratic ideals and can only be tolerated if
the executive flawlessly adheres to every constitutional safeguard.

The Court heavily scrutinized the "grounds of detention." The judge ruled
that "grounds" do not merely mean the statutory conclusions (e.g.,
"threat to public order"); they must include the basic facts and material
particulars upon which that conclusion was formed. Providing vague,
sweeping generalizations completely destroys the detenu's fundamental
right to make an effective representation under Article 22(5). The Court
further held that the State cannot use the "public interest" privilege of
Article 22(6) as a blanket shield to hide a lack of evidence. The Court
found the District Magistrate's "subjective satisfaction" was perverse
and legally unsupportable, as peaceful protests do not constitute a
threat to national security. The detention was deemed a mala fide attempt
to bypass the criminal justice system.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the constitutional safeguards of Preventive
Detention (Article 22(5)). It establishes the absolute legal principle
that the communication of grounds must include specific factual
particulars, not vague statutory boilerplate. Failure to provide these
facts destroys the detenu's right to representation and renders the
detention order inherently unconstitutional and void.

cases.title: Mera Lawyer v. Bar Council of India (Article 19(1)(g) vs. Monopoly of the Legal Profession)
cases.facts:
"Mera Lawyer," incorporated as LexImperia Pvt. Ltd., is a revolutionary
legal-tech platform. It utilizes an advanced AI model to provide citizens
with highly accurate, initial legal drafting, contract analysis, and
predictive case outcomes based on Indian jurisprudence. The platform
democratized legal access for thousands of citizens who could not afford
traditional lawyers.

Viewing this as an existential threat, the Bar Council of India (BCI)
passed a sweeping resolution. Relying on the Advocates Act, 1961, the BCI
declared that providing legal analysis or drafting via AI constitutes the
"unauthorized practice of law." They ordered internet service providers
to block the "Mera Lawyer" platform and threatened disciplinary action
against any registered advocate associated with the company. Aryan, the
founder, filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court, challenging the
BCI's resolution as an unconstitutional restriction on his freedom of
trade and profession (Article 19(1)(g)) and a violation of the public's
right to access justice.
cases.issues:
Does the provision of AI-generated legal analysis and drafting by a
corporate entity constitute the "practice of law" reserved exclusively
for enrolled advocates under the Advocates Act, 1961?

Does a blanket ban on AI legal-tech platforms by the Bar Council violate
the platform developers' fundamental right to carry on any trade or
business under Article 19(1)(g)?

How does the Constitution balance the statutory monopoly of the legal
profession against technological innovation and the public's right to
affordable legal information?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mera Lawyer / LexImperia)
Mera Lawyer argued that the BCI was acting as an illegal, protectionist
cartel. They argued that their AI does not "represent" clients in court,
nor does it establish an attorney-client fiduciary relationship. It
operates as a highly advanced search engine and document generator-an
informational tool. They invoked Article 19(1)(g), arguing that creating
and selling software is a constitutionally protected trade. Banning a
technology simply because it is more efficient and cheaper than human
lawyers is not a "reasonable restriction" in the public interest (Article
19(6)); it is anti-competitive monopolization that actively harms
impoverished citizens seeking basic legal literacy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Bar Council of India)
The BCI fiercely defended its statutory monopoly. They argued that the
"practice of law" includes drafting, advising, and interpreting statutes,
all of which the AI performs. Under the Advocates Act, only human beings
enrolled with the Bar, bound by strict ethical codes, confidentiality,
and fiduciary duties, can practice law. They argued that an AI cannot be
held accountable for malpractice or bad advice. Allowing corporations to
practice law through algorithms destroys the accountability of the
justice system. The restriction, they argued, is a perfectly reasonable
safeguard to protect the public from unregulated, robotic legal advice.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled predominantly in favor of Mera Lawyer. The Court
struck down the BCI's blanket ban on the platform but instituted
regulatory guidelines requiring the AI to display clear disclaimers that
its outputs do not constitute formal legal counsel. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment harmonizing the legal profession
with the AI revolution. The judge strictly interpreted the Advocates Act.
The Court ruled that the "practice of law" possessing a statutory
monopoly is specifically the act of representing a client before a
judicial body and providing bespoke, fiduciary legal counsel.

The Court distinguished this from the provision of legal information and
automated drafting. The judge ruled that Mera Lawyer functions as a
highly sophisticated legal tool, not a human advocate. Restricting the
development of beneficial technology solely to protect the financial
monopoly of lawyers violates Article 19(1)(g). The Court reasoned that
access to justice is a constitutional imperative. Banning a tool that
makes legal frameworks accessible to the masses is antithetical to the
public interest. However, acknowledging the BCI's valid concerns
regarding accountability, the Court mandated that such platforms cannot
represent users in court and must prominently display warnings that their
AI-generated drafts require final review by a human advocate, striking a
balance between innovation and public safety.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a monumental precedent for Legal Tech and Freedom of Trade
(Article 19(1)(g)). It establishes the legal principle that the provision
of AI-driven legal information, automated drafting, and predictive
analysis does NOT constitute the unauthorized "practice of law," and the
Bar Council cannot constitutionally ban such platforms, terminating the
absolute monopoly over basic legal literacy.

cases.title: Singh v. Union of India (Article 16(4A) and Quantifiable Data for Reservation in Promotions)
cases.facts:
The Central Government passed an executive order implementing massive,
accelerated reservations in promotions for Scheduled Castes (SC) and
Scheduled Tribes (ST) across all senior administrative tiers of the civil
services. Several general category civil servants, including Mr. Singh,
who were superseded by junior officers, filed a writ petition in the
Supreme Court.

They challenged the order, arguing that the Government failed to collect
any contemporary, objective "quantifiable data" demonstrating that SCs
and STs were inadequately represented in those specific senior cadres, as
mandated by the Supreme Court's constitutional bench in M. Nagaraj v.
Union of India and Jarnail Singh. The Government argued that historical
disadvantage is self-evident, and demanding microscopic quantifiable data
for every department paralyzes the constitutional mandate of Article
16(4A).
cases.issues:
Under Article 16(4A) of the Constitution, is the collection of
"quantifiable data" showing inadequacy of representation a mandatory
condition precedent before the State can implement reservations in
promotions?

Can the State rely on the general, historical backwardness of SCs and
STs, or must the data be specific to the cadre or grade where the
promotion is being applied?

How does the Court balance the mandate of administrative efficiency
(Article 335) with the goal of substantive social justice in senior
government roles?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Singh - General Category)
Mr. Singh anchored his case strictly in the Nagaraj and Jarnail Singh
jurisprudence. He argued that Article 16(4A) is an enabling provision,
not a mandatory rule. Before exercising this discretionary power, the
State is constitutionally bound to satisfy three criteria: backwardness,
inadequacy of representation, and overall administrative efficiency.
Singh argued the Government executed a blanket, blind quota without
auditing the actual demographics of the senior departments. If SC/ST
officers are already adequately represented in a specific senior tier,
forcing further accelerated promotions destroys meritocracy, demoralizes
the workforce, and violates the right to equality of opportunity for
general category candidates (Article 16(1)).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued for a broader, less rigid interpretation of social
justice. They contended that requiring exhaustive, cadre-by-cadre
quantifiable data is a bureaucratic trap designed to endlessly delay
affirmative action. They argued that the Supreme Court in Jarnail Singh
already removed the requirement to prove "backwardness" for SCs and STs.
They asserted that the overall lack of marginalized representation in the
highest echelons of government is a well-documented national reality. The
State argued that administrative efficiency (Article 335) is actually
enhanced, not degraded, by having a diverse leadership that reflects the
populace it governs.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Mr. Singh. The Court struck down the
specific executive order granting accelerated promotions due to the total
absence of quantifiable data regarding inadequacy of representation. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigorous defense of the constitutional boundaries
of affirmative action. The judge reaffirmed the core tenets of the
Nagaraj and Jarnail Singh judgments. While the State does not need to
prove the backwardness of SCs/STs, the constitutional requirement to
prove "inadequacy of representation" remains absolute and non-negotiable.

The Court ruled that Article 16(4A) is an exception to the general rule
of equality of opportunity. Exceptions must be strictly justified. The
State cannot rely on assumptions, historical generalizations, or broad
national demographics. The State must collect objective, contemporary,
and quantifiable data specific to the cadre or grade where the
reservation is being applied. If the data shows they are adequately
represented in that specific tier, the constitutional justification for
reservations in promotions evaporates. By implementing a blanket
promotion policy without conducting any empirical demographic audit, the
Government acted arbitrarily, violating Article 14 and Article 16(1).
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the prerequisites for Reservations in
Promotions (Article 16(4A)). It establishes the absolute legal principle
that the State must collect contemporary, cadre-specific "quantifiable
data" proving inadequacy of representation before implementing
promotional quotas, striking down blind or blanket affirmative action
policies that ignore empirical administrative demographics.

cases.title: Begum v. State of Kerala
cases.facts:
Fatima Begum, a Muslim widow residing in Kerala, had only daughters.
Under the specific provisions of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat)
Application Act, 1937, because she had no sons, her deceased husband's
brothers laid claim to a significant portion of his estate, drastically
reducing the inheritance of Fatima and her daughters.

Fatima filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court, challenging the
constitutionality of these specific, discriminatory inheritance rules
within Muslim Personal Law. She argued they blatantly violated her
fundamental right to Equality (Article 14) and Prohibition of
Discrimination on grounds of sex (Article 15). The All India Muslim
Personal Law Board intervened, arguing that personal laws are derived
from divine religious texts and are fundamentally protected under the
Right to Freedom of Religion (Article 25), explicitly shielding them from
secular judicial scrutiny under Part III of the Constitution.
cases.issues:
Are "Personal Laws" based on religious texts considered "Laws in force"
