under Article 13 of the Constitution, making them subject to fundamental
rights scrutiny?

Does a religious personal law that inherently discriminates against women
in matters of inheritance violate the fundamental rights to Equality
(Article 14) and Dignity (Article 21)?

Does the Constitutional guarantee of Freedom of Religion (Article 25)
grant religious communities absolute immunity to enforce patriarchal
property laws?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Fatima Begum)
Fatima relied heavily on the progressive trajectory of the Shayara Bano
(Triple Talaq) and Mary Roy judgments. She argued that the Constitution
is the supreme law of the land. Any law, whether secular or religious,
that regulates civil matters like property and inheritance must conform
to Part III of the Constitution. She argued that the Shariat Application
Act is a statutory law passed by the legislature, thus qualifying as
"State action" under Article 13. Discriminating against daughters solely
because of their biological sex is a grotesque violation of Article 15.
She argued that Article 25 explicitly subjects religious freedom to
public order, morality, and other fundamental rights, meaning gender
equality permanently supersedes discriminatory religious orthodoxy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Personal Law Board)
The Board anchored its defense in the 1951 Bombay High Court judgment of
State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali, which held that personal laws do not
fall within the definition of "laws" under Article 13 and are immune from
fundamental rights challenges. They argued that inheritance rules are an
inextricable part of Islamic theology. The Constitution guarantees
minorities the right to manage their own religious affairs (Article 26)
and practice their religion (Article 25). They argued that imposing
majoritarian secular laws on minority personal laws destroys India's
pluralistic fabric and constitutes judicial overreach into divine
scripture.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Fatima Begum. Overruling Narasu Appa
Mali, the Constitutional Bench declared that discriminatory inheritance
provisions within personal laws are subject to fundamental rights and
struck down the gender-biased clauses, granting Fatima and her daughters
equal inheritance. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a monumental, historic judgment dismantling
patriarchal religious immunity. The Constitutional Bench formally
overturned the archaic Narasu Appa Mali doctrine. The judge ruled that
any personal law, once codified or recognized by state statutes (like the
Shariat Application Act), unquestionably becomes "law in force" under
Article 13. Therefore, it must face the crucible of Part III of the
Constitution.

The Court rigorously analyzed Article 25. The judge affirmed that the
freedom of religion is fiercely protected, but the Constitution
explicitly subordinates this freedom to the rights of Equality (Article
14) and Non-Discrimination (Article 15). The Court drew a sharp line
between "essential religious practices" (how one prays) and civil/secular
activities associated with religion (how one inherits property). Property
distribution is a secular, civil matter. The Court held that in a modern
republic, religious texts cannot be weaponized to legally subjugate women
or strip them of their constitutional right to equal economic dignity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case historicizes the supremacy of Constitutional Morality over
Discriminatory Personal Laws (Articles 13, 14, 15, & 25). It establishes
the absolute legal principle that Personal Laws are subject to
Fundamental Rights scrutiny, declaring that gender-discriminatory
religious laws regarding civil matters like inheritance are
unconstitutional and void.

cases.title: Union of India v. LifeCare Foundation
cases.facts:
Mr. Kapoor, a 70-year-old man, executed a legally notarized "Advance
Medical Directive" (Living Will). The document explicitly stated that if
he ever fell into an irreversible, persistent vegetative state with no
hope of recovery, he refused any artificial life support, including
ventilators and artificial nutrition. Five years later, he suffered a
massive stroke, entering a permanent vegetative state. The hospital
ethics committee, fearing criminal prosecution for homicide, refused to
honor the Living Will and placed him on a ventilator against the pleas of
his family. The LifeCare Foundation filed a writ petition in the Supreme
Court, demanding the legal enforcement of Advance Medical Directives,
arguing that forcing a brain-dead patient to exist on machines violates
their Right to Die with Dignity under Article 21.
cases.issues:
Is the "Right to Die with Dignity" recognized as an intrinsic facet of
the fundamental Right to Life under Article 21 of the Constitution?

Are "Advance Medical Directives" (Living Wills) legally valid and
enforceable in India?

Does withdrawing artificial life support from a terminally ill patient
based on their prior written consent constitute a criminal offense, or is
it a protected constitutional right?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (LifeCare Foundation)
The Foundation relied on the landmark Supreme Court judgment in Common
Cause v. Union of India. They argued that Article 21 is not merely about
preserving the biological shell of a human body; it guarantees a life of
dignity. When medical science can offer no cure but only artificially
prolong the agony of death, forcing treatment upon an individual violates
their bodily autonomy and subjects them to cruel, degrading treatment.
They argued that an adult of sound mind has the absolute sovereign right
to refuse medical treatment. An Advance Directive is simply the execution
of that right in advance. Honoring it is the ultimate respect for
individual liberty.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India / Hospital)
The Government and the Hospital expressed deep ethical and legal
anxieties. They argued that the sanctity of life is paramount.
Recognizing Living Wills could create a slippery slope toward active
euthanasia or the premature termination of life by greedy relatives
trying to inherit estates. The hospital argued that withdrawing life
support is an active step that causes death, potentially opening doctors
to murder charges under Section 302 of the IPC. They argued that without
a strict, rigid legislative framework passed by Parliament, the courts
should not judicially legislate matters of life and death.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the LifeCare Foundation. The Court
reaffirmed the legal validity of Advance Medical Directives (Living
Wills) and laid down streamlined, binding guidelines for their execution
and implementation, directing the hospital to withdraw life support from
Mr. Kapoor. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profoundly compassionate judgment centering on
human autonomy. The judge explicitly recognized that the Right to Life
under Article 21 inherently encompasses the Right to Die with Dignity.
The Court drew a strict jurisprudential boundary between active
euthanasia (lethal injection) and passive euthanasia (withdrawing
artificial support).

The judge reasoned that an adult of sound mind has an absolute,
indefeasible right to refuse medical treatment. An Advance Medical
Directive is a constitutional extension of that right, allowing a person
to dictate their medical autonomy even after they lose consciousness. The
Court held that artificially prolonging the dying process of a brain-dead
patient using machines, against their explicitly stated prior wishes,
strips them of all human dignity. To prevent misuse, the Court
established robust procedural safeguards (witnesses, medical board
approvals), but affirmed that doctors acting upon a verified Living Will
are completely immune from civil or criminal liability.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case permanently enshrines the Right to Die with Dignity and the
Validity of Advance Medical Directives under Article 21. It establishes
the legal principle that passive euthanasia (withdrawing life support)
based on a patient's informed consent or a verified Living Will is a
fundamental constitutional right, protecting individual bodily autonomy
until the very end of life.

cases.title: MediaWatch v. Union of India (Article 19(1)(a) - Statutory Regulation of Digital News and OTT Platforms)
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Central Government promulgated the highly controversial
"Digital Media Ethics Code." This code placed all independent digital
news portals and OTT streaming platforms under the direct regulatory
control of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The Code
mandated a three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, with the final tier
being an executive "Inter-Departmental Committee" possessing the
absolute, unilateral power to demand the removal of any digital news
article or documentary they deemed "detrimental to public order or
decency."

MediaWatch, an alliance of independent digital journalists, filed a writ
petition challenging the Code. They argued that granting the executive
branch unilateral power to delete news articles without a court order
creates an architecture of censorship and fundamentally crushes the
Freedom of the Press guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a). The Government
argued the digital space was an unregulated "wild west" spreading fake
news, requiring strict oversight under Article 19(2).
cases.issues:
Does granting the executive branch the unilateral, extra-judicial power
to censor and delete digital news content violate the Freedom of Speech
and Expression under Article 19(1)(a)?

Do the provisions of the Digital Media Ethics Code constitute an
unreasonable restriction on free speech that fails the test of Article
19(2)?

Does subjecting digital news media to greater executive control than
traditional print media violate the guarantee of Equality under Article
14?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MediaWatch)
MediaWatch argued that the digital press is the lifeblood of modern
democracy. They relied on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, which struck
down arbitrary digital censorship. They argued the new Code bypasses the
judiciary entirely. Granting a committee of government bureaucrats the
power to dictate what constitutes "truth" or "decency," and the power to
instantly erase journalism critical of the state, has a devastating
"Chilling Effect" on free speech. They argued this is prior restraint and
censorship by executive fiat. Furthermore, they argued it violates
Article 14: traditional newspapers are regulated by the independent Press
Council, while digital news is now directly subordinated to government
ministries.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the digital medium has infinite reach and
instantaneous impact, unlike print media. The proliferation of
coordinated fake news and inflammatory content frequently triggers
actual, physical riots. Therefore, waiting for a lengthy judicial process
to remove dangerous content is unviable. The State invoked Article 19(2),
arguing the regulations are reasonable restrictions strictly in the
interest of sovereignty, security, and public order. They asserted the
three-tier system prioritizes self-regulation, with the government
committee acting only as a last-resort safety valve to prevent digital
anarchy.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of MediaWatch. The Court struck down the
specific provisions of the Digital Media Ethics Code that granted the
executive committee unilateral takedown powers, declaring them
unconstitutional and violative of Article 19(1)(a) and 14. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of the Fourth Estate. The judge
ruled that the fundamental right to freedom of the press cannot be
subjugated to executive whims. While the State has the power to regulate
under Article 19(2), those restrictions must be reasonable and strictly
proportional.

The Court heavily scrutinized the "Inter-Departmental Committee."
Granting bureaucrats the power to act as the ultimate arbiters of
journalistic truth and decency, with the power to erase content without a
prior judicial hearing, completely destroys the separation of powers. It
replaces the rule of law with executive censorship. The Court held that
the State cannot bypass the courts simply because digital news spreads
quickly. Furthermore, subjecting digital journalism to draconian
government oversight while print journalism enjoys independent regulation
creates an arbitrary, unconstitutional classification under Article 14.
The Court affirmed that independent journalism must remain free from the
coercive shadow of the State.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strongly protects Freedom of the Digital Press (Article
19(1)(a)) against Executive Censorship. It establishes the absolute legal
principle that granting the executive branch unilateral, extra-judicial
powers to censor or delete digital news content constitutes an
unreasonable restriction and violates the Constitution, ensuring that the
press cannot be regulated directly by the ministries it is meant to
scrutinize.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Deep Learning Institute
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Central Government mandated that all initial screenings for
nationalized bank loans be conducted using a proprietary AI model named
"Equity-AI," developed by the Deep Learning Institute. By 2026, data
revealed that Equity-AI systematically rejected loan applications from
specific pin codes historically associated with certain marginalized
communities, despite applicants having high individual credit scores. The
algorithm had "learned" historical socioeconomic biases from the 50 years
of training data provided by the State. A Public Interest Litigation
(PIL) was filed under Article 32, alleging that the State's reliance on a
biased "black-box" algorithm violated the fundamental right to equality
under Article 14.
cases.issues:
Does the use of an algorithm that produces discriminatory outcomes, even
without explicit "human" intent, violate the Right to Equality under
Article 14?

Can the State delegate "subjective satisfaction" in financial
distributive justice to an opaque, private-sector algorithm?

Does the Constitutional guarantee of "Equal Protection of the Laws"
include a right to "Algorithmic Transparency"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (PIL Petitioners)
The Petitioners argued that Article 14 strikes at "arbitrariness" in
State action. Relying on E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, they argued
that an algorithm that discriminates based on geographic proxies for
caste or religion is "manifestly arbitrary." They asserted that the State
cannot hide behind "technological neutrality." If the output is
discriminatory, the State action is unconstitutional. They demanded the
right to audit the source code, arguing that "due process" in the 21st
century requires the transparency of the logic that governs a citizen's
life.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Equity-AI is objective and eliminates human
corruption and nepotism. They contended that banking is a commercial
function requiring efficiency. The algorithm evaluates thousands of data
points that humans cannot. They argued that "pin-code clustering" was a
legitimate risk-assessment metric, not a proxy for discrimination.
Furthermore, they claimed "trade secret" privilege over the algorithm's
internal weights, arguing that full transparency would allow bad actors
to "game" the national financial system.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Petitioners. The Court issued a
writ of Mandamus directing the Government to suspend Equity-AI until a
"Constitutional Compliance Audit" was conducted by an independent
judicial committee. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Constitutionalism. The
judge ruled that Article 14 is not just a shield against intended
discrimination, but also against unintended systemic disparate impact.
The Court held that the State's duty to ensure equality is non-delegable.
If the State uses a tool that automates historical prejudice, the State
is the violator. The judge famously remarked, "The Constitution does not
stop at the edge of a computer screen." The Court ruled that "Trade
Secrets" cannot override "Fundamental Rights." Any algorithm used for
public distributive justice must meet the standards of Reasonable
Classification-it must be intelligible and have a rational nexus to a
legitimate goal. A "black box" that cannot explain why it rejected a
citizen fails the test of Article 14.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Accountability. It
reinforces the legal principle that State-sponsored AI must be
transparent and its logic must be subject to judicial review under
Article 14. It confirms that disparate impact caused by technology is as
unconstitutional as direct discrimination by a human official.

cases.title: State of Tamil Nadu v. The Governor
cases.facts:
Between 2024 and 2025, the State Legislature of Tamil Nadu passed 15
high-stakes bills regarding public health and education. The Governor of
the state neither granted assent nor returned the bills for
reconsideration. Instead, the Governor sat on the bills for over 18
months without taking any action. The State Government filed a writ
petition in the Supreme Court, arguing that the Governor's indefinite
silence constituted a "Pocket Veto" not recognized by the Constitution,
effectively paralyzing the will of the democratically elected
legislature.
cases.issues:
Under Article 200, does the Governor have the power to sit on a Bill
indefinitely, or does the phrase "as soon as possible" imply a mandatory
timeline?

Can the Supreme Court issue a writ of Mandamus to a constitutional
functionary like a Governor to discharge a specific duty?

Does the Governor's inaction violate the Basic Structure feature of
"Parliamentary Democracy" and "Federalism"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State Government)
The State argued that the Governor is a symbolic head, not a parallel
center of power. Relying on Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, they
argued the Governor must act on the aid and advice of the Council of
Ministers. They contended that Article 200 provides three options:
Assent, Withhold Assent, or Reserve for President. "Indefinite Inaction"
is a fourth, unconstitutional option. They argued that "as soon as
possible" means within a reasonable time, usually weeks, not years. The
Governor's silence was a mala fide attempt to subvert the mandate of the
people.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Governor's Office)
The Governor's counsel relied on Article 361, which grants the Governor
absolute immunity from being answerable to any court for the exercise of
their powers. They argued that the "satisfaction" of the Governor is
subjective and non-justiciable. They contended that certain bills were so
complex and potentially unconstitutional that the Governor required
extensive time for "due deliberation" to protect the national interest.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State Government. The Court held
that the Governor cannot sit on bills indefinitely and must either grant
assent, withhold it, or return the bill within a reasonable timeframe.
The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound lesson on Constitutional Morality. The
judge ruled that while Article 361 provides personal immunity, the
actions of the Governor's office are fully subject to judicial review if
they result in a constitutional vacuum. The Court interpreted the phrase
"as soon as possible" in Article 200 as a constitutional mandate for
speed.

The judge reasoned that in a Parliamentary Democracy, the Governor cannot
use their office to veto legislation by stealth. To allow a Governor to
kill a bill through silence would be to grant an unelected official more
power than the elected legislature, which violates the Basic Structure.
The Court ruled that if a Governor disagrees with a bill, they must
return it; if the legislature passes it again, the Governor must grant
assent. Indefinite delay is a subversion of the legislative process.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Article 200 (Assent to Bills) and the Doctrine of
Parliamentary Supremacy. It establishes the legal principle that
Constitutional heads cannot use delay as a tool to stifle legislation,
and that the phrase "as soon as possible" imposes a time-bound duty upon
the Governor.

cases.title: Dr. Ayesha v. National Medical Council
cases.facts:
Dr. Ayesha, a devout surgeon, refused to perform a specific elective
reproductive procedure (legal under Indian law) on a patient, citing her
deeply held religious beliefs protected under Article 25. The National
Medical Council (NMC) initiated disciplinary action, arguing that a
doctor's professional duty to provide legal healthcare is secular and
absolute. Dr. Ayesha filed a writ petition, arguing that forcing her to
act against her conscience violates her fundamental right to "freedom of
conscience and free profession of religion."
cases.issues:
Does the Right to Freedom of Conscience (Article 25) include a
"Conscientious Objection" clause for professionals in the
public/regulated sector?

Can the State mandate a professional to perform an act that violates
their core religious tenets if that act is otherwise legal and a part of
their job?

How is the balance struck between the "Freedom of Conscience" of the
provider and the "Right to Health" (Article 21) of the patient?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Ayesha)
Dr. Ayesha argued that Article 25 protects not just "belief" but
"conscience." Forcing her to perform a procedure she considers a sin is a
form of state-sponsored spiritual violence. She relied on the "Essential
Religious Practices" test, arguing her refusal was rooted in a
foundational doctrine of her faith. She contended that as long as other
doctors are available to perform the procedure, the State has no
"compelling interest" to force her specifically to violate her soul.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (NMC)
The NMC argued that the medical profession is a "secular activity
associated with religious practice" which the State can regulate under
Article 25(2)(a). They contended that when a doctor enters a regulated,
state-licensed profession, they voluntarily subordinate their private
beliefs to the professional code of ethics. Allowing "conscientious
objection" would lead to a fragmented healthcare system where patients
are denied legal rights based on the private whims of their doctors,
creating a "religious veto" over secular law.
cases.judgment:
The High Court delivered a balanced judgment. It upheld the NMC's power
to discipline but ruled that the State must provide "Reasonable
Accommodation" for religious beliefs where possible. The Plaintiff
partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explored the Limits of Religious Liberty in the Public Sphere.
The judge ruled that the "Right to Health" under Article 21 is a
paramount right of the patient. However, the "Freedom of Conscience" in
Article 25 is also fundamental. The Court rejected the idea of an
absolute "religious veto."

The judge ruled that in a pluralistic society, the State must apply the
Doctrine of Reasonable Accommodation. If a hospital has ten surgeons and
nine are willing to perform the procedure, forcing the tenth (Dr. Ayesha)
to do it is an unnecessary violation of her conscience. However, if Dr.
Ayesha is the only doctor available (e.g., in a remote village), her
professional duty to the patient's life and health (Article 21) must
supersede her private religious objection (Article 25). The Court held
that the NMC must create guidelines for conscientious objection that
ensure no patient is denied care while respecting the diversity of belief
among providers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case introduces the Doctrine of Reasonable Accommodation to Article
25 jurisprudence. It establishes that Fundamental Rights are not absolute
and must be harmonized; religious conscience can be respected in the
professional sphere only if it does not infringe upon the fundamental
rights (like Health and Equality) of other citizens.

cases.title: Association of Tribal Rights v. Union of India
cases.facts:
In a protected tribal region in North-East India, a traditional customary
law mandated that tribal land could only be inherited by the eldest male
child. Women were entirely barred from land ownership. In 2025, the
Parliament passed the "Tribal Land Modernization Act," which overrode
these customs to grant equal inheritance rights to tribal women. The
Tribal Council challenged the Act, arguing that under Article 13, "custom
and usage" having the force of law are protected, and the State cannot
interfere with their distinct cultural identity protected under Article
29.
cases.issues:
Are "Customs and Usages" having the force of law subject to the "crucible
of fundamental rights" under Article 13?

Can the State use legislation to abolish gender-discriminatory customs in
tribal societies?

In the clash between Article 29 (Right to conserve culture) and Article
15 (Prohibition of sex discrimination), which takes precedence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tribal Council)
The Council argued that their customs are the bedrock of their survival
as a distinct people. They relied on Article 29, which guarantees the
right to "conserve" their culture. They argued that land ownership is the
physical manifestation of their cultural structure. They contended that
"modernization" is a euphemism for cultural genocide, and the
Constitution protects pluralism, not a forced, majoritarian sameness.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Article 13 is clear: any "law" (which includes
custom) that is inconsistent with fundamental rights is void. They relied
on Article 15, arguing that gender-based exclusion from property is a
violation of the "Basic Structure" of equality. They contended that
cultural rights under Article 29 are not a license to practice
discrimination or maintain a state of "perpetual inequality" for women.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Union of India. The Court upheld
the Act, declaring that discriminatory customs must yield to the
fundamental right to equality. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a seminal ruling on Transformative Constitutionalism.
The judge ruled that the "Right to Culture" (Article 29) is a shield for
diversity, not a sword for discrimination. The judge interpreted Article
13 strictly: no custom, however ancient or "essential" to a culture, can
survive if it violates the "Golden Triangle" of Articles 14, 19, and 21.

The Court reasoned that "culture" is not a static museum piece; it must
evolve with the values of human dignity. Stripping women of property
rights is a violation of their Right to Life (Article 21) and Equality
(Article 14). The Court held that the Constitution's primary goal is the
emancipation of the individual. Therefore, the State has a "positive
obligation" to intervene and excise discriminatory elements from
customary laws to ensure that every citizen, regardless of their tribe or
gender, enjoys the full bloom of constitutional liberty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Supremacy of Fundamental Rights over Custom
(Article 13). It establishes that cultural and educational rights
(Article 29 & 30) are subordinate to the rights of Equality and Non-
Discrimination (Articles 14 & 15), affirming the role of the State as an
agent of social reform.

cases.title: MegaBank v. The Privacy Commissioner
cases.facts:
Mr. Varma, a businessman, was acquitted of financial fraud charges in
2018. Despite his acquittal, every time a potential business partner or
bank searched his name on the internet, the first ten results were news
articles about his initial arrest and "alleged" crimes. This "digital
ghost" prevented him from securing loans or contracts. In 2025, Varma
approached the Privacy Commissioner, demanding that Google and news
portals de-link these articles. The Commissioner ordered the de-linking.
MegaBank and several media houses challenged this order, arguing it
violated the public's "Right to Know" and the freedom of the press under
Article 19(1)(a).
cases.issues:
Does the fundamental Right to Privacy (Article 21) include the "Right to
be Forgotten" in the digital age?

How does the Court balance the individual's "Right to be Forgotten"
against the public's "Right to Information" and the "Right to History"?

Can the State compel private search engines to curate information based
on an individual's personal rehabilitation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MegaBank & Media)
The Appellants argued that "Truth" cannot be illegal. The articles were
factually accurate at the time of publication. They argued that the
"Right to be Forgotten" is a form of digital censorship that allows
individuals to "whitewash" their past. They contended that banks have a
"legitimate interest" in knowing the full history of a borrower.
Furthermore, they argued that Articles once published become part of the
"public record" and the "collective memory" of the nation, which the
State cannot authorize individuals to erase.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Mr. Varma & Commissioner)
Varma relied on the Puttaswamy judgment, which explicitly mentioned the
"Right to be Forgotten." He argued that in the digital era, "information
is eternal," meaning a past mistake or even a false accusation becomes a
"life sentence" from which there is no escape. He contended that his
acquittal proved his innocence, yet the internet continued to punish him.
He argued that his "Right to Dignity" and "Right to a Fresh Start"
(Article 21) should allow him to control his digital footprint once the
information has served its original purpose.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Mr. Varma. The Court recognized the
"Right to be Forgotten" as a subset of Article 21, but limited it to "de-
linking" rather than "deletion." The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly sophisticated judgment on Informational
Privacy. The judge ruled that the "Right to be Forgotten" is essential to
human dignity. If a person is acquitted, or if the information is old and
no longer relevant to the public interest, the continuous prominence of
that information becomes an "unreasonable burden."

The Court applied the Balance of Interests test. The judge ruled that the
"Right to Information" is not absolute. While the articles can remain in
the newspaper's archives (the "Right to History"), the search engine (the
gateway to information) must de-link them from the person's name search
to prevent the "digital shadow" from destroying their future. The Court
held that "Rehabilitation" is a constitutional goal, and the digital era
must accommodate the human need to move past the past.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case formally enshrines the Right to be Forgotten under Article 21.
It establishes the legal principle of Informational Self-Determination,
ruling that individuals have a qualified right to have outdated or
irrelevant personal information de-linked from public search results to
protect their dignity and future prospects.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Global Climate Alliance
cases.facts:
To meet its renewable energy targets, the Central Government approved a
massive 100,000-hectare solar park in the Great Indian Bustard (GIB)
habitat in Rajasthan. The GIB is a critically endangered bird. The
project involved thousands of miles of overhead power lines. Scientific
data proved these lines would lead to the imminent extinction of the GIB.
The Global Climate Alliance filed a PIL, arguing that the "Right to Life"
under Article 21 includes the right to a "living, biodiverse planet" and
that the State cannot destroy one fundamental ecological component (an
endangered species) to satisfy another (green energy).
cases.issues:
Does the Right to Life (Article 21) extend to the protection of
endangered species and the preservation of "Ecological Integrity"?

How does the Court resolve the "Green vs. Green" dilemma-where a climate
mitigation project (solar) destroys a local biodiversity component (the
GIB)?

Can the "Precautionary Principle" be used to halt a project of national
importance for the sake of an endangered bird?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Climate Alliance)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 is not "anthropocentric" (human-
centered) but "biocentric." They relied on T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v.
Union of India, arguing that the survival of humans is inextricably
linked to the survival of the ecosystem. The extinction of a flagship
species like the GIB is a "permanent loss to the heritage of India." They
argued that the Government must find "alternative routes" or "underground
cabling," even if more expensive, to ensure that the "Right to a Clean
Environment" does not come at the cost of the "Right to Species
Survival."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued for the "Doctrine of Proportionality" in a
developing nation. India is one of the most climate-vulnerable nations on
earth. Rapidly shifting to solar power is the only way to protect the
"Right to Life" of 1.4 billion humans from lethal heatwaves and floods.
They argued that the "survival of the many" (humans) must take precedence
over the "survival of the one" (a bird species). They contended that
underground cabling was technically and financially unfeasible, and the
project was essential for national energy security.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Climate Alliance. The Court
issued a "Prohibitory Injunction" against overhead lines in the priority
GIB habitat, ordering mandatory underground cabling. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound ruling on Earth Jurisprudence. The judge
ruled that Article 21 encompasses the Right against the Adverse Effects
of Climate Change, but this right cannot be realized through the
"Ecological Bankruptcy" of the nation.

The judge rejected the anthropocentric argument. The Court ruled that the
State is a "Trustee" of all natural resources (the Public Trust
Doctrine). The judge reasoned that "Sustainable Development" requires the
State to protect the "Ecological Integrity" of the land. If the State
destroys a unique, ancient lineage of life (the GIB), it violates its
fiduciary duty to future generations. The Court held that the
"Precautionary Principle" mandates that the cost of underground cabling-
however high-is a "necessary cost of development" that the State must
bear to ensure that its "Green Vision" is not a "Lethal Vision" for the
rest of the web of life.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case expands Article 21 to include Ecological Integrity. It
establishes the Biocentric Principle in Indian law, ruling that
environmental protection must encompass the rights of non-human species
to exist, and that climate mitigation projects must be harmonized with,
not achieved at the cost of, local biodiversity.

cases.title: The State of Vindhya v. The Union of India
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Central Government introduced the "National Education
Incentive Scheme." Under this scheme, the Center offered massive
financial grants to states, but with a strict condition: the states must
adopt a uniform, federally-mandated curriculum that replaced local
languages with a national link language in primary schools. The State of
Vindhya, citing its distinct linguistic heritage protected under Article
29, refused to adopt the curriculum. In retaliation, the Center withheld
Vindhya's entire share of the "Divisible Pool" of taxes (GST and Income
Tax) authorized by the Finance Commission. Vindhya filed a suit under
Article 131, arguing the Center was using "Financial Coercion" to destroy
the "Federal Autonomy" of the states.
cases.issues:
Can the Central Government use discretionary grants or the "Divisible
Pool" of taxes as a tool of coercion to force States to surrender their
legislative autonomy?

Does "Federalism" as a Basic Structure feature protect the "Fiscal
Autonomy" of the States?

Is a dispute over the withholding of constitutional tax shares a "legal
right" actionable under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
(Article 131)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State of Vindhya)
Vindhya argued that the "Divisible Pool" of taxes is a Constitutional
Entitlement of the states, not a "bounty" given at the whim of the
Center. They relied on S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, arguing that states
are not mere administrative units but "sovereign within their own
sphere." They contended that "Cooperative Federalism" has been replaced
by "Coercive Federalism." By starving a state of its constitutional
revenue over a disagreement on education (a State/Concurrent list
subject), the Center was effectively executing an "Economic Emergency"
without declaring one, violating the Basic Structure.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Center argued that Article 282 (Discretionary Grants) gives them the
absolute power to set conditions for funding to ensure "national
standards." They contended that education is a matter of "National
Integration." They argued that the dispute was "political," not "legal,"
and therefore outside the scope of Article 131. The Center maintained
that a State that refuses to align with national development goals cannot
demand the same level of federal financial support.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State of Vindhya. The Court
ordered the immediate release of the tax shares, declaring the Center's
action unconstitutional. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Fiscal Federalism. The judge
ruled that the "Divisible Pool" of taxes is a Vested Constitutional Right
of the states under Article 270 and 280. The Center is a mere "collecting
agent" for the states' share.

The judge ruled that the Center cannot use constitutional revenue to
"blackmail" states into surrendering their legislative powers. The Court
held that Federalism is the bedrock of the Constitution. If the Center
can starve a state into submission, the "State List" becomes a "Dead
List." The judge reasoned that "Cooperative Federalism" means the Center
and States are "partners," not "master and servant." While the Center can
set conditions for discretionary grants (Article 282), it can never
withhold the mandatory tax shares authorized by the Finance Commission.
The action was deemed a mala fide abuse of executive power aimed at
destroying the linguistic and legislative diversity of the Union.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines Fiscal Federalism as a Basic Structure feature. It
establishes the legal principle that mandatory tax shares of States are a
Constitutional Entitlement that the Center cannot withhold for political
or legislative leverage, protecting the financial and legislative
autonomy of the States under the Doctrine of Federal Supremacy in their
own spheres.

cases.title: Ananya v. The State of Haryana
cases.facts:
The State of Haryana implemented a "33% Horizontal Reservation" for women
in all State Government jobs. However, the legislation included a "Socio-
Economic Filter": any woman whose family income exceeded ₹12 Lakhs per
annum (the 'Creamy Layer') was excluded from the reservation. Ananya, a
highly qualified daughter of two senior government officials, was denied
the reservation benefit despite being the top-ranked female candidate.
She challenged the filter, arguing that gender-based reservation is meant
to combat "universal patriarchal oppression," not "economic
backwardness," and therefore the "Creamy Layer" concept applicable to
OBCs cannot be imported into gender reservations.
cases.issues:
Is the "Creamy Layer" principle (based on economic status)
constitutionally applicable to reservations made for women under Article
15(3)?

Is gender-based discrimination a "universal disadvantage" that transcends
class, or can the State distinguish between "privileged" and
"underprivileged" women?

Does Article 14 permit the State to sub-classify a protected group
(women) to ensure that benefits reach the "most backward" members of that
group?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ananya)
Ananya argued that Article 15(3) is a "special provision" for women based
on the biological and social reality of patriarchy. She relied on Indra
Sawhney v. Union of India, arguing that the "Creamy Layer" was a specific
tool for "Backward Classes" (OBCs) to ensure they aren't siphoned by the
affluent. She contended that a wealthy woman still faces the same glass
ceilings, safety issues, and systemic sexism as a poor woman. By adding
an income filter, the State is treating gender reservation as a "Poverty
Alleviation" scheme rather than a "Representation" scheme, which violates
the intent of Article 15(3).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Haryana)
The State argued the Doctrine of Substantive Equality. They contended
that a woman from a multi-millionaire family has a massive "head-start"
in education and networking compared to a woman from a rural,
impoverished background. They argued that "universalizing" the
reservation would allow the "privileged elite" women to capture all 33%
of the seats, leaving marginalized women exactly where they were. The
State contended that Article 14 mandates them to "classify" so that the
"most needy" receive the State's limited resources.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State of Haryana. The Court
upheld the "Creamy Layer" filter for women's reservations. The Defendant
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a pragmatic judgment on Intersectional Equality. The
judge ruled that Article 14 is a "Dynamic Equality." While patriarchy is
universal, its impact is not. A woman with massive economic and
educational capital is not "backward" in the same sense as a woman
without those tools.

The judge ruled that the State has the power under Article 15(3) to
design reservations that achieve Substantive Social Justice. If the State
finds that "Elite Capture" is preventing the benefits from reaching the
grass-roots, the State is required by Article 14 to sub-classify. The
Court held that the "Creamy Layer" is a valid constitutional tool to
ensure that affirmative action does not become a "privilege of the
privileged." The judge reasoned that the "equality of opportunity"
(Article 16) is best served when the State prioritizes those who have
suffered the dual burden of gender and class.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Constitutional Validity of the Creamy Layer in
Gender Reservations. It reinforces the principle of Substantive Equality
(Article 14), ruling that the State can sub-classify protected groups to
prevent the monopolization of benefits by the affluent, ensuring that
affirmative action serves as an instrument of genuine social mobility.

cases.title: The AI Ethics Board v. The News Portal (Article 19(1)(a) and the 'Right to Human Content')
cases.facts:
In 2026, "IndiaDaily," a massive news portal, fired its entire staff of
500 journalists and replaced them with a proprietary Generative AI
system. The AI generated 5,000 articles a day, often indistinguishable
from human writing. However, the AI had no "moral compass" and frequently
"hallucinated" facts, leading to widespread misinformation. The
Government-mandated "AI Ethics Board" issued a directive: "All news
outlets must ensure at least 50% of their content is authored by human
beings to protect the integrity of the public discourse." IndiaDaily
challenged this in the High Court, arguing it was an unconstitutional
restriction on their "Freedom of Trade" (Article 19(1)(g)) and "Freedom
of Expression" (Article 19(1)(a)).
cases.issues:
Does the "Freedom of Speech" (Article 19(1)(a)) protect speech generated
entirely by an Artificial Intelligence algorithm?

Can the State mandate "Human Authorship" as a "reasonable restriction" to
protect the "Sovereignty and Integrity of India" or "Public Order"?

Does the right to "receive information" under Article 19(1)(a) include a
right to know if information is "Human-made" or "Machine-made"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (IndiaDaily)
IndiaDaily argued that the "Medium" of speech is irrelevant; only the
"Content" matters. They contended that if the State can regulate who
(human vs. machine) speaks, the State is effectively practicing
"Censorship by Proxy." They relied on Shreya Singhal, arguing that
Article 19(1)(a) is technology-neutral. They contended that they were
exercising their "Right to Trade" by using the most efficient technology
available, and a "Human Quota" was an arbitrary, Luddite restriction that
had no "rational nexus" to stopping fake news.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (AI Ethics Board)
The Board argued that the "Public Square" is a human space. They
contended that AI-generated misinformation is a "clear and present
danger" to public order (Article 19(2)). Because AI has no legal
personality and cannot be jailed for defamation or sedition, "Machine
Speech" lacks accountability. They argued that citizens have a "Right to
the Truth," and in the age of Deepfakes, "Human Authorship" is the only
remaining proxy for accountability and ethical journalism.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the AI Ethics Board. The Court upheld
the "50% Human Content" mandate. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a visionary judgment on Human-Centric Jurisprudence.
The judge ruled that the Constitution is a "Social Contract" between
humans. Article 19(1)(a) was designed to protect the "human spirit" and
the "human right to dissent."

The judge ruled that Machine Speech is not Fundamental Speech. An
algorithm has no "Conscience" (Article 25) and no "Dignity" (Article 21).
Therefore, the State can regulate it much more strictly than human
speech. The Court held that the "Right to Information" includes the Right
to Authenticity. If the public discourse is flooded by un-checked, non-
accountable machine hallucinations, the democratic process itself
collapses. The "Human Quota" was deemed a "reasonable restriction" in the
interest of "Public Order" and "Decency," as it ensures that at least
half of the nation's information stream is backed by a human being who is
legally and ethically responsible for the words published.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Human Primacy in Speech. It
establishes the legal principle that Artificial Intelligence does not
possess Fundamental Rights, and that the State can impose "Human-Centric"
regulations on digital platforms to protect the integrity of information
and public order in the age of algorithmic automation.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Heritage Restoration Society
cases.facts:
The Central Government passed the "Ancient Cities Modernization Act,"
which allowed for the demolition of 200 "minor" heritage buildings (over
100 years old but not nationally protected) in Varanasi to build a high-
speed transit corridor. The Heritage Restoration Society filed a writ
petition, arguing that Article 49 of the Directive Principles (Protection
of monuments and places of national importance) must be read into the
"Right to Life" (Article 21). They argued that the "Right to Heritage" is
an essential part of the "Right to Identity" and "Right to Environment."
The Government argued that development is a "sovereign necessity" and
Article 49 is non-enforceable in a court of law.
cases.issues:
Can the "Directive Principles of State Policy" (Article 49) be elevated
to the status of an "Enforceable Fundamental Right" by reading them into
Article 21?

Does the "Right to Life" include the right to reside in a culturally and
historically intact environment?

How does the Court balance the "Right to Development" against the "Right
to Heritage"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Heritage Society)
The Society relied on the "Integrated Approach" of Kesavananda Bharati
and Minerva Mills, arguing that Fundamental Rights and Directive
Principles are "two wheels of the same chariot." They contended that
Article 21 is an "Empty Shell" without the cultural and historical
environment that gives meaning to life. They argued that Varanasi's
heritage is a "Global Public Good," and the State is a mere "Trustee" of
this history, not an owner who can demolish it for a railway.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued a strict reading of Article 37: Directive
Principles are "non-justiciable." They contended that the transit
corridor would lift millions out of poverty and reduce carbon emissions.
They argued that "sentimental value" of old buildings cannot halt
"structural survival" of a modern city. The State argued that the
judiciary should not act as an "architectural censor" of executive
infrastructure projects.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Heritage Restoration Society. The
Court stayed the demolition and ordered a "Heritage Impact Assessment."
The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Cultural Rights. The judge ruled
that the "Right to Life" is not a "Right to Animal Existence." Human life
is a "Cultural Life."

The judge adopted the Doctrine of Harmonious Construction. While Article
49 is a Directive, it informs the content of Article 21. The Court ruled
that the "Right to a Decent Environment" includes the "Right to a
Cultural Environment." The judge reasoned that the State has a "Duty of
Care" towards the historical soul of a city. Demolishing 200 heritage
buildings without an expert audit is a "manifestly arbitrary" act. The
Court held that "Development" and "Heritage" are not enemies; the State
must pursue "Heritage-Sensitive Development." The judge famously stated,
"A nation that destroys its past has no future to look forward to,"
making heritage protection an implicit facet of the constitutional right
to dignity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Fundamental Right to Heritage under Article 21.
It reinforces the principle that Directive Principles (Article 49) must
be used to expand the scope of Fundamental Rights, and that the State
holds a "Public Trust" duty to protect the cultural and historical
environment of the people.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Algorithmic Justice Project
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Home Affairs implemented "Sentinel-AI," an
automated risk-assessment tool used to determine the eligibility of
undertrial prisoners for bail. The AI analyzed 50 variables, including
socioeconomic background, family history, and "predictive recidivism
scores." An audit by the Algorithmic Justice Project revealed that the AI
systematically assigned higher risk scores to individuals from specific
marginalized tribal communities (STs), even when their criminal records
were identical to "low-risk" upper-caste counterparts. The State argued
that the AI was "mathematically objective" and simply processed
historical data. The Project filed a writ of Mandamus to halt the use of
Sentinel-AI, alleging a violation of Article 14 (Equality) and Article 21
(Personal Liberty).
cases.issues:
Can a "Black Box" algorithm satisfy the "Reasonable Classification" test
under Article 14 if its internal logic is proprietary and opaque?

Does the use of historical data that encodes systemic bias constitute
"State-sponsored Discrimination" under Article 15?

Is there a fundamental Right to "Human Intervention" in judicial or
quasi-judicial decision-making affecting personal liberty under Article
21?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Justice Project)
The Petitioners argued that Article 14 strikes at "manifest
arbitrariness." An algorithm that produces discriminatory outcomes based
on caste-proxies is the epitome of arbitrariness. Relying on Maneka
Gandhi v. Union of India, they argued that "procedure established by law"
under Article 21 must be just, fair, and reasonable. A procedure that
automates prejudice through a machine is fundamentally unfair. They
contended that "mathematical objectivity" is a myth when training data is
poisoned by historical systemic bias.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Sentinel-AI was a "Scientific Advancement"
aimed at reducing the massive backlog of bail applications. They
contended that the algorithm eliminates human "subjective bias" and
corruption. They argued that tribal status was not an explicit variable,
and if the AI found correlations in socioeconomic data, it was merely
reflecting statistical reality. They claimed "Sovereign Privilege" over
the source code, arguing that transparency would allow criminals to "game
the system."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Justice Project. The Court issued
a "Stay" on Sentinel-AI, declaring that no machine can replace the
"Judicial Mind" in matters of life and liberty. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Digital Constitutionalism. The
judge ruled that the "Right to Equality" includes the Right against
Algorithmic Bias.

The judge reasoned that an "Intelligible Differentia" must be human-
readable and legally justifiable. If the State cannot explain why a
machine rejected a citizen's liberty, the State has abdicated the Rule of
Law. The Court held that "Historical Data" is often a record of
"Historical Injustice"; therefore, automating the past is a violation of
the transformative nature of the Constitution. The Court mandated a
"Human-in-the-Loop" requirement for all AI systems affecting Fundamental
Rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Algorithmic Transparency. It
reinforces that Article 14 prohibits disparate impact caused by
technology and establishes that Judicial Power cannot be delegated to
non-human entities.

cases.title: State of Vindhya v. The Union Trust
cases.facts:
A 500-year-old religious denomination, the "Ananda Sect," became extinct
as its last ordained priest died without appointing a successor. The Sect
held massive properties worth ₹2,000 Crores in the State of Vindhya. The
State Government passed a law to take over the properties under the
"Doctrine of Escheat" (State taking ownerless property) to build public
hospitals. The "Union Trust," representing the lay followers of the sect,
challenged the law under Article 26, arguing that the "denomination"
survives through its followers, and the State has no right to secularize
religious property.
cases.issues:
Does a "Religious Denomination" under Article 26 cease to exist upon the
death of its clergy, or does it reside in the body of its lay followers?

Can the State invoke the "Doctrine of Escheat" over religious endowments
protected by fundamental rights?

Does the "Right to Manage Religious Affairs" include the right to prevent
the State from converting a temple into a hospital?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The State argued that the Sect was a "clerical order." With no priests,
the legal entity had vanished. They contended that the property was now
"ownerless" and, as the sovereign, the State is the ultimate heir
(Ultimus Haeres). They relied on the Directive Principles (Article 47) to
argue that using idle wealth for public health is a superior
constitutional goal than maintaining empty shrines.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union Trust)
The Trust relied on the Shirur Mutt case, arguing that a denomination
consists of all persons who share a common faith and organization. Lay
followers are the heart of the denomination. They argued that Article
26(c) gives the denomination the right to "own and acquire" property, and
this right is not contingent on the survival of a specific leader.
Converting religious land to secular use, they argued, is a violation of
the "Essential Religious Practices" of the community.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Union Trust. The Court struck
down the State's takeover, ordering the Trust to manage the properties
according to the sect's original tenets. The Respondent prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a profound ruling on Religious Autonomy. The judge
ruled that the State is a "Secular Entity" and must remain neutral. The
judge reasoned that the "Doctrine of Escheat" applies to private
property, but Religious Endowments are held in Trust for the Deity. Since
the "Deity" is a "Juristic Person" who never dies, the property can never
be "ownerless." The Court held that Article 26 protects the community's
right to their sacred space, and the State cannot use "Public Utility" as
a pretext to dismantle religious institutions, as this would violate the
Basic Structure of Secularism.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Juristic Personality of the Deity and the
Autonomy of Religious Denominations (Article 26). It establishes that the
State's power of Escheat is subordinate to the fundamental rights of
religious communities.

cases.title: MegaGrid Corp v. The Forest Rights Alliance
cases.facts:
To achieve 100% rural electrification, the Central Government authorized
MegaGrid Corp to install massive, high-intensity LED streetlights every
50 meters across a protected forest zone inhabited by the "Nocturnal
Tribes." The tribes filed a PIL, arguing that the perpetual artificial
light destroyed the ecosystem, killed their sacred nocturnal insects, and
caused them "Circadian Despair." They claimed a fundamental "Right to
Darkness" as a subset of the "Right to a Clean Environment" under Article
21.
cases.issues:
Does the "Right to Environment" under Article 21 include the right to be
free from "Light Pollution"?

How does the Court balance the "Right to Development" (Electricity)
against the "Right to Cultural and Ecological Preservation"?

Can "Light" be considered a "Pollutant" under Indian Environmental
Jurisprudence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Alliance)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 protects the "Quality of Life."
For a tribe that has lived in harmony with the night for millennia,
darkness is an essential resource. They relied on international "Dark
Sky" movements, arguing that light pollution is a silent killer of
biodiversity. They contended that "Constant Day" is a form of
psychological torture and a violation of their Right to Sleep and Right
to Privacy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MegaGrid)
The Corporation argued that electricity is a "Human Right." They
contended that darkness is a proxy for "backwardness," and the State has
a duty under the Directive Principles to provide modern infrastructure.
They argued that "Light" cannot be a pollutant because it is essential
for public safety and the prevention of crime in forest areas.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court delivered a "Compromise Judgment." It recognized the
"Right to Darkness" but allowed the lights with strict "Dimming and
Shielding" mandates. The Plaintiff partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explored the Limits of Anthropocentric Development. The judge
ruled that Article 21 is an "evolving container" that now includes the
Right to Circadian Integrity.
[Image showing the effect of light pollution on the human circadian
rhythm and ecology]
The judge reasoned that the "Right to a Clean Environment" means an
environment that respects the natural cycles of life. However, the Court
used the Doctrine of Harmonious Construction. It ruled that development
and darkness are not binary. The Court ordered MegaGrid to use "Warm-
spectrum, Motion-sensor lighting" that preserves the darkness when no
humans are present, thus protecting the tribe's culture and the forest's
ecology while providing safety.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case expands Article 21 to include the Right against Light
Pollution. It establishes the Circadian Rights Doctrine, affirming that
the State must mitigate the ecological impact of infrastructure on the
natural cycles of light and dark.

cases.title: The Citizen Journalists v. The Union of India (Article 19(1)(a) and the 'Right to Record')
cases.facts:
In 2026, during a major public protest, the police utilized a "Signal
Jamming" vehicle and issued an order prohibiting all citizens from using
mobile phone cameras to record police action, citing "operational
secrecy" and "privacy of officers." Several citizen journalists were
arrested and their phones confiscated. They filed a writ petition,
arguing that the "Right to Record" public officials in the discharge of
their duties is a fundamental component of Freedom of the Press under
Article 19(1)(a).
cases.issues:
Is the act of "Digital Recording" of public events a protected form of
"Expression" under Article 19(1)(a)?

Can the State invoke the "Privacy of Public Servants" to prevent the
documentation of state action in public spaces?

Does a "Camera Ban" constitute an "Unreasonable Restriction" that fails
the test of Article 19(2)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Journalists)
The Petitioners argued that the "Right to Know" is well-established. If a
citizen cannot record, the right to "seek and receive information"
becomes hollow. They argued that cameras are the "modern pens" of the
citizenry. Recording police action ensures Accountability, which is a
basic feature of democracy. They contended that a public servant in a
public uniform on a public street has zero "expectation of privacy"
regarding their official acts.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that live-streaming police tactics allows rioters to
coordinate and ambush officers, threatening "Public Order" under Article
19(2). They argued that "Doxxing" (releasing officer identities) leads to
the harassment of their families, violating the officers' Right to
Privacy under Article 21. They claimed that the "Right to Record" is not
a recognized fundamental right and can be restricted during emergencies.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Journalists. The Court declared
the "Right to Record" state action as a fundamental right. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a resounding victory for Democratic Transparency. The
judge ruled that Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to use the
"technological tools of the age." The judge reasoned that a camera is a
tool of Truth.

The Court held that the State cannot use "Privacy" as a cloak for
"Impunity." A public official performing a public duty is accountable to
the public eye. The Court ruled that while "Live-streaming" could be
restricted in specific tactical anti-terror operations, a blanket ban on
recording police at a protest is a "draconian restriction" that destroys
the "Check and Balance" of the Fourth Estate. The "Right to Record" was
held to be an essential safeguard against custodial violence and
administrative overreach.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Fundamental Right to Record Public Officials. It
establishes that State Secrecy cannot override Democratic Accountability
and that cameras in public spaces are protected instruments of Freedom of
Expression.

cases.title: Dr. Mehta v. The State of Gujarat
cases.facts:
The State Government implemented a "100% Reservation" policy for in-
service government doctors for all "Super-Specialty" (DM/MCh) medical
seats in state-run colleges. Dr. Mehta, a highly ranked private
candidate, was denied admission despite having a much higher score than
the in-service candidates. He challenged the policy, arguing that at the
level of "Super-Specialty," reservation is unconstitutional as it
destroys "Institutional Excellence" and violates Article 14.
cases.issues:
Can the State provide 100% reservation in "Super-Specialty" medical
courses under Article 15(4)?

Is there a "Point of No Return" for Affirmative Action where "Merit" must
become the sole criterion?

How does the Court balance "Social Justice" with the "Right to Life"
(Article 21) which requires the highest quality of specialized surgeons?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Mehta)
Dr. Mehta relied on Preeti Srivastava v. State of M.P. and Indra Sawhney.
He argued that while reservation is vital at the entry-level (MBBS), it
cannot be allowed at the level where surgeons are learning to perform
heart transplants or brain surgery. He contended that at this stage, the
"Interests of the Nation" and the "Sanctity of Life" demand the absolute
best candidates, regardless of caste or service status. 100% reservation
is a "Total Exclusion of Merit," which is per se unconstitutional.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that rural India has zero super-specialists. By
reserving seats for "in-service" doctors (who are bonded to work for the
government), the State ensures that specialized care reaches the poor,
not just the urban elite. They argued that Article 15(4) is an "enabling
provision" with no upper limit for specific social goals. "Merit," they
argued, is a social construct that ignores the privilege of private
candidates.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Dr. Mehta. The Court struck down the
100% reservation, capping it at 15%. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Equilibrium of Equality. The judge
ruled that Article 14 is a "double-edged sword." It protects marginalized
groups, but it also protects the Right to Excellence.

The judge reasoned that "Social Justice" cannot be achieved by
compromising "National Health." The Court held that at the "Super-
Specialty" level, the level of skill required is so high that any
dilution of standards poses a direct threat to the Right to Life (Article
21) of the patients. The judge ruled that 100% reservation is an
"Expropriation of Opportunity" that violates the Basic Structure. The
Court established the Doctrine of Merit-Centricity in High-Tech
Education, ruling that the State can provide "incentives" for rural
service, but it cannot "exclude" the most talented minds from the
nation's highest operating theaters.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Limits of Affirmative Action. It establishes the
legal principle that Reservation cannot be absolute in Super-Specialty
education, as the Constitutional mandate for "Efficiency of
Administration" (Article 335) and the "Right to Health" (Article 21)
require the primacy of competitive merit.

cases.title: The Secular Alliance v. The Ministry of Culture
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Ministry of Culture launched the "Divya Darshan Scheme,"
utilizing ₹5,000 Crores of taxpayer money to provide free air travel and
luxury accommodation exclusively to pilgrims visiting ten specific major
religious sites of a particular faith. The Secular Alliance filed a writ
petition, arguing that the scheme violated Article 27, which states that
"No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are
specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or
maintenance of any particular religion."
cases.issues:
Does the use of general tax revenue to fund a specific religious
pilgrimage constitute the "promotion or maintenance of a particular
religion" under Article 27?

Is there a distinction between "Promotion of Religion" and "Promotion of
Tourism/Culture"?

Can the State argue that "Equal Funding for All Religions" (Sarva Dharma
Sambhava) justifies religious expenditures?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Alliance)
The Petitioners argued that Article 27 is an absolute bar. The State
cannot be a "Travel Agent for a Deity." They contended that using tax
money from an atheist or a member of a different faith to fund a specific
religion's pilgrimage is a "Constitutional Breach of Trust." They argued
that the scheme was not "Tourism" but a direct financial subsidy to
religious institutions, which violates the Secular Basic Structure.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Ministry)
The Ministry argued that the scheme was intended to boost the "Spiritual
Economy" and domestic tourism. They contended that "Secularism" in India
is not a "Wall of Separation" but "Neutrality." They argued that as long
as the State eventually launches similar schemes for other faiths,
Article 27 is not violated. They claimed the expenditure was for the
"Welfare of Senior Citizens" (the primary beneficiaries), not the
promotion of faith.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Secular Alliance. The Court
struck down the scheme as unconstitutional. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining ruling on Fiscal Secularism. The judge
ruled that Article 27 is a "Negative Right" of the taxpayer. The State
cannot pick a specific religion and spend the general pool of taxes on
its "promotion."

The judge reasoned that while the State can provide "Secular Facilities"
(like roads or toilets) for large gatherings, it cannot fund the "Core
Religious Act" (the pilgrimage itself). The judge rejected the "Equal
Funding" argument, ruling that "Multi-Religious Promotion" is not
"Secularism." secularism means the State has "no religion." If the State
spends tax money on religion, it is "appropriating" the conscience of the
taxpayer. The Court held that the "Promotion of Tourism" was a mere
"colorable device" to hide a direct religious subsidy.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case robustly enforces Article 27. It establishes the legal
principle that Tax Revenue cannot be used for the direct funding of
religious activities, and that "Spiritual Tourism" schemes must be
strictly secular in their benefits to pass the constitutional test.

cases.title: Ananya v. The Passport Office
cases.facts:
Ananya, a human rights lawyer, was a fierce critic of the government. In
2026, the Passport Office revoked her passport under the Passport Act,
citing "Interests of the general public" and "Prejudice to friendly
relations with foreign nations," based on her speeches at international
forums. Ananya was effectively trapped within India. She filed a writ
petition, arguing that the "Right to Travel Abroad" is a fundamental
facet of personal liberty under Article 21 and cannot be curtailed based
on "Political Speech."
cases.issues:
Is the "Right to Travel Abroad" an absolute fundamental right, or can it
be restricted based on "Executive Discretion"?

Does "Political Criticism" of the home State at an international forum
constitute "Prejudice to Friendly Relations"?

What is the scope of judicial review over "Subjective Satisfaction" in
national security matters?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ananya)
Ananya relied on the Maneka Gandhi case. She argued that the "Right to
Travel" is a part of her "Universal Dignity." Revoking a passport to
prevent a citizen from speaking abroad is "Executive Gagging." She
contended that "Friendly Relations with Foreign States" is a narrow
exception meant to prevent the incitement of war or terrorism, not to
protect the Government from "reputational embarrassment."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that Ananya was "Maliciously De-branding India" on the
global stage, which discouraged Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and
weakened the nation's "Soft Power." They claimed that her travel posed a
"Strategic Threat" to the national interest. They argued that under the
Passport Act, the State has broad "Sovereign Discretion" to decide who
represents the country abroad.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Ananya. The Court ordered the immediate
restoration of her passport. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Global Liberty. The judge ruled
that the "Right to Travel" is a "Human Right" recognized under Article
21.

The judge reasoned that a "Friendly Relation" with a foreign state is not
so fragile that it can be broken by the speech of a single lawyer. The
Court held that the State cannot equate its "Political Ego" with
"National Security." To trap a critic within the borders is a form of
"Internal Exile." The Court ruled that unless the State can prove the
citizen is involved in espionage or violent incitement, the right to
cross borders for the purpose of speech and movement is absolute.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Article 21 and the Maneka Gandhi Precedent. It
establishes the legal principle that Political Dissent is not a ground
for revoking a passport and that the "Interests of the General Public"
exception must be interpreted narrowly to prevent executive overreach.

cases.title: The Privacy Collective v. The Smart City
cases.facts:
A "Smart City" project in Bangalore installed 50,000 AI-enabled CCTV
cameras with Real-time Facial Recognition System (FRRS). The system was
linked to the Aadhaar database and was programmed to track the movement
of "known protesters" and "frequent dissenters" across the city. The
Privacy Collective filed a writ petition, arguing that constant tracking
of an individual's physical location in the public sphere violates the
"Right to Anonymity" and the "Right to be Let Alone" under Article 21.
cases.issues:
Does the fundamental Right to Privacy (Article 21) include a "Right to
Public Anonymity"?

Does "Mass Surveillance" via FRRS create a "Chilling Effect" on the
Freedom of Assembly (Article 19(1)(b))?

Does the State's interest in "Crime Prevention" justify the permanent
tracking of law-abiding citizens?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Collective)
The Petitioners argued that privacy does not end when you leave your
house. The "Right to be Let Alone" means the right to walk the streets
without being "Digital Tagged." They argued that FRRS is a "Digital
Leash" that makes people afraid to attend protests or meet political
dissidents, thereby destroying Article 19. They contended that the system
fails the Proportionality Test as it treats every citizen as a "Potential
Criminal."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Smart City)
The State argued that there is "no expectation of privacy" in a public
street. They contended that FRRS is a "Force Multiplier" for the police
that has reduced kidnapping and theft by 40%. They argued that tracking
"known dissenters" was necessary for "Predictive Policing" and to prevent
riots. They claimed the data was stored on a secure server and only
accessed during active investigations.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Privacy Collective. The Court
ordered the decommissioning of the FRRS until a specific "Data Protection
Law" was passed by Parliament. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment on Public Sphere Privacy. The
judge ruled that the "Right to Privacy" is a "Right to Control one's
Identity."

The judge reasoned that "Anonymity is the shield of liberty." If the
State knows where every citizen is at every second, the "Democratic
Spirit" is crushed by a "Permanent Gaze." The Court held that the FRRS
failed the Puttaswamy test because there was no "Specific Law"
authorizing its use. The judge ruled that "Administrative Guidelines" are
not enough to authorize mass surveillance. The Court held that the State
cannot build a "Digital Panopticon" under the guise of "Smart
Development." Any surveillance must be "Targeted," not "Mass," and must
have judicial oversight.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Right to Public Anonymity under Article 21. It
establishes the legal principle that Mass Facial Recognition is
unconstitutional in the absence of a strict, transparent legislative
framework and judicial warrants.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Gig Workers Union
cases.facts:
In 2026, the Central Government passed the "Digital Economy Act," which
explicitly classified all gig workers (delivery partners, ride-share
drivers) as "Independent Contractors," thereby excluding them from all
labor laws, including minimum wage, health insurance, and pension
schemes. The Gig Workers Union filed a writ petition, arguing that
"Exclusion from Social Security" violates their fundamental "Right to
Work with Dignity" under Article 21 and the Directive Principle of
Article 42 (Just and humane conditions of work).
cases.issues:
Can the State use "Contractual Nomenclature" (Contractor vs Employee) to
deny fundamental social protections to a massive workforce?

Does the "Right to Life" (Article 21) include the right to a "Minimum
Social Security Net"?

How does the Court balance "Economic Flexibility" with "Constitutional
Social Justice"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Workers)
The Union argued that "Economic Reality" must override "Legal Fiction."
The workers are "algorithmically controlled" and "economically dependent"
on the platforms. They relied on Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corp,
arguing that the Right to Life includes the Right to Livelihood. They
contended that working 14 hours a day without health insurance or a
safety net is "Modern Slavery" and a violation of Article 23 (Prohibition
of forced labor).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that the Gig Economy is based on "Flexibility" and
"Choice." They contended that forcing platforms to provide benefits would
kill the industry, leading to massive unemployment. They argued that
"Social Security" is a Directive Principle (Article 41) and is "Non-
Justiciable," meaning the Court cannot compel the State to spend money it
does not have.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Gig Workers Union. The Court
ordered the State to create a "Mandatory Social Security Fund" for all
gig workers. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a defining ruling on Economic Dignity. The judge
ruled that the Constitution is a "Social Document" meant to protect the
weak.

The judge reasoned that the "Right to Life" is not a "Right to Bare
Survival." It is a "Right to a Meaningful Life." The Court held that a
worker who powers the nation's digital economy cannot be left to die in a
medical emergency. The judge ruled that while the State can categorize
workers, it cannot "Exempt" itself from the Positive Obligations of a
Welfare State. The Court invoked the Doctrine of Constitutional
Integration, reading the Directive Principles into Article 21. The judge
held that "Economic Stability" of an industry cannot be built on the
"Constitutional Destitution" of its workers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Fundamental Right to Social Security under
Article 21. It reinforces that Directive Principles (Article 41 & 42) are
the soul of Fundamental Rights, and the State must ensure basic dignity
for all forms of labor, including the gig economy.

cases.title: The State of Uttarakhand v. The Himalayan People
cases.facts:
To build a massive "Char Dham All-Weather Road," the State Government
began the blasting of Himalayan mountains. This caused massive
