landslides, the drying up of perennial springs, and the "Sinking" of a
historic mountain town. The Himalayan People filed a PIL, arguing that
the "Ganges River" and the "Himalayan Glaciers" are "Living Juristic
Persons" with their own fundamental rights, and the road project was an
act of "Assault" upon their physical integrity under Article 21.
cases.issues:
Can non-human natural entities (Rivers/Glaciers/Mountains) be recognized
as "Juristic Persons" with Fundamental Rights under the Indian
Constitution?

Does the "Right to Life" of a human include the right to the
"Uninterrupted Flow" and "Physical Integrity" of the ecosystem?

How does the Court resolve the conflict between "National Infrastructure"
and "Ecological Personhood"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The People)
The Petitioners relied on the Salmond definition of personhood. They
argued that if a "Corporation" or a "Deity" can be a person, why not a
"Glacier" that sustains millions? They contended that the Himalayas are
the "Sacred Ancestors" of the nation. They argued that nature has an
"Intrinsic Right to Exist" independent of human utility, and destroying
it is a violation of the Public Trust Doctrine.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that "Personhood" is a human attribute. They contended
that granting rights to mountains would make all development
(dams/roads/tunnels) a criminal offense. They argued that the "Needs of
the Living" (devotees and travelers) must take precedence over the
"Rights of Rocks." They claimed the project was vital for "National
Defense" on the border.
cases.judgment:
The High Court (and later affirmed by SC) ruled in favor of Nature. The
Court declared the Himalayas and its Glaciers as "Living Juristic
Entities" and appointed the citizens as their "Legal Guardians." The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a visionary ruling on Biocentric Constitutionalism.
The judge ruled that the Constitution is not a "Death Warrant" for the
environment.

The judge reasoned that the "Right to Life" (Article 21) is dependent on
the "Life of the Earth." If the mountains sink, the people sink. The
Court held that the legal concept of "Personhood" is a tool for
protection. By granting personhood to the Himalayas, the Court gave the
mountains a "Voice in the Room." [Image representing the concept of Legal
Personhood for Nature/Ecosystems]
The judge ruled that the State is a "Trustee," not an "Owner." The
project was ordered to be "Radically Re-designed" to respect the
"Structural Integrity" of the mountains, declaring that the "Rights of
Nature" are an unshakeable prerequisite for the "Rights of Man."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Doctrine of Ecological Personhood. It establishes
the legal principle that Nature has an inherent right to exist and
flourish, and that Article 21 includes the protection of the Earth's
"Life-Support Systems" as a fundamental right.

cases.title: "Life-Support Systems" as a fundamental right.
cases.facts:
The State of Punjab enacted a law providing for "preferential treatment"
to the Balmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs within the Scheduled Castes (SC) quota,
acknowledging they were the most backward among the backward. This sub-
classification was challenged as violating Article 341 of the
Constitution, which treats the President's list of SCs as a homogenous
monolith. The matter reached a seven-judge Constitution Bench in 2024 to
determine if states have the power to sub-divide the SC list for more
targeted affirmative action.
cases.issues:
- Does the sub-classification of Scheduled Castes for the purpose of
reservation violate the "monolithic" nature of the Presidential list
under Article 341?
- Can the State use empirical data to prove that certain sub-castes have
failed to reap the benefits of reservation, justifying "preferential"
quotas within the quota?
- Does the "Creamy Layer" principle apply to Scheduled Castes and
Scheduled Tribes as it does to OBCs?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Opponents of Sub-
classification)
The Appellants relied on the 2004 judgment in E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of
Andhra Pradesh. They argued that Article 341 creates a single, unified
class of Scheduled Castes. Only the President can notify the list, and
only Parliament can exclude or include castes. They contended that sub-
classification amounts to "tinkering" with the list, which is a fraud on
the Constitution and leads to "vote-bank" politics by State governments.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Punjab &
Proponents)
The State argued that Article 14 (Equality) mandates treating unequals
unequally. They presented empirical data showing that Mazhabi Sikhs and
Balmikis remained at the very bottom of the social hierarchy, while other
SC sub-castes captured the majority of government jobs and seats. They
contended that "Substantive Equality" (Article 16(4)) grants the State
the power to ensure the "weakest of the weak" receive protection, rather
than allowing a "Creamy Layer" to monopolize benefits.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (7-judge bench) ruled in favor of the State of Punjab,
overruling E.V. Chinnaiah. The Court upheld the validity of sub-
classification within the Scheduled Caste categories. The Defendant
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Intersectional Social
Justice. The judge ruled that Scheduled Castes are not a "homogenous
monolith." The Court reasoned that Article 341 is only for the
"identification" of castes; once identified, the State has the power
under Article 16(4) to "classify" them based on their actual degree of
backwardness. The judge noted that the "Creamy Layer" exclusion is now
applicable to SCs/STs to ensure that benefits reach the grass-roots.
However, the Court mandated that any sub-classification must be based on
objective, quantifiable empirical data and is subject to judicial
review.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Sub-classification. It
reinforces that Substantive Equality (Article 14 & 16) requires the
State to proactively identify and uplift the most marginalized within a
reserved category, effectively ending the legal fiction of SC/ST
homogeneity.

cases.title: Citizen Rights Union v. MeitY (Article 19(1)(a) & 21 - The AI Intermediary Rules, 2026)
cases.facts:
In February 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
(MeitY) notified the "IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Amendment Rules,
2026." These rules mandated that all social media platforms
(Intermediaries) remove "harmful synthetically generated information"
(Deepfakes) within two hours of a government or user notification.
Failure to comply would result in the immediate loss of "Safe Harbor"
protection (Section 79 IT Act). The rules also required the
"traceability" of the first originator of AI-generated content. A civil
rights union challenged these rules as an unconstitutional "prior
restraint" on speech.
cases.issues:
- Is a mandatory "two-hour takedown" window operationally realistic, or
does it incentivize "Defensive Censorship" by platforms, violating
Article 19(1)(a)?
- Does the "Traceability" mandate for AI content violate the fundamental
Right to Privacy (Article 21) as established in Puttaswamy?
Are the 2026 Rules ultra vires (beyond the powers of) the parent IT
Act, 2000?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Rights Union)
The Petitioners argued that two hours is insufficient for human review of
complex content. They contended this forces platforms to use "over-
blocking" algorithms that will stifle legitimate satire, parody, and
political dissent. Relying on Shreya Singhal, they argued that
"Traceability" breaks end-to-end encryption, creating a "Chilling Effect"
where citizens are afraid to use AI tools for creative expression due to
absolute state surveillance.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MeitY/Union of India)
The Government argued that deepfakes represent a "Clear and Present
Danger" to national security and women's dignity (non-consensual deepfake
pornography). They contended that in a viral digital environment, 24
hours is too long; a deepfake can destroy a reputation or spark a riot in
minutes. They argued that "Traceability" is a "reasonable restriction"
under Article 19(2) to combat coordinate misinformation campaigns and
foreign interference in elections.
cases.judgment:
The High Court issued an interim stay on the "Traceability" clause but
upheld the "Accelerated Takedown" window for "highly sensitive content"
(like deepfake nudity). The matter is pending final SC disposal. A split
verdict on immediate impact.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Algorithmic Accountability. The
judge ruled that while deepfakes are a lethal threat, the State cannot
mandate the destruction of digital privacy architecture for all citizens
to catch a few bad actors. However, regarding the takedown speed, the
Court applied the Doctrine of Proportionality. For "catastrophic
harms" (pornography, incitement to riot), a 2-hour window was deemed a
"Reasonable Restriction" given the technological capacity of major
platforms. The Court warned that the rules must not become a tool for the
"Executive Veto" over political parody.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Proportionality of Takedown Timelines. It
reinforces that Fundamental Rights apply to Synthetic Media and that
the State must balance the "Right to Reputation" (Article 21) with the
"Freedom of Expression" (Article 19).

cases.title: State of UP v. Lalta Prasad Vaish
cases.facts:
For decades, a jurisdictional battle raged between the Union and the
States over "Industrial Alcohol" (alcohol not fit for human consumption).
The Union argued it had exclusive power under Entry 52 of List I
(Industries in public interest), while States claimed power under Entry 8
of List II (Intoxicating liquors). In 2024, a nine-judge Constitution
Bench heard the matter to decide if States could regulate and tax
industrial alcohol, which is used for chemical processes but often
diverted for illegal drinking.
cases.issues:
- Does "Intoxicating Liquor" under Entry 8, List II include "Industrial
Alcohol," or is it limited only to potable alcohol?
- Does the Union's power to regulate "Industries" (Entry 52, List I) oust
the State's power to regulate the trade and production of alcohol within
its borders?
- How is the Doctrine of Pith and Substance applied to overlapping
entries in the Seventh Schedule?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The Union argued that "Industrial Alcohol" is a vital industrial raw
material. Under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951,
Parliament has "occupied the field." They contended that if every state
taxes industrial alcohol differently, it would destroy the national
chemical industry and violate the "Economic Unity of India" (Article
301).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State Governments)
The States argued that they bear the entire "Social Cost" of alcohol.
They contended that industrial alcohol is frequently diverted to make
"hooch" (spurious liquor), causing mass deaths. To prevent this, they
must have the power to regulate, track, and tax it. They argued that
Entry 8, List II is a specific entry that should prevail over the general
"Industries" entry of the Union.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (9-judge bench) ruled in favor of the States (8:1
majority). The Court held that States possess the power to regulate and
tax industrial alcohol. The Respondent prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Federalism. The judge ruled that
the Constitution must be interpreted to preserve State Autonomy. The
Court reasoning was that "Intoxicating Liquors" is a broad term that
encompasses all liquids containing alcohol. The judge ruled that the
Union's power under Entry 52, List I is not absolute; it cannot be used
to "usurp" specific powers granted to States. The Court held that the
"Pith and Substance" of the State's power was to control a substance that
has direct impacts on public health and order, which are primary State
responsibilities.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Federal Supremacy in State
Spheres. It establishes that State legislative powers are not
subordinate to the Union's industrial policy, protecting the fiscal and
regulatory autonomy of States under the Basic Structure of
Federalism.

cases.title: ADR v. Union of India (Article 19(1)(a) - The Electoral Bonds Case, 2024)
cases.facts:
In 2018, the Government introduced "Electoral Bonds," allowing
individuals and corporations to donate unlimited money to political
parties anonymously through the State Bank of India. The Association for
Democratic Reforms (ADR) challenged the scheme, arguing that anonymizing
political funding prevents voters from knowing who is "buying" political
influence, thereby violating the "Right to Know" under Article 19(1)(a).
cases.issues:
- Does the "Right to Know" under Article 19(1)(a) include the right to
know the source of funding of political parties?
- Can the State use the "Right to Privacy" of the donor as a ground to
restrict the "Right to Information" of the voter?
- Does the scheme fail the Proportionality Test for restricting
fundamental rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (ADR)
The Petitioners argued that "Free and Fair Elections" are a basic feature
of the Constitution. Democracy requires an "informed electorate." They
contended that the scheme allows for a "quid pro quo" between
corporations and the ruling party, and by hiding these transactions, the
State is institutionalizing corruption. They argued the donor's privacy
(Article 21) cannot override the voter's right to information (Article
19).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the scheme was intended to "curb black money"
in politics by moving donations into the banking system. They contended
that donors have a "Right to Confidentiality" to prevent political
victimization by rival parties. They argued that the public interest in
clean funding justified the restriction on information.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in favor of ADR. The Court struck
down the Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional and ordered the
disclosure of all bond data. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Transparency in Democracy.
The judge ruled that the "Right to Know" is a prerequisite for a
functioning democracy. The Court rejected the "privacy" argument, stating
that a corporation donating massive sums to a political party is a
"political act," not a private one.

The judge applied the Proportionality Test: While curbing black money
is a legitimate goal, providing absolute anonymity to donors is a
disproportionate measure that destroys the voter's right to information.
The Court famously noted that the "Right to Privacy" does not extend to
"buying policy" through anonymous donations. The scheme was deemed to
have created an "Information Asymmetry" that favored the ruling party.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Right to Information of the Voter as a
fundamental right. It establishes the legal principle that Corporate
and Political Transparency is essential to the Basic Structure of Free
and Fair Elections.

cases.title: Bilkis Bano v. Union of India
cases.facts:
In 2022, the State of Gujarat granted "remission" (early release) to 11
convicts sentenced to life imprisonment for the gang rape of Bilkis Bano
and the murder of her family during the 2002 riots. The remission was
challenged in the Supreme Court. The convicts had been sentenced by a
court in Maharashtra, but the Gujarat government granted remission based
on a 2022 Supreme Court order (obtained by one convict by suppressing
facts) that directed Gujarat to consider the application.
cases.issues:
- Which State government has the "Competent Jurisdiction" to grant
remission to a prisoner-the state where the crime occurred or the state
where the trial was held?
- Can the "Right to Liberty" of a convict (Article 21) be revoked if the
remission was obtained through "Fraud on the Court"?
- Does the State's power of remission violate the victim's "Right to
Justice" under Article 21?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Bilkis Bano)
The Petitioner argued that under the CrPC, the "Appropriate Government"
for remission is the government of the state where the trial took place
(Maharashtra). They contended that the Gujarat government acted ultra
vires and in "tandem" with the convicts. They argued that releasing
brutal gang-rapists after only 14 years, without considering the impact
on the victim, is a violation of the "Rule of Law."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Gujarat &
Convicts)
The Defendants argued that the convicts had spent 14 years in jail and
were eligible for rehabilitation. They relied on the 1992 Remission
Policy of Gujarat. They contended that since the Supreme Court had
previously directed Gujarat to hear the matter, the State was merely
following a judicial mandate.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bilkis Bano. The Court quashed the
remission order and directed the convicts to surrender and return to jail
within two weeks. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a scathing judgment on Procedural Integrity. The
judge ruled that the Gujarat government was "usurping" the power of the
Maharashtra government. The Court famously declared that "Fraud and
Justice never dwell together." Because the convicts had obtained the
previous SC order by suppressing the fact that the Maharashtra court had
sentenced them, the entire basis of the remission was void. The Court
held that the Rule of Law requires that even the State must act
within the strict boundaries of its jurisdiction. The judge noted that
the State of Gujarat acted in bad faith by not filing a review against
the earlier incorrect SC direction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Rule of Law. It establishes that the
"Appropriate Government" for remission is strictly the State where the
trial was concluded, and that any state action founded on "Fraud on
the Court" is a nullity.

cases.title: Ananya v. The Online Gaming Authority (Article 19(1)(g) vs. Public Morality)
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Parliament passed the "Promotion and Regulation of Online
Gaming Act," which imposed a 28% GST on the full face value of bets and
allowed the government to block any game it deemed "addictive" or
"harmful to youth." Ananya, a professional E-sports player and game
developer, challenged the Act. She argued that classifying "Games of
Skill" (like Rummy or Fantasy Cricket) alongside "Gambling" violated her
right to trade under Article 19(1)(g).
cases.issues:
- Does the high taxation and the "Subjective Veto" of the government over
online games constitute an "Unreasonable Restriction" under Article
19(6)?
- Is there a Constitutional distinction between "Games of Skill" and
"Games of Chance" (Gambling)?
- Can "Public Morality" be used to ban a legitimate digital trade?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ananya)
The Petitioner relied on the K.R. Lakshmanan (Horse Racing) judgment.
She argued that "Games of Skill" are a protected trade. Imposing
"punitive taxation" and granting the executive the power to block games
without a clear definition of "addiction" is "Manifestly Arbitrary" under
Article 14. She contended that e-sports is a global industry and the
State's "Paternalistic Morality" is destroying the digital economy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that online gaming is a "res extra commercium"
(activity outside commerce) similar to alcohol or lottery. They presented
data on "digital debt" and suicides among youth due to gaming addiction.
They contended that under the Directive Principles (Article 47), the
State has a duty to protect public health and that high taxes are a "Sin
Tax" meant to discourage harmful behavior.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Ananya regarding the skill-based
distinction. The Court struck down the "Addiction Veto" but upheld the
tax. The Plaintiff partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Economic Rights in the Digital Age.
The judge ruled that the Constitution recognizes the distinction between
Skill and Chance. A game where a player's knowledge and strategy
predominate is a legitimate trade protected under Article 19(1)(g). The
Court ruled that "Public Morality" is a subjective concept and cannot be
used to grant the executive "Unfettered Discretion" to block businesses.
However, the Court upheld the GST, stating that the "Power to Tax" is a
sovereign legislative function and courts will not interfere with the
quantum of tax unless it is "Confiscatory" (so high it destroys the
business entirely).
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Predominance of Skill Test. It establishes
that the State cannot treat legitimate digital E-sports as illegal
gambling and that regulatory restrictions must be "Narrowly Tailored"
to avoid violating the Freedom of Trade.

cases.title: State of Karnataka v. The Metaverse Trust
cases.facts:
A religious organization created a "Virtual Temple" in the Metaverse
where devotees could perform Darshan and Aarti using VR headsets. The
State Government passed a law prohibiting the collection of "Digital
Donations" for virtual religious acts, arguing that religious practices
must be physical and traditional to be protected. The Trust challenged
the law, arguing that "Freedom of Religion" (Article 25) is technology-
neutral and that they have the right to manage their religious affairs
(Article 26) in any medium.
cases.issues:
- Does Article 25 protect the "Right to Worship" in a purely virtual or
digital environment?
- Can the State regulate "Digital Rituals" as "Secular Activities" under
Article 25(2)(a)?
- Is a "Virtual Temple" a "Religious Denomination" under Article 26?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Metaverse Trust)
The Petitioners argued that faith resides in the mind, not just the body.
For homebound or disabled devotees, the Metaverse provides the only way
to exercise their Article 25 rights. They contended that "Darshan" is a
spiritual experience that is equally valid in VR. They argued that the
collection of donations is an "Essential Religious Practice" to maintain
the digital infrastructure, and the State's ban was an act of "Digital
Persecution."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State)
The State argued that religion is an inherently physical and communal
social activity. They contended that "Virtual Rituals" are a commercial
simulation, not a religious practice. They relied on Article 25(2)(a),
arguing that the financial transactions (donations) in the Metaverse are
a "Secular Activity" which the State can regulate to prevent money
laundering and cyber-fraud.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the Metaverse Trust. The Court struck
down the ban on digital donations. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a visionary judgment on Technological Neutrality of
Rights. The judge ruled that Fundamental Rights do not evaporate in
Cyberspace. If a community recognizes a digital space as sacred, the
State has no right to declare it "invalid." The judge reasoned that
Article 25 protects the "conscience" of the individual. If an individual
feels a spiritual connection through VR, it is a protected religious act.
The Court held that while the State can regulate the manner of
donations (to prevent fraud), it cannot "Prohibit" them, as that would
selectively penalize a new form of worship, violating the Secular
neutrality of the State.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Digital Religious Freedom. It
reinforces that Fundamental Rights are evolving and medium-
independent, and that the State must respect the "Essential Religious
Practices" of a community even when they are performed in virtual
environments.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Climate Justice Collective
cases.facts:
In the summer of 2025, a record-breaking heatwave caused 5,000 deaths in
north India. The "Climate Justice Collective" filed a PIL, arguing that
the State's failure to provide "Heat-Resilient Infrastructure" (cooling
centers, green roofs, and water access) and its continued approval of
deforestation projects was a direct violation of the Right to Life
under Article 21. They demanded the Court recognize the "Right to a
Survivable Temperature" as a fundamental right.
cases.issues:
- Does the "Right to Life" (Article 21) include a positive obligation on
the State to mitigate the impacts of extreme climate events like
heatwaves?
- Can the "Precautionary Principle" be used to compel the State to spend
massive public funds on "Climate Adaptation"?
- Is the State's failure to regulate carbon-heavy industries a violation
of the fundamental rights of its citizens?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Collective)
The Petitioners relied on the M.K. Ranjitsinh judgment (2024), where
the SC recognized the right against adverse climate change. They argued
that "bare survival" is impossible at 50°C. The State's "Heat Action
Plans" were mere paper documents with no funding. They contended that
under the Public Trust Doctrine, the State must protect the
"Atmospheric Commons" and has a duty to ensure that urban environments
remain habitable for the poor who cannot afford air conditioning.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that climate change is a global phenomenon. No
single State can "guarantee" a temperature. They contended that "Climate
Adaptation" is a matter of broad policy and budgetary allocation, which
is a non-justiciable executive function. They argued that the Court
should not act as a "Super-Legislature" by mandating specific
infrastructure projects.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Collective. The Court formally
recognized the "Right to Survivable Habitats" and issued mandatory
guidelines for "National Heat-Stress Mitigation." The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on Human Rights in the
Anthropocene. The judge ruled that Article 21 is a "Dynamic Right" that
must respond to the existential threat of the 21st century.

The judge reasoned that the State has a Positive Duty to protect its
citizens from foreseeable environmental disasters. If the State knows
that 50°C heat is coming and fails to provide "Cooling Infrastructure,"
it is a "State-sponsored violation of the Right to Life." The Court held
that Environmental Justice is inextricable from Social Justice. The
judge famously remarked, "A Constitution that cannot protect a citizen
from the burning sun is a failing document." The Court ordered the
creation of a "Climate Compensation Fund" for victims of extreme weather
events.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Fundamental Right to Survivable Habitats. It
establishes the legal principle that Climate Change Mitigation is a
Constitutional Mandate, reading the Directive Principles (Article 48A)
into the Right to Life (Article 21).

cases.title: Association of Retired Judges v. State of UP
cases.facts:
In 2024, the State Government of UP issued a summons to several retired
and sitting High Court judges to appear before a legislative committee to
explain certain "administrative delays" in the court system. During the
hearing, government officials made disparaging oral comments about the
judges' efficiency. The Association of Retired Judges filed a writ
petition, arguing that the executive has no power to "harass" or
"intimidate" the judiciary under the guise of accountability.
cases.issues:
- Does the summoning of judges by the executive violate the
Independence of the Judiciary, which is a part of the Basic
Structure?
- Can the executive branch "Audit" the performance of the judicial branch
under the concept of "Checks and Balances"?
- What is the scope of Article 235 (Control over subordinate courts)
regarding executive interference?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Judges)
The Petitioners relied on the All India Judges Association case. They
argued that the judiciary must be "Insulated" from the executive.
Summoning judges to a legislative committee creates a "Master-Servant"
hierarchy that destroys the "Separation of Powers." They contended that
"Administrative Control" over the courts belongs exclusively to the High
Courts and Supreme Court, not the State Government.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of UP)
The State argued that "No branch is above the law." They contended that
because the State funds the judicial infrastructure, the legislature has
a right to "Audit" how public money is being spent and why cases are
delayed. They argued that "Judicial Accountability" is essential for
democracy and that judges are "Public Servants" under the law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Judges. The Court issued strict
guidelines (2024) prohibiting the "casual summoning" of government
officials and judges by the executive. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive ruling on Inter-Branch Comity. The
judge ruled that the Independence of the Judiciary is a "Basic
Feature" that cannot be diluted by executive "Audit."

The judge reasoned that while accountability is vital, it must be
"Internal." The High Courts have the power of "Superintendence" under
Article 227. The executive cannot use the "Power of the Purse" (funding)
to exert "Power over the Person" (judges). The Court held that oral
comments disparaging judges "chills" judicial bravery. The judge noted
that the executive should use affidavits and documents to seek
information, rather than demanding physical appearance, to preserve the
"Dignity of the Office."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Separation of Powers. It establishes the
legal principle that the Judiciary is not answerable to the Executive
for its administrative or judicial functions, safeguarding the Basic
Structure from executive overreach.

cases.title: The Privacy Collective v. The Biometric Border Force
cases.facts:
In 2025, the Border Security Force (BSF) implemented a mandatory "DNA-at-
the-Border" policy for all individuals entering India from "high-risk"
neighboring countries. The BSF argued this was necessary to prevent
"Illegal Infiltration" and to build a "Terrorist DNA Database." A privacy
collective challenged the policy, arguing that the forced extraction of
DNA from millions of travelers, without any suspicion of a crime, was a
violation of the Right to Bodily Autonomy and Informational
Privacy under Article 21.
cases.issues:
- Does the "Right to Privacy" (Article 21) include an absolute "Right
to Genetic Privacy"?
- Can "National Security" be used as a blanket justification for the mass
collection of biological data from non-suspects?
- Does the policy violate the "Presumption of Innocence" and Article 14
(Equality) by targeting specific nationalities?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Collective)
The Petitioners relied on the Selvi and Puttaswamy judgments. They
argued that DNA is the "Blueprint of the Soul." Forced extraction is an
"Intrusive Search" of the body. They contended that "Mass Surveillance"
of genetic data is inherently disproportionate. By targeting specific
nationalities, the State was practicing "Racial/National Profiling,"
which is a "Manifestly Arbitrary" classification under Article 14.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (BSF/Union of India)
The State argued that "Sovereignty" includes the right to decide who
enters the country. They contended that "Biometric Warfare" is a real
threat and that DNA is the only "Unforgeable ID." They argued that
travelers have a "Reduced Expectation of Privacy" at international
borders and that the data would be deleted after 10 years if no criminal
match was found.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Privacy Collective. The Court
struck down the "Mass DNA" policy, allowing only "Targeted DNA"
collection based on individual suspicion. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a seminal judgment on Biological Integrity. The
judge ruled that the "Human Genome" is the ultimate private property.

The judge applied the Proportionality Test: While "Border Security"
is a compelling aim, the "Mass Collection" of DNA from innocent travelers
is "Draconian." The Court held that the State cannot treat every traveler
as a "Potential Terrorist." The judge reasoned that DNA reveals not just
the person, but their entire family lineage, violating the privacy of
millions not even present at the border. The Court ruled that "Targeted
Collection" (with a warrant or individualized suspicion) is the "Least
Restrictive Means" to achieve security. The judge famously stated, "The
Border is not a Lawless Zone where the Constitution stops breathing."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Fundamental Right to Genetic Privacy under
Article 21. It reinforces that State Surveillance must be Targeted
and Proportional, preventing the creation of a "Genetic Panopticon"
under the guise of National Security.

cases.title: State of Uttar Pradesh v. The Residents
cases.facts:
In 2024 and 2025, state authorities in various jurisdictions utilized
heavy machinery to demolish the residential and commercial properties of
individuals accused of participating in riots or serious crimes, often
within 24 hours of the alleged offense. The State argued these were
"encroachment clearances." However, no prior judicial hearing was
granted, and the demolitions targeted specific individuals before any
criminal conviction. A batch of petitions challenged this practice. In
late 2024 and early 2025, the Supreme Court delivered a definitive ruling
on "Bulldozer Justice."
cases.issues:
- Does the summary demolition of property as a punitive measure against
an "accused" violate the fundamental Right to Shelter under Article
21?
- Does "Bulldozer Justice" bypass the Presumption of Innocence and
the Separation of Powers?
- Can administrative "satisfaction" regarding encroachments override the
constitutional right to property under Article 300A without due process?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Aggrieved Residents)
The Petitioners argued that the State cannot act as judge, jury, and
executioner. Relying on Olga Tellis, they argued the Right to Shelter
is a facet of Article 21. Summary demolitions serve as extra-judicial
punishment, violating the Rule of Law. They argued that even if an
encroachment exists, the State must provide a reasonable notice and a
fair hearing before deprivation of property (Article 300A).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State Authorities)
The State argued they were simply enforcing municipal laws and removing
illegal structures built on public land. They contended that the "timing"
of the demolitions (following a crime) was coincidental to administrative
drives. They argued that "encroachers" have no vested right to a home
built on stolen land.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Residents. The Court declared
summary punitive demolitions unconstitutional, established mandatory
guidelines requiring 15 days' notice and a personal hearing, and held
that officials who violate these rules face personal financial liability.
The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Substantive Due Process. The
judge ruled that the "Power of the State" must be exercised within the
"Boundaries of the Law." The Court reasoned that using a bulldozer to
punish a person for a crime not yet proven in court is a "Direct Assault"
on the Separation of Powers. The judge held that the "Right to a Home" is
essential to human dignity and that the State cannot bypass the judiciary
to administer instant, elective justice. The Court established that
"Administrative Efficiency" is no excuse for "Constitutional Barbarism."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case enshrines the Doctrine of Accountability for State Action.
It establishes that due process is a prerequisite for property
deprivation, and that the State cannot use municipal laws as a cloak
for extra-judicial punitive measures.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Digital Rights Alliance
cases.facts:
In late 2024, the Supreme Court heard a case where a trial court had
imposed a bail condition requiring an accused (a foreign national) to
"drop a pin" on Google Maps continuously for the police to monitor his
real-time location. The Alliance challenged this, arguing it amounted to
"digital shackling."
cases.issues:
- Does a bail condition mandating continuous electronic surveillance
violate the Right to Privacy under Article 21?
- Can the State use technology to convert "Liberty on Bail" into "Virtual
Confinement"?
Does the Puttaswamy proportionality test apply to judicial orders in
criminal procedure?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Alliance)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 protects the privacy of the
accused. Constant tracking is a form of "surveillance" that destroys the
dignity of an individual. They contended that less intrusive means (like
periodic check-ins at a police station) were sufficient and that "Digital
Shackling" was a disproportionate restriction on movement (Article 19).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that the accused was a flight risk and a foreign
national. Technology provides a "middle path" between jail and absolute
freedom. They contended that the accused "consented" to the tracking in
exchange for his release on bail.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Alliance. The Court struck down
the "Google Maps Pin" condition as unconstitutional. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court ruled that Bail is for ensuring presence at trial, not for
continuous surveillance. The judge reasoned that privacy is an
"inalienable right" that does not evaporate just because a person is an
accused. The Court held that "Constant Tracking" via Google Maps is a
"profound intrusion" that fails the proportionality test. The judge noted
that technology should facilitate liberty, not create a "Digital
Panopticon" for undertrials.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes that Bail Conditions must be Proportional. It
reinforces that Article 21 protects an accused from intrusive digital
surveillance and that judicial discretion cannot override the
fundamental right to privacy.

cases.title: All India Judges Association v. Union of India, 2025
cases.facts:
In 2025, a Constitution Bench decided a dispute regarding whether serving
judicial officers (Civil Judges) can apply for the post of District Judge
through "direct recruitment" (reserved for advocates with 7 years of
practice) without resigning from their current posts.
cases.issues:
- Does Article 233(2) exclude serving judicial officers from the
"Advocate" category for direct recruitment?
- Can the State create a "Bar" between the lower judiciary and the higher
judicial services?
- Does the combined experience of Bar and Bench satisfy the "7 years"
requirement?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Judicial Officers)
The Petitioners argued that a Civil Judge is also a legally trained
professional. They contended that "resigning to apply" is a
discriminatory and irrational hurdle that deprives the District Court of
experienced talent. They argued for a purposive interpretation of Article
233 to include those with Bar + Bench experience.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (High Courts/Bar)
The Bar argued that the "Direct Recruitment" quota is specifically
designed to bring "fresh blood" and independent perspectives from the Bar
into the judiciary. They contended that allowing Civil Judges to compete
in this quota would lead to a "Service Monopoly" and destroy the
incentive for senior advocates to join the bench.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled that judicial officers with previous Bar
experience are eligible for direct recruitment. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court interpreted Article 233 as a Complete Code. The judge ruled
that the Constitution does not intend to penalize those who join the
lower judiciary. The Court held that if a person had 7 years of combined
experience, they are eligible. The reasoning focused on Institutional
Excellence-the judiciary needs the best minds, whether they come
directly from the Bar or have served in the lower ranks.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Judicial Independence and Career Mobility. It
establishes that the "Advocate" requirement in Article 233 includes the
cumulative experience of legal practice and judicial service.

cases.title: The State of Maharashtra v. The Transgender Union
cases.facts:
In March 2026, Parliament passed the "Transgender Persons (Protection of
Rights) Amendment Act, 2026." The Act replaced the "Self-Identification"
model (from the NALSA judgment) with a "Medical Certification"
model. A transgender person now requires a certificate from a District
Magistrate based on a medical board's assessment to be legally
recognized. The Union challenged this as "Decolonization in Reverse."
cases.issues:
- Does mandatory medical certification for gender identity violate the
Right to Self-Determination under Article 21?
- Does the Act's "closed list" of socio-cultural identities (hijra,
kinner, etc.) violate the right to equality under Article 14 by excluding
trans-men and non-binary persons?
- Can the State use the "Rationale of the 1871 Criminal Tribes Act" to
surveil gender non-conforming communities?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Transgender Union)
The Petitioners argued that "Identity resides in the mind, not the
anatomy." Relying on NALSA, they argued that forcing a person to
undergo a medical exam to prove their gender is a "Violent Intrusion"
into privacy. They contended the Act was "Over-inclusive and Under-
inclusive," effectively erasing millions of trans-identities not on the
"Closed List."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that certification is necessary to prevent the
"Misuse of Welfare Benefits." They contended that "Objective Criteria"
are required for state-sponsored affirmative action and that the medical
board ensures the "Biological Integrity" of the classification.
cases.judgment:
The High Court issued a stay on the "Medical Filter" provision, pending a
Supreme Court review. A landmark verdict is expected in late 2026.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered an interim ruling on Human Dignity. The judge
noted that the State cannot reach into the "most intimate layer of a
person's self-knowledge." The Court reasoned that a protection regime
that "erases more identities than it recognizes" fails the test of
Article 14. The judge remarked that the NALSA principles are part of
the "Soul of the Constitution" and cannot be amended away by executive
suspicion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reasserts the Right to Gender Identity as a Fundamental
Right. It establishes that Self-Identification is a facet of Articles
14, 15, 19, and 21, and any state-imposed medical filter is prima
facie unconstitutional.

cases.title: The Opposition Parties v. The Union of India
cases.facts:
In April 2026, the Government introduced the 131st Constitutional
Amendment Bill to increase the Lok Sabha strength to 850 seats and
implement 33% women's reservation immediately, using 2011 Census data.
Southern states challenged the Bill, arguing that redrawing boundaries
based on old or unadjusted population data would "punish" states that
successfully implemented family planning, violating the Basic Structure
of Federalism.
cases.issues:
- Does redrawing electoral boundaries based on population (Article 82)
without a recent census violate the Principle of Equal
Representation?
- Can a constitutional amendment alter the "Federal Equilibrium" to favor
more populous states?
- Does the immediate implementation of Women's Reservation bypass the
"Post-2026 Census" requirement originally mandated in the Nari Shakti
Vandan Adhiniyam?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Southern States)
The Petitioners argued that "Democracy is not just about numbers; it's
about Federal Comity." They contended that the 131st Amendment would
reduce their political voice in the Union. Relying on the Kuldip Nayar
case, they argued that the "Federal Balance" is a basic feature that
cannot be destroyed by a population-based seats-grab.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that "One Person, One Vote" is the core of Article
14. They contended that a citizen in Uttar Pradesh should not have a
"weaker vote" than a citizen in Tamil Nadu. The seat expansion was a
"Democratic Necessity" to manage the massive increase in the electorate
since 1971.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court has referred the matter to a 9-Judge Bench. An interim
order allows the seat expansion but mandates a "Federal Compensation
Formula."
cases.reasoning:
The Court explored the Conflict between Individual Equality (Article
14) and Federal Equality. The judge noted that the "Constitutional
Freeze" on delimitation was an "Accord" between states. Breaking that
accord without a new census is a "High-Stakes Constitutional Gamble." The
judge reasoned that "Representation" must be balanced with "Stability."
The Court held that the 131st Amendment must provide "Weightage" to
states that have achieved national goals (like health and education) to
prevent a "Tyranny of Numbers."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Federal Equity. It reinforces
that Federalism (Basic Structure) protects States from being
politically marginalized due to demographic success, and that
Delimitation is subject to "Constitutional Fair-Play."

cases.title: Sita Soren v. Union of India, 2024
cases.facts:
A seven-judge bench in 2024 revisited the 1998 P.V. Narasimha Rao
judgment. The issue was whether legislators enjoy absolute immunity from
criminal prosecution for taking bribes to vote or speak in a certain way
in the House.
cases.issues:
- Does the immunity under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) protect a legislator
who accepts a bribe to influence their conduct in Parliament/Assembly?
- Is the "Act of Bribery" distinct from the "Act of Voting/Speaking"?
- Does granting immunity for corruption violate the Basic Structure of
Parliamentary Democracy?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Central Bureau of
Investigation)
The CBI argued that "Corruption is not a Privilege." They contended that
the immunity was meant to protect "Freedom of Speech," not "Freedom of
Sale." Bribery is a criminal act that is complete the moment the money is
taken, regardless of whether the speech is later delivered.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Accused Legislators)
The Defendants relied on the literal text: "No member shall be liable to
any proceedings... in respect of anything said or any vote given." They
argued that any inquiry into "why" they voted a certain way would allow
the Executive to harass the Legislature, destroying the Independence of
the House.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in favor of the Union/CBI. The Court
overruled the 1998 judgment, declaring that bribery is not protected by
legislative immunity. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Constitutional Morality. The
judge ruled that "Privilege is not an exemption from the general
law." The reasoning was that bribery "subverts the very foundation of
democracy." The Court held that the "nexus" between the bribe and the
speech does not make the bribe a "protected act." The judge famously
stated, "The Constitution does not create a class of citizens who are
above the law." Immunity extends only to acts indispensable to the
legislative function; taking a bribe is not indispensable-it is
parasitic.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reasserts the Supremacy of the Rule of Law over Parliamentary
Privilege. It establishes that bribery is a separate criminal offense
not covered by Articles 105 or 194, protecting the integrity of the
democratic process.

cases.title: In re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955
cases.facts:
Section 6A was added to the Citizenship Act following the 1985 Assam
Accord. it granted citizenship to migrants who entered Assam from
Bangladesh between 1966 and 1971. Petitioners challenged this as
discriminatory, arguing it singled out Assam and violated the "Right to
Culture" (Article 29) of indigenous people by enabling illegal migration.
cases.issues:
- Does Section 6A violate Article 14 by creating a "State-Specific"
citizenship rule that is different for the rest of India?
- Does the "Demographic Alteration" caused by Section 6A infringe upon
the fundamental right of indigenous citizens to "Conserve their Culture"
under Article 29?
- Is the Parliament's power to regulate citizenship (Article 11)
absolute?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Indigenous Groups)
The Petitioners argued that Assam was being treated as a "dumping ground"
for migrants. They contended that Article 14 requires a "Uniform Law" for
citizenship. They provided data on the loss of linguistic and political
dominance of the indigenous Assamese people, claiming Section 6A was a
"Constitutional Breach of Trust."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that Section 6A was a "Political Settlement" to end
a decade of ethnic violence. They contended that "Reasonable
Classification" (Article 14) allows for state-specific rules based on
"Historical Necessity." Parliament has the plenary power to define who is
a citizen.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (5-judge bench) ruled in favor of the Union. The Court
upheld Section 6A as constitutionally valid. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Constitutional Pragmatism. The
judge ruled that the "Assam Accord" was a unique response to a unique
crisis. The Court reasoned that Article 14 does not mandate "Uniformity"
but "Rationality." Singling out Assam was rational because the migration
crisis was specific to that border. The Court held that while Article 29
protects culture, it does not grant a "Veto" over the State's power to
manage borders and citizenship. The judge noted that striking down 6A
after 40 years would create millions of "Stateless Persons," which is a
humanitarian catastrophe.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Parliament's Plenary Power over Citizenship
(Article 11). It establishes that state-specific legislative
classifications are valid if they have a rational nexus to a historical
or geopolitical objective, and that "Political Necessity" can justify
departures from uniform laws.

cases.title: Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL, 2024
cases.facts:
A nine-judge bench in 2024 decided whether "Royalty" paid by mining
companies to the State is a "Tax" and whether States have the power to
tax mineral rights. The Union argued that mineral regulation belongs
exclusively to Parliament under Entry 54, List I.
cases.issues:
- Is "Royalty" a "Tax" under the Constitution?
- Do States have the power to levy taxes on "Mineral Rights" under Entry
50, List II?
- Can the Union use "Regulation" to "Oust" the State's power of taxation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State Governments)
The States argued that "Fiscal Autonomy" is a part of Federalism. They
contended that Royalty is a contractual payment, while Tax is a sovereign
levy. They argued that Entry 50, List II explicitly gives them the power
to tax mineral rights, and the Union cannot "silently steal" this power.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India & Mining
Corps)
The Union argued that if every state taxes minerals differently, the
"National Economy" and "Industrial Development" would collapse. They
relied on the Doctrine of Occupied Field, arguing that the MMDR Act
(a Central law) had already taken over the entire domain of minerals.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (9-judge bench) ruled in favor of the States. The Court
held that Royalty is NOT a tax and that States do have the power to tax
mineral rights. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive ruling on Fiscal Federalism. The
judge ruled that the power to tax is an "Independent Power" that cannot
be taken away by mere "Regulation." The Court reasoned that "Royalty" is
a payment for the use of the land, while "Tax" is for the benefit of the
State exchequer. The judge held that federalism requires that States have
their own "Sources of Revenue" to fulfill their duties under the
Directive Principles.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Supremacy of the State's Power to Tax in its
own list. It clarifies the distinction between Royalty and Tax and
prevents the "Centralization of Fiscal Power" through the backdoor of
industrial regulation.

cases.title: Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft, 2025
cases.facts:
In 2025, a five-judge bench decided whether courts have the power to
"Modify" an arbitral award (change the amount) or if they can only "Set
Aside" (cancel) the award in toto. This has huge implications for the
"Ease of Doing Business" in India.
cases.issues:
- Does the power to "Set Aside" an award include the power to "Correct"
or "Modify" it?
- Does a "Zero-Modification" rule violate the Right to Justice
(Article 21) by forcing parties back to square one?
- Can the Supreme Court use Article 142 to modify awards while lower
courts cannot?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Pro-Modification)
The Petitioner argued that if a judge finds a mathematical error or a
small illegality, cancelling the entire award leads to "Endless
Litigation." They contended that "Justice" requires the power to fix the
error and finalize the dispute.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Anti-Modification)
The Respondent argued that Arbitration is a "Private Contract." If judges
begin changing the amounts awarded by arbitrators, the "Finality of
Arbitration" is destroyed, and the system becomes just another layer of
the court system.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled that while Courts under Section 34 generally
cannot modify awards, the Appellate Courts possess a limited power to
"Vary" or "Sever" specific portions. The Plaintiff partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Pragmatic Justice. The judge ruled
that a "Complete Reset" of a 10-year arbitration because of a minor error
is "Unjust." The judge reasoned that the "Power of Severance" allows a
court to remove the "bad part" and keep the "good part." The Court held
that Articles 136 and 142 allow the SC to do "Complete Justice," ensuring
that India becomes a "Global Arbitration Hub" by providing finality to
commercial disputes.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of Severability in Arbitral
Awards. It reinforces that the judiciary is a partner in
arbitration, not just a supervisor, and that "Procedural Fairness"
includes "Economic Efficiency."

cases.title: Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal, 2024
cases.facts:
A seven-judge bench in 2024 revisited the 1967 Aziz Basha judgment to
determine if Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) can be classified as a
"Minority Institution" despite being established by a Central Act of
Parliament.
cases.issues:
- Does the "Establishment by Statute" automatically strip an institution
of its minority character under Article 30?
- What is the "Test of Establishment"-is it the source of funds, the
administrative control, or the legislative act?
- Can the State regulate the admission policy of a minority institution
that receives 100% state funding?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (AMU)
The University argued that the "Founding Spirit" and the "Soul of the
Institution" were Muslim. They contended that Article 30 protects the
right to "Establish and Administer." The Central Act was merely a legal
"Recognition" of their existing institution. They argued that "Funding"
does not destroy "Minority Status."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that AMU is a "National Institution" created by a
"Sovereign Act." They contended that once an institution is established
by a law of Parliament, it belongs to the nation, not a community. They
relied on Aziz Basha, stating that a minority cannot "establish" a
University through a public statute.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (7-judge bench) ruled that Minority Status is a
matter of factual inquiry, not just a statutory label. The Aziz Basha
logic was significantly diluted. The matter was referred to a regular
bench for a final factual determination.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Substantive Minority Rights. The
judge ruled that the "Source of the Idea" and the "Effort of the
Community" are more important than the "Legislative Seal." The Court
reasoned that Article 30 would be a "Dead Letter" if the State could take
over an institution simply by passing a law to "recognize" it. The judge
held that the Right to Administer is the core of Article 30, and
state funding is a welfare measure that does not extinguish fundamental
rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Purposeful Test for Minority Institutions.
It reinforces that Article 30 protects the "Community Character" of an
institution, even if it operates under a state statute, provided its
"Genesis" was minority-led.

cases.title: Harish Rana v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
Harish Rana, a 32-year-old man, had been in a Persistent Vegetative State
(PVS) for 13 years following a catastrophic accident. He had no cognitive
function and was kept alive solely through Clinically Assisted Nutrition
and Hydration (CANH). His parents, witnessing his prolonged state of
"biological existence" without quality of life, approached the court
seeking the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. This was the first
major test of the guidelines laid down in the Common Cause (2018)
judgment in a non-terminal but irreversible PVS scenario.
cases.issues:
- Is Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH) considered
"medical treatment" that can be legally withdrawn?
- Does the Right to Die with Dignity under Article 21 extend to
individuals who have not left an "Advance Medical Directive" but are in a
permanent vegetative state?
- How should the Court determine the "Best Interest" of a patient who is
unable to signify consent?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Parents of Harish)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 protects the right to a "Dignified
Life," which inherently includes a "Dignified Death." They contended that
Harish was in a state of "perpetual suffering" and that keeping his body
alive mechanically for over a decade was a violation of his human
dignity. They argued that CANH is a medical intervention, not a natural
process, and the family, as his natural guardians, should have the right
to choose the withdrawal of such treatment in his best interest.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State/Medical Board)
The State argued the "Sanctity of Life" principle. They contended that
Harish was not "brain dead" and was breathing spontaneously. Therefore,
withdrawing nutrition would be an act of intentional killing (homicide).
They argued that in the absence of a Living Will, the State must act as
the ultimate protector of life (Parens Patriae) and cannot authorize
the starvation of a citizen.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (2026) ruled in favor of the Parents. The Court
permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment (CANH),
marking a historic first for passive euthanasia in a PVS case in India.
The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Dignity of the Human Spirit.
The judge ruled that artificial nutrition and hydration are "medical
treatments," not basic care like washing or holding a hand. The Court
reasoned that keeping a person in a "biological limbo" for 13 years
against the reality of zero neurological recovery is "cruel and unusual."
The judge held that when a patient is in an irreversible PVS, their "Best
Interest" lies in being allowed to pass away with peace and dignity
rather than being subjected to the "tyranny of technology."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Right to Passive Euthanasia (Article 21). It
establishes that artificial nutrition is a medical intervention that
can be withheld or withdrawn in the best interest of a PVS patient,
even without a prior Advance Directive.

cases.title: Transgender Rights Alliance v. Union of India
cases.facts:
In early 2026, Parliament passed the "Transgender Persons (Protection of
Rights) Amendment Act." The amendment replaced the open-ended, self-
identification model with a "categorical and exhaustive list" of socio-
cultural identities (e.g., Hijra, Kinner) and mandated medical board
examinations for legal recognition. Trans men and non-binary individuals,
not belonging to these traditional communities, found themselves legally
erased. A petition was filed on April 21, 2026, challenging the Act as a
"prejudice of visibility" encoded in statute.
cases.issues:
- Does the legislative erasure of trans men and non-binary identities
from the statutory definition of "transgender" violate the right to
Equality (Article 14)?
- Does mandatory medical certification violate the Right to Self-
Perceived Gender Identity recognized in NALSA?
- Is "Visibility" a valid constitutional ground for granting or denying
fundamental rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Alliance)
The Petitioners argued that the 2026 Act systematically dismantles the
NALSA mandate. They contended that "Identity resides in the mind, not
the anatomy." By privileging "trans-feminine" socio-cultural groups over
"trans-masculine" individuals who live in private, the State was
practicing hostile discrimination. They argued that medical "gatekeeping"
is a form of state surveillance over the body, violating the Right to
Privacy (Article 21).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the amendment was necessary to provide a
"Clear and Verifiable Framework" for affirmative action. They contended
that "Self-Identification" was prone to misuse for siphoning welfare
benefits. The medical board, they argued, ensures "Objective Reality" in
a legal system that requires categorical certainty for reservations and
social security.
cases.judgment:
The matter is currently before a CJI-led bench (as of late April 2026).
The Court has issued a notice and granted an interim stay on the
mandatory medical board requirement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court's interim reasoning focused on Legislative Arbitrariness.
The judge noted that a law designed to "protect rights" cannot begin by
"extinguishing identities." The Court observed that "Privacy" includes
the right to define one's own gender, and any medical intervention forced
by the State is prima facie a violation of bodily autonomy. The judge
famously remarked, "A person's soul cannot be audited by a medical
board."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reasserts the Doctrine of Self-Identification. It
establishes that Fundamental Rights are inclusive, not exhaustive,
and that the State cannot use "Socio-cultural Visibility" as a metric to
deny constitutional protection to marginalized citizens.

cases.title: Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
A PIL was filed seeking the implementation of a national policy for
menstrual hygiene, including the provision of free sanitary napkins and
separate toilets in all government-aided schools. In January 2026, the
Supreme Court delivered a definitive judgment linking menstrual hygiene
to the fundamental right to education and dignity.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the Right to Menstrual
Health?
- Can the State's failure to provide menstrual hygiene management (MHM)
be considered a violation of the Right to Education (Article 21A)?
- Is menstrual health a "multiplier right"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Jaya Thakur)
The Petitioner argued that the lack of menstrual facilities is the
primary reason for female dropouts in rural schools. They contended that
menstrual health is a matter of Human Dignity. Without access to
basic hygiene, a girl child's Article 21A right is "effectively
suspended" for five days every month, creating a gender-based educational
gap.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that health is a "State Subject" and they are already
providing grants under the Swachh Bharat mission. They contended that
the Court should not mandate specific budgetary allocations for sanitary
products as it is an executive policy decision.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The Court declared
Menstrual Health as a Fundamental Right under Article 21. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Substantive Equality. The judge
ruled that the Right to Education is a "Multiplier Right"-it is the
gateway to all other rights. The Court reasoned that dignity is not an
abstract concept; it requires physical infrastructure. The judge held
that menstrual hygiene is "inextricably linked" to the Right to Health
and the Right to Education. The Court ordered the Union to formulate a
"Uniform National Policy" with a specific focus on school-going girls,
declaring that the biological reality of a woman cannot be a
constitutional barrier to her progress.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Constitutional Recognition of Menstrual
Health. It reinforces that Article 21 is a positive right,
mandating the State to provide the physical infrastructure necessary for
the exercise of human dignity.

cases.title: Rachana Gangu v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
Following reports of rare but fatal Adverse Events Following Immunization
(AEFI) during the COVID-19 mass vaccination drive, families of the
deceased filed a petition seeking compensation. They argued that while
the vaccine was for the public good, the individuals who suffered lethal
side effects should not bear the entire burden of a state-sponsored
health intervention.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Health (Article 21) include a right to
compensation for "unavoidable harm" in mass public health programs?
- Can the State be held liable under a "No-Fault Liability" framework
for vaccine deaths?
- How does the Court balance the need for public trust in science with
the individual's right to life?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Families)
The Petitioners argued that since the State "strongly encouraged" (and in
many cases mandated) vaccination to protect the population, the State
assumes a "Strict Duty of Care." They contended that a "Social Contract"
exists: an individual risks their health for the herd, and if harm
occurs, the herd (via the State) must compensate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that vaccines are inherently probabilistic. They
contended that legally attributing individual deaths to a vaccine would
create "scientific panic" and paralyze future public health responses.
They argued that since there was no "negligence" on the part of the
State, no compensation is due under traditional tort law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Families. The Court
directed the Union to formulate a "No-Fault Compensation Policy" for
vaccine-related deaths. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Distributive Justice. The judge
ruled that Article 21 protects the individual from the "Tyranny of the
Majority." The judge reasoned that if an individual sacrifices their life
for the "collective immunity" of the nation, the nation owes that
individual's family a debt of gratitude and compensation. The Court held
that "No-Fault Liability" is the only constitutional response to mass
public health interventions, ensuring that "Public Policy" does not
become "Public Peril" for the unlucky few.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of No-Fault Compensation in Public
Health. It reinforces that the State's "Parens Patriae" duty includes
financial restitution for systemic risks undertaken by citizens in the
interest of national security or health.

cases.title: Hamsaanandini Nanduri v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
The Social Security Code, 2020, provided maternity benefits to adoptive
mothers, but only if the adopted child was "under the age of three
months." An adoptive mother of an older child challenged this
restriction, arguing it was arbitrary and ignored the biological and
psychological reality of the bonding period required for any child.
cases.issues:
- Does the "3-month age limit" for an adoptive child to trigger maternity
benefits violate Article 14 (Equality)?
- Is the "Maternity Right" a biological right (linked to birth) or a
social/parental right (linked to caregiving)?
- Does this restriction discriminate against older orphans?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Adoptive Mother)
The Petitioner argued that an older child requires more time and care
to bond and adjust to a new home than a newborn. They contended that the
3-month limit was "Manifestly Arbitrary" and had no rational nexus to the
goal of the Maternity Benefit Act. It treated adoptive mothers as
"secondary mothers," violating their dignity under Article 21.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the 3-month limit was a "Policy Choice" based
on the biological recovery period associated with traditional childbirth.
They contended that expanding the benefit to all adoptive mothers would
impose an unmanageable financial burden on employers and the State.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The
Court struck down the 3-month limit as unconstitutional. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Soul of Motherhood. The judge
ruled that motherhood is a "Social and Emotional Function," not merely a
"Biological Event." The Court reasoned that discriminating between a
"biological" and "adoptive" mother violates the very essence of
Substantive Equality. The judge held that every child, regardless of
age, has a Right to be Cared For (Article 21), and the State cannot
create arbitrary hurdles that penalize the adoption of older children.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Parity of Motherhood Rights. It reinforces
that Constitutional Benefits must be based on Functional Reality, not
arbitrary biological markers, protecting the rights of both the parent
and the adopted child.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Fact-Check Unit (Article 19(1)(a) - The IT Rules 2023 Challenge)
cases.facts:
In 2023, the government amended the IT Rules to establish a "Fact-Check
Unit" (FCU) with the power to label any information related to the
"business of the government" as "fake, false, or misleading." Platforms
were then required to take down such content. The Bombay High Court
struck this down in 2024, and the matter reached the Supreme Court in
early 2026.
cases.issues:
- Can the State act as the "Sole Arbiter of Truth" regarding its own
affairs under Article 19(1)(a)?
- Is the FCU a "Reasonable Restriction" under Article 19(2), or does it
constitute Vague and Overbroad Censorship?
- Does the "Chilling Effect" on digital journalism violate the Basic
Structure?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Journalists/Kunal Kamra)
The Petitioners argued that the FCU creates an "Inquisitorial System"
where the government is the prosecutor, judge, and executioner of truth.
They contended that "Business of the Government" is a term so vague that
it could include any criticism of policy. This violates the Shreya
Singhal principle against vague speech restrictions.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that "Fake News" on social media is a threat to the
"Sovereignty and Integrity of India." They contended that the FCU is
merely a "Protective Filter" and that the government is the best-placed
entity to verify facts concerning its own departments.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (2026) upheld the High Court's ruling, striking down
the FCU provision. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Democratic Dissent. The judge
ruled that "Truth is a marketplace, not a state-run monopoly." The Court
reasoned that allowing the government to decide what is "fake" about
itself is a "Conflict of Interest" that destroys the Fourth Estate. The
judge held that Article 19(2) does not include a "Right against
Falsehood" as a ground for restriction. The Court famously remarked, "The
State cannot be the master of the citizen's mind."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine against Vague Restrictions on
Speech. It establishes the legal principle that the State cannot
bypass judicial oversight to act as a digital censor of political
information, safeguarding the freedom of the press in the digital age.

cases.title: Rohith Nathan v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
A dispute arose regarding the determination of the "Creamy Layer" for
Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The Government attempted to include
"Parental Salary" as a component of the income limit for all OBC
candidates, including those whose parents were in private service or
self-employed.
cases.issues:
- Can the "Creamy Layer" status be decided based on "Parental Salary"
alone, or must it be based on "Gross Annual Income"?
- Does treating PSU/Private employees differently from Government
employees (whose salary is excluded from the income test) violate
Article 14?
- What is the "Test of Social Advancement" versus "Economic Advancement"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (OBC Candidates)
The Petitioners argued that for government employees, "Salary" is
excluded and only "Wealth/Rank" matters. By including "Salary" for
private/PSU employees, the State created a "Hostile Discrimination." They
contended that "Creamy Layer" is meant to identify "Social Advancement,"
not just "Financial Liquidity."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that for the self-employed and private sector, "Salary"
and "Income" are the only available metrics for assessment. They
contended that the 8-Lakh limit is a "Uniform Economic Bar" to ensure
reservations reach the "truly backward."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Candidates. The
Court struck down the inclusion of salary for certain categories. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Class vs. Caste. The judge ruled
that the "Creamy Layer" test must be Uniform and Non-Discriminatory.
The Court reasoned that "Social Advancement" is the primary metric. If a
senior government officer's son is excluded based on "Rank" regardless of
salary, a private sector equivalent must be judged by a similar "Status"
metric, not just a raw salary figure. The judge held that the State
cannot "Change the Goalposts" for different sections of the same class.

Layer. It establishes that Income and Salary are distinct concepts in
reservation law, and the State must maintain a "Level Playing Field"
for all OBC candidates regardless of their parents' employer.

cases.title: Yogamaya M.G. v. Union of India, 2026 (Advocates Act & Article 19(1)(g) - Bar Council Elections)
cases.facts:
The Bar Council of India (BCI) introduced a rule prohibiting the office
bearers of local Bar Associations (Presidents/Secretaries) from
contesting elections to the State Bar Councils. This was challenged as an
unconstitutional restriction on the right to practice a profession and
the right to association.
cases.issues:
- Can a statutory body (BCI) impose "Additional Disqualifications" on
candidates that are not found in the parent Advocates Act, 1961?
- Does the rule violate the Right to Form Associations under Article
19(1)(c)?
- Does the rule create an "Arbitrary Classification" among advocates?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Yogamaya)
The Petitioner argued that the BCI is a "Delegate of Parliament" and
cannot legislate new restrictions. They contended that being a leader of
a local bar is a "qualification," not a "disqualification." The rule was
characterized as a "Protectionist Measure" by entrenched Bar Council
members.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Bar Council of India)
The BCI argued the "One Person, One Post" principle. They contended that
allowing local bar leaders to sit on State Councils leads to a "Conflict
of Interest" and "Administrative Paralysis," as they would prioritize
local populist demands over professional regulation.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (April 2026) directed the BCI to "Reconsider and
Withdraw" the rule. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Professional Democracy. The judge
ruled that the BCI's power is "Regulatory," not "Sovereign." The Court
reasoned that the right to contest an election is a "Statutory Right"
that cannot be curtailed by "Subordinate Legislation" (Rules) unless the
parent Act allows it. The judge held that the rule was "Manifestly
Arbitrary" under Article 14 as it penalized successful professional
leadership.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Limits of Delegated Legislation. It
establishes that Statutory Bodies cannot impose "Invisible Bars" on the
