cases.title: Association of Christian Schools v. State of A.P., 2026
cases.facts:
A person born into a Scheduled Caste (SC) converted to Christianity. He
was later accused of a crime, and the victim attempted to invoke the
SC/ST Act against him. The appellant argued that upon conversion to
Christianity, his "SC Status" was legally extinguished, and thus he could
not be prosecuted under the special Act.
cases.issues:
- Does conversion to a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism
result in an "Immediate and Complete" loss of SC status?
- Can the State "Caste-Certificate" override the Constitution
(Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950?
- Is the "Caste System" legally recognized within the Christian or Muslim
faith in India?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Convert)
The Appellant argued that the 1950 Presidential Order is clear: no person
who professes a religion different from the Hindu, Sikh, or Buddhist
religion shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste. They
contended that since Christianity is "Egalitarian," the legal "Stigma of
Untouchability" (the basis for SC status) is theoretically erased upon
conversion.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The State/Victim)
The State argued that "Caste follows the person, not the prayer." They
contended that converted Christians continue to suffer the same social
and economic discrimination as their Hindu counterparts, and therefore
the "Protective Umbrella" of the SC/ST Act should remain.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Appellant. The Court
held that Conversion to Christianity extinguishes SC status. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strictly Textualist Interpretation of the
Constitution. The judge ruled that the Constitution (Scheduled Castes)
Order, 1950, is a "Sovereign Directive." The Court reasoned that the
judiciary cannot "Add or Subtract" religions from the Presidential list.
The judge held that the law assumes the caste system is "Alien to
Christianity." While the social reality might be different, the "Legal
Reality" is that a convert loses the statutory protections and benefits
reserved for the Scheduled Castes.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Exclusivity of the Presidential List (Article
341). It establishes the legal principle that Religious Conversion
results in the loss of Caste-based Statutory protections, barring a
constitutional amendment to include other religions.

cases.title: Ali Khan Mahmudabad v. State of Haryana, 2026 (Article 19(1)(a) & 21 - The 'Academic Magnanimity' Case)
cases.facts:
A prominent professor was threatened with criminal prosecution for a
Facebook post that critiqued a government military operation using
"allegorical language." The State sought sanction to prosecute him for
"Promoting Enmity" (Section 153A IPC). The case reached the Supreme Court
in March 2026.
cases.issues:
- Can "Allegorical or Metaphorical Speech" be criminalized under the
guise of "Public Order"?
- Does the "Right to Academic Freedom" provide a higher threshold of
protection for speech?
- How does the Court handle the "Subjective satisfaction" of the State in
granting prosecution sanctions?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Professor)
The Petitioner argued that "Writing between the lines" is the hallmark of
intellectual life. They contended that a professor has a "Duty to
Critique" and that a "Literalist Interpretation" by the police would
result in the "Death of the University." They argued the post did not
incite any violence.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Haryana)
The State argued that the post was "Cryptic but Inflammatory" and
designed to demoralize the armed forces during a sensitive period. They
contended that even "High Learning" does not grant a license to undermine
national security.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) recorded the State's refusal to prosecute
and dismissed the matter, citing "Academic Magnanimity."
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Constitutional Tolerance. The judge
(CJI Surya Kant) observed that while "cryptic writing" can create
problems, the Court must trust the "Prudence of Learned Minds." The judge
reasoned that the State must show "Maturity" in handling dissent from the
intelligentsia. The Court held that unless there is a "Clear and Present
Incitement" to violence, the State should not unleash the criminal
machinery against academic thought.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of State Magnanimity. It
reinforces that Article 19(1)(a) protects intellectual and allegorical
critique, and that the "Sanction to Prosecute" should be used with
extreme caution to prevent the harassment of academics.

cases.title: Harish Rana v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
Harish Rana, a 32-year-old man, had been in a Persistent Vegetative State
(PVS) for over 13 years following a catastrophic accident. He possessed
no cognitive function and was kept alive solely through Clinically
Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH). His parents, witnessing his
prolonged state of "biological limbo," approached the court seeking the
withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. This case marked the first major
application of the Common Cause (2018) guidelines in a non-terminal but
irreversible PVS scenario where no "Advance Medical Directive" existed.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Die with Dignity under Article 21 extend to
individuals in a persistent vegetative state who cannot signify consent?
- Is Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH) considered
"medical treatment" that can be legally withdrawn, or is it basic care?
- What is the threshold for a judicial "Best Interest" determination for
patients in biological abeyance?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Parents of Harish)
The Petitioners argued that Article 21 protects the right to a "Dignified
Life," which inherently includes the right to a "Dignified Death." They
contended that keeping Harish alive mechanically for over a decade
against the reality of zero neurological recovery was a violation of his
human dignity. They argued that CANH is an intrusive medical
intervention, not a natural process, and should be withdrawable in his
best interest.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State/Medical Board)
The State argued the "Sanctity of Life" principle. They contended that
Harish was not "brain dead" as he was breathing spontaneously.
Withdrawing nutrition, they argued, would be an act of intentional
killing (homicide). In the absence of a Living Will, the State must act
as Parens Patriae and prevent the "starvation" of a citizen.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Parents. The Court
permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment (CANH),
marking the first legally sanctioned passive euthanasia for a PVS patient
in India. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment positioned "between medicine and mercy."
The judge ruled that artificial nutrition and hydration are "medical
treatments," not basic care. The Court reasoned that keeping a person in
a "biological limbo" for 13 years with no hope of recovery is a violation
of the human spirit. The judge held that when a patient is in an
irreversible PVS, their "Best Interest" lies in being allowed to pass
away naturally, rather than being subjected to the "tyranny of
technology."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Right to Passive Euthanasia (Article 21). It
establishes that CANH is a medical intervention that can be withdrawn
in the best interest of a PVS patient, even without a prior Advance
Directive, provided strict medical boards certify the irreversibility of
the condition.

cases.title: Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
A PIL was filed seeking a national policy for menstrual hygiene, focusing
on the provision of free sanitary napkins and separate toilets in all
government schools. In early 2026, the Supreme Court delivered a
transformative judgment linking menstrual hygiene to the fundamental
right to education and dignity.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the Right to Menstrual
Health?
- Can the lack of menstrual hygiene infrastructure be considered a
violation of the Right to Education (Article 21A)?
- Is menstrual health a "multiplier right" in gender equality
jurisprudence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dr. Jaya Thakur)
The Petitioner argued that the lack of menstrual facilities is the
primary driver of female dropouts in rural India. They contended that
menstrual health is a matter of Human Dignity. Without access to
basic hygiene, a girl child's Article 21A right is "effectively
suspended" for several days every month, creating a systemic, biological
educational gap.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that they already provide grants under existing
missions. They contended that the Court should not mandate specific
budgetary allocations for sanitary products, as fiscal management is an
executive policy function and health is primarily a "State Subject" under
the Seventh Schedule.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The Court declared
Menstrual Health as a Fundamental Right under Article 21. The
Plaintiff prevailed.

ruled that the Right to Education (Article 21A) is a "Multiplier Right"-

infrastructure. The Court held that menstrual hygiene is "inextricably

that biological reality cannot be a constitutional barrier to a citizen's
progress.

Health. It reinforces that Article 21 imposes a positive obligation
on the State to provide the physical infrastructure necessary for the
exercise of human dignity.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Fact-Check Unit (Article 19(1)(a) - The IT Rules 2023 Challenge, 2026)

Unit" (FCU) with the power to label any information related to the
"business of the government" as "fake, false, or misleading." In 2024,
the Bombay High Court struck this down as unconstitutional. The matter
reached the Supreme Court in early 2026.
cases.issues:
- Can the State act as the "Sole Arbiter of Truth" regarding its own
affairs under Article 19(1)(a)?
- Does the FCU constitute an Unreasonable Restriction under Article
19(2) due to "Vagueness"?
- Does the risk of losing "Safe Harbor" (Section 79 IT Act) incentivize
digital platforms to practice "Defensive Censorship"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Union of India)
The State argued that "Fake News" on social media is a threat to the
"Sovereignty and Integrity of India." They contended that the FCU is
merely a "Protective Filter" and that the government is the best-placed
entity to verify facts concerning its own departments.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Journalists / Kunal
Kamra)
The Petitioners argued that the FCU creates an "Inquisitorial System"
where the government is the prosecutor and judge of its own truth. They
contended that "Business of the Government" is so broad it could include
any criticism of policy. This violates the Shreya Singhal principle
against vague speech restrictions.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) upheld the Bombay High Court's ruling,
striking down the FCU provision. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Democratic Dissent. The judge
ruled that "Truth is a marketplace, not a state-run monopoly." The Court
reasoned that allowing the government to decide what is "fake" about its
own conduct is a "Conflict of Interest" that destroys the Fourth Estate.
The judge held that Article 19(2) does not include a "Right against
Falsehood" as a ground for restriction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine against Vague Restrictions on
Speech. It establishes the legal principle that the State cannot
bypass judicial oversight to act as a digital censor of political
information.

cases.title: Hamsaanandini Nanduri v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
The Social Security Code, 2020, provided maternity benefits to adoptive
mothers, but only if the adopted child was "under the age of three
months." An adoptive mother of a child older than three months challenged
this restriction as being "manifestly arbitrary."
cases.issues:
- Does the "3-month age limit" for an adoptive child to trigger maternity
benefits violate Article 14 (Equality)?
- Is "motherhood" under the Constitution a biological event or a
caregiving function?
- Does this restriction discriminate against older orphans by making
their adoption less financially viable for parents?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Adoptive Mother)
The Petitioner argued that an older child requires more time and care
to bond and adjust to a new home than a newborn. They contended that the
3-month limit had no "Rational Nexus" to the goal of the Maternity
Benefit Act and treated adoptive mothers as "secondary," violating their
dignity under Article 21.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that the 3-month limit was a "Policy Choice" based
on the biological recovery period associated with traditional childbirth.
They contended that expanding the benefit would impose an unmanageable
financial burden on the private sector and the State.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The
Court struck down the 3-month age limit as unconstitutional. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Soul of Motherhood. The judge
ruled that motherhood is a "Social and Emotional Function," not merely a
"Biological Event." The Court reasoned that discriminating between
"biological" and "adoptive" mothers violates the essence of Substantive
Equality. The judge held that every child, regardless of age, has a
Right to be Cared For (Article 21).
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Parity of Motherhood Rights. It reinforces
that Constitutional Benefits must be based on Functional Reality,
protecting the rights of both the parent and the adopted child.

cases.title: Union of India v. Rohith Nathan, 2026
cases.facts:
For decades, a disparity existed in determining the "Creamy Layer" for
OBC candidates. For children of government servants, "Salary" was
excluded from the income test, while for children of Public Sector Unit
(PSU) and private sector employees, "Salary" was included. This often led
to PSU employees' children being excluded from reservations while
government officers' children were included.
cases.issues:
- Does treating PSU employees differently from Government employees
regarding "Creamy Layer" status violate Article 14?
- Can "Salary" be used as the sole metric for "Social Advancement" under
the Indra Sawhney guidelines?
- Is there a "Hostile Discrimination" between similarly placed categories
of employees?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (OBC Candidates)
The Petitioners argued that the "Source of Employment" does not alter the
social backwardness of a family. They contended that including salary for
PSU employees while excluding it for government servants was an arbitrary
and irrational distinction that penalized children of PSU workers.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that government employees have a "Rank-based"
classification that serves as a proxy for social advancement. They
contended that for the private sector/PSU, raw income is the only
available metric to ensure reservations reach the "truly backward."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Candidates. The
Court struck down the distinction, ordering a uniform application of the
income threshold. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Uniform Equality. The judge ruled
that the "Creamy Layer" test must be Non-Discriminatory. The Court
reasoned that "Social Advancement" is the primary metric. If a senior
government officer's child is excluded based on "Rank," a private sector
equivalent must be judged by a similar status, not just a raw salary
figure. The State cannot "change the goalposts" for different sections of
the same class.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Indra Sawhney Guidelines. It establishes
that Income and Salary are distinct concepts in reservation law,
mandating a level playing field for all OBC candidates.

cases.title: Transgender Persons Amendment Challenge, 2026
cases.facts:
In March 2026, a Bill was introduced (and subsequently challenged) to
replace the "Self-Identification" model for transgender persons with a
"Medical Certification" model. The Bill also removed "trans-man" and
"trans-woman" from certain welfare definitions, focusing strictly on
socio-cultural groups like Hijras and Kinners.
cases.issues:
- Does mandatory medical certification for gender identity violate the
Right to Self-Determination under Article 21?
- Does the Act's "closed list" of identities violate the right to
equality by excluding non-binary persons?
- Can the State use medical "gatekeeping" as a filter for fundamental
rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Transgender Union)
The Petitioners argued that "Identity resides in the mind, not the
anatomy." Relying on NALSA, they argued that forcing a medical exam is
a "Violent Intrusion" into privacy. They contended the Bill was "Under-
inclusive," effectively erasing millions of trans-identities not on the
"Closed List."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that certification is necessary to prevent the
"Misuse of Welfare Benefits." They contended that "Objective Criteria"
are required for state-sponsored affirmative action.
cases.judgment:
The High Court (April 2026) issued a stay on the "Medical Filter"
provision. A landmark verdict is expected in late 2026.
cases.reasoning:
The Court's interim reasoning focused on Human Dignity. The judge
noted that the State cannot reach into the "most intimate layer of a
person's self-knowledge." The judge remarked that the NALSA principles
are part of the "Soul of the Constitution" and cannot be amended away by
executive suspicion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reasserts the Right to Gender Identity. It establishes that
Self-Identification is a facet of Articles 14 and 21, and any state-
imposed medical filter is prima facie unconstitutional.

cases.title: The Opposition Parties v. The Union of India
cases.facts:
In April 2026, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was introduced
to increase the Lok Sabha strength to 850 seats and implement 33% women's
reservation immediately using 2011 Census data. The Bill was defeated in
the Lok Sabha on April 19, 2026, failing to secure the mandatory two-
thirds majority.
cases.issues:
- Does redrawing electoral boundaries based on population (Article 82)
using old data (2011) violate the Basic Structure of Federalism?
- Can a constitutional amendment alter the "Federal Equilibrium" to favor
more populous states?
- Does the immediate implementation of Women's Reservation bypass the
"Post-2026 Census" requirement originally mandated?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Opponents of the Bill)
The Petitioners argued that "Democracy is about Federal Comity." They
contended that the 131st Amendment would "punish" states that
successfully implemented family planning. Relying on the Kuldip Nayar
case, they argued the "Federal Balance" is a basic feature.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The Government argued that "One Person, One Vote" is the core of Article
14. They contended that the seat expansion was a "Democratic Necessity"
to manage the massive increase in the electorate since 1971.
cases.judgment:
The Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha for lack of the two-thirds
majority. However, the Supreme Court is currently hearing a "Pre-emptive
Reference" on the federal formula for future Delimitation.
cases.reasoning:
The legislative reasoning for the defeat centered on the "Federal
Conflict". States with lower populations argued that a purely numbers-
based expansion would reduce their political voice to a nullity. The
failure to pass the Bill highlights the strength of Federal Equity in
the Indian legislative process.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Federalism as a Basic Structure. It establishes
that Delimitation is subject to "Federal Fair-Play", and population-
based seat distribution cannot be altered without a national consensus
between the states.

cases.title: Rachana Gangu v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
Parents who lost children to rare but fatal side effects after COVID-19
vaccination filed a petition seeking compensation. They argued that while
the vaccine was for the public good, the individuals who suffered lethal
outcomes should not bear the entire burden of a state-led program.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Health (Article 21) include a right to
compensation for "unavoidable harm" in mass programs?
- Can the State be held liable under a "No-Fault Liability" framework
for vaccine deaths?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (The Families)
The Petitioners argued that since the State "strongly encouraged"
vaccination, the State assumes a "Strict Duty of Care." They contended
that a "Social Contract" exists: an individual risks their health for the
"herd immunity," and if harm occurs, the State must compensate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Union of India)
The State argued that vaccines are inherently probabilistic. They
contended that legally attributing individual deaths would create
"scientific panic." They argued that since there was no "negligence," no
compensation is due under traditional tort law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Families. The Court
directed the Union to formulate a "No-Fault Compensation Policy" for
serious adverse events. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Distributive Justice. The judge
ruled that Article 21 protects the individual from the "Majority
Interest." The judge reasoned that if an individual sacrifices their life
for the nation's immunity, the nation owes that individual's family
restitution. The Court held that "No-Fault Liability" is the only
constitutional response to state-led systemic risks.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of No-Fault Compensation. It
reinforces that the State's "Parens Patriae" duty includes financial
restitution for systemic risks undertaken by citizens.

permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment (CANH),
marking the first legally sanctioned passive euthanasia for a PVS patient
in India. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment positioned "between medicine and mercy."
The judge ruled that artificial nutrition and hydration are "medical
treatments," not basic care. The Court reasoned that keeping a person in
a "biological limbo" for 13 years with no hope of recovery is a violation
of the human spirit. The judge held that when a patient is in an
irreversible PVS, their "Best Interest" lies in being allowed to pass
away naturally, rather than being subjected to the "tyranny of
technology."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the Right to Passive Euthanasia (Article 21). It
establishes that CANH is a medical intervention that can be withdrawn
in the best interest of a PVS patient, even without a prior Advance
Directive, provided strict medical boards certify the irreversibility of
the condition.

cases.title: Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
A PIL was filed seeking a national policy for menstrual hygiene, focusing
on the provision of free sanitary napkins and separate toilets in all
government schools. In early 2026, the Supreme Court delivered a
transformative judgment linking menstrual hygiene to the fundamental
right to education and dignity.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Life (Article 21) include the Right to Menstrual
Health?
- Can the lack of menstrual hygiene infrastructure be considered a
violation of the Right to Education (Article 21A)?
- Is menstrual health a "multiplier right" in gender equality
jurisprudence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioner argued that the lack of menstrual facilities is the
primary driver of female dropouts in rural India. They contended that
menstrual health is a matter of Human Dignity. Without access to
basic hygiene, a girl child's Article 21A right is "effectively
suspended" for several days every month, creating a systemic, biological
educational gap.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The State argued that they already provide grants under existing
missions. They contended that the Court should not mandate specific
budgetary allocations for sanitary products, as fiscal management is an
executive policy function and health is primarily a "State Subject" under
the Seventh Schedule.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The Court declared
Menstrual Health as a Fundamental Right under Article 21. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Substantive Equality. The judge
ruled that the Right to Education (Article 21A) is a "Multiplier Right"-
the gateway to all other rights. Dignity requires physical
infrastructure. The Court held that menstrual hygiene is "inextricably
linked" to the Right to Health. The Court ordered the Union to formulate
a "Uniform National Policy" with a specific focus on schools, declaring
that biological reality cannot be a constitutional barrier to a citizen's
progress.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Constitutional Recognition of Menstrual
Health. It reinforces that Article 21 imposes a positive obligation
on the State to provide the physical infrastructure necessary for the
exercise of human dignity.

cases.title: Union of India v. The Fact-Check Unit (Article 19(1)(a) - The IT Rules 2023 Challenge, 2026)
cases.facts:
In 2023, the government amended the IT Rules to establish a "Fact-Check
Unit" (FCU) with the power to label any information related to the
"business of the government" as "fake, false, or misleading." In 2024,
the Bombay High Court struck this down as unconstitutional. The matter
reached the Supreme Court in early 2026.
cases.issues:
- Can the State act as the "Sole Arbiter of Truth" regarding its own
affairs under Article 19(1)(a)?
- Does the FCU constitute an Unreasonable Restriction under Article
19(2) due to "Vagueness"?
- Does the risk of losing "Safe Harbor" (Section 79 IT Act) incentivize
digital platforms to practice "Defensive Censorship"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The State argued that "Fake News" on social media is a threat to the
"Sovereignty and Integrity of India." They contended that the FCU is
merely a "Protective Filter" and that the government is the best-placed
entity to verify facts concerning its own departments.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Petitioners argued that the FCU creates an "Inquisitorial System"
where the government is the prosecutor and judge of its own truth. They
contended that "Business of the Government" is so broad it could include
any criticism of policy. This violates the Shreya Singhal principle
against vague speech restrictions.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) upheld the Bombay High Court's ruling,
striking down the FCU provision. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fierce defense of Democratic Dissent. The judge
ruled that "Truth is a marketplace, not a state-run monopoly." The Court
reasoned that allowing the government to decide what is "fake" about its
own conduct is a "Conflict of Interest" that destroys the Fourth Estate.
The judge held that Article 19(2) does not include a "Right against
Falsehood" as a ground for restriction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine against Vague Restrictions on
Speech. It establishes the legal principle that the State cannot
bypass judicial oversight to act as a digital censor of political
information.

cases.title: Hamsaanandini Nanduri v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
The Social Security Code, 2020, provided maternity benefits to adoptive
mothers, but only if the adopted child was "under the age of three
months." An adoptive mother of a child older than three months challenged
this restriction as being "manifestly arbitrary."
cases.issues:
- Does the "3-month age limit" for an adoptive child to trigger maternity
benefits violate Article 14 (Equality)?
- Is "motherhood" under the Constitution a biological event or a
caregiving function?
- Does this restriction discriminate against older orphans by making
their adoption less financially viable for parents?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioner argued that an older child requires more time and care
to bond and adjust to a new home than a newborn. They contended that the
3-month limit had no "Rational Nexus" to the goal of the Maternity
Benefit Act and treated adoptive mothers as "secondary," violating their
dignity under Article 21.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Government argued that the 3-month limit was a "Policy Choice" based
on the biological recovery period associated with traditional childbirth.
They contended that expanding the benefit would impose an unmanageable
financial burden on the private sector and the State.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Petitioner. The
Court struck down the 3-month age limit as unconstitutional. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on the Soul of Motherhood. The judge
ruled that motherhood is a "Social and Emotional Function," not merely a
"Biological Event." The Court reasoned that discriminating between
"biological" and "adoptive" mothers violates the essence of Substantive
Equality. The judge held that every child, regardless of age, has a
Right to be Cared For (Article 21).
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Parity of Motherhood Rights. It reinforces
that Constitutional Benefits must be based on Functional Reality,
protecting the rights of both the parent and the adopted child.

cases.title: Union of India v. Rohith Nathan, 2026
cases.facts:
For decades, a disparity existed in determining the "Creamy Layer" for
OBC candidates. For children of government servants, "Salary" was
excluded from the income test, while for children of Public Sector Unit
(PSU) and private sector employees, "Salary" was included. This often led
to PSU employees' children being excluded from reservations while
government officers' children were included.
cases.issues:
- Does treating PSU employees differently from Government employees
regarding "Creamy Layer" status violate Article 14?
- Can "Salary" be used as the sole metric for "Social Advancement" under
the Indra Sawhney guidelines?
- Is there a "Hostile Discrimination" between similarly placed categories
of employees?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioners argued that the "Source of Employment" does not alter the
social backwardness of a family. They contended that including salary for
PSU employees while excluding it for government servants was an arbitrary
and irrational distinction that penalized children of PSU workers.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The State argued that government employees have a "Rank-based"
classification that serves as a proxy for social advancement. They
contended that for the private sector/PSU, raw income is the only
available metric to ensure reservations reach the "truly backward."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Candidates. The
Court struck down the distinction, ordering a uniform application of the
income threshold. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Uniform Equality. The judge ruled
that the "Creamy Layer" test must be Non-Discriminatory. The Court
reasoned that "Social Advancement" is the primary metric. If a senior
government officer's child is excluded based on "Rank," a private sector
equivalent must be judged by a similar status, not just a raw salary
figure. The State cannot "change the goalposts" for different sections of
the same class.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Indra Sawhney Guidelines. It establishes
that Income and Salary are distinct concepts in reservation law,
mandating a level playing field for all OBC candidates.

cases.title: Transgender Persons Amendment Challenge, 2026
cases.facts:
In March 2026, a Bill was introduced (and subsequently challenged) to
replace the "Self-Identification" model for transgender persons with a
"Medical Certification" model. The Bill also removed "trans-man" and
"trans-woman" from certain welfare definitions, focusing strictly on
socio-cultural groups like Hijras and Kinners.
cases.issues:
- Does mandatory medical certification for gender identity violate the
Right to Self-Determination under Article 21?
- Does the Act's "closed list" of identities violate the right to
equality by excluding non-binary persons?
- Can the State use medical "gatekeeping" as a filter for fundamental
rights?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioners argued that "Identity resides in the mind, not the
anatomy." Relying on NALSA, they argued that forcing a medical exam is
a "Violent Intrusion" into privacy. They contended the Bill was "Under-
inclusive," effectively erasing millions of trans-identities not on the
"Closed List."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Government argued that certification is necessary to prevent the
"Misuse of Welfare Benefits." They contended that "Objective Criteria"
are required for state-sponsored affirmative action.
cases.judgment:
The High Court (April 2026) issued a stay on the "Medical Filter"
provision. A landmark verdict is expected in late 2026.
cases.reasoning:
The Court's interim reasoning focused on Human Dignity. The judge
noted that the State cannot reach into the "most intimate layer of a
person's self-knowledge." The judge remarked that the NALSA principles
are part of the "Soul of the Constitution" and cannot be amended away by
executive suspicion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reasserts the Right to Gender Identity. It establishes that
Self-Identification is a facet of Articles 14 and 21, and any state-
imposed medical filter is prima facie unconstitutional.

cases.title: The Opposition Parties v. The Union of India
cases.facts:
In April 2026, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was introduced
to increase the Lok Sabha strength to 850 seats and implement 33% women's
reservation immediately using 2011 Census data. The Bill was defeated in
the Lok Sabha on April 19, 2026, failing to secure the mandatory two-
thirds majority.
cases.issues:
- Does redrawing electoral boundaries based on population (Article 82)
using old data (2011) violate the Basic Structure of Federalism?
- Can a constitutional amendment alter the "Federal Equilibrium" to favor
more populous states?
- Does the immediate implementation of Women's Reservation bypass the
"Post-2026 Census" requirement originally mandated?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioners argued that "Democracy is about Federal Comity." They
contended that the 131st Amendment would "punish" states that
successfully implemented family planning. Relying on the Kuldip Nayar
case, they argued the "Federal Balance" is a basic feature.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Government argued that "One Person, One Vote" is the core of Article
14. They contended that the seat expansion was a "Democratic Necessity"
to manage the massive increase in the electorate since 1971.
cases.judgment:
The Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha for lack of the two-thirds
majority. However, the Supreme Court is currently hearing a "Pre-emptive
Reference" on the federal formula for future Delimitation.
cases.reasoning:
The legislative reasoning for the defeat centered on the "Federal
Conflict". States with lower populations argued that a purely numbers-
based expansion would reduce their political voice to a nullity. The
failure to pass the Bill highlights the strength of Federal Equity in
the Indian legislative process.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces Federalism as a Basic Structure. It establishes
that Delimitation is subject to "Federal Fair-Play", and population-
based seat distribution cannot be altered without a national consensus
between the states.

cases.title: Rachana Gangu v. Union of India, 2026
cases.facts:
Parents who lost children to rare but fatal side effects after COVID-19
vaccination filed a petition seeking compensation. They argued that while
the vaccine was for the public good, the individuals who suffered lethal
outcomes should not bear the entire burden of a state-led program.
cases.issues:
- Does the Right to Health (Article 21) include a right to
compensation for "unavoidable harm" in mass programs?
- Can the State be held liable under a "No-Fault Liability" framework
for vaccine deaths?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioners argued that since the State "strongly encouraged"
vaccination, the State assumes a "Strict Duty of Care." They contended
that a "Social Contract" exists: an individual risks their health for the
"herd immunity," and if harm occurs, the State must compensate.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The State argued that vaccines are inherently probabilistic. They
contended that legally attributing individual deaths would create
"scientific panic." They argued that since there was no "negligence," no
compensation is due under traditional tort law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Families. The Court
directed the Union to formulate a "No-Fault Compensation Policy" for
serious adverse events. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Distributive Justice. The judge
ruled that Article 21 protects the individual from the "Majority
Interest." The judge reasoned that if an individual sacrifices their life
for the nation's immunity, the nation owes that individual's family
restitution. The Court held that "No-Fault Liability" is the only
constitutional response to state-led systemic risks.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes the Doctrine of No-Fault Compensation. It
reinforces that the State's "Parens Patriae" duty includes financial
restitution for systemic risks undertaken by citizens.

cases.title: Association of Christian Schools v. State of A.P., 2026
cases.facts:
A person born into a Scheduled Caste (SC) converted to Christianity. He
was later accused of a crime, and the victim attempted to invoke the
SC/ST Act against him. The appellant argued that upon conversion, his "SC
Status" was legally extinguished.
cases.issues:
- Does conversion to a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism
result in an "Immediate and Complete" loss of SC status under the
1950 Order?
- Can a State Government order override the Constitution (Scheduled
Castes) Order, 1950?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Appellant argued that the 1950 Presidential Order is clear: no person
who professes a religion different from Hinduism, Sikhism, or Buddhism
shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste. They contended that
since Christianity is "Egalitarian," the legal "Stigma of Untouchability"
is theoretically erased.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The State argued that "Caste follows the person." They contended that
converted Christians continue to suffer the same social and economic
discrimination as their Hindu counterparts, and thus the "Protective
Umbrella" of the SC/ST Act should remain.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (March 2026) ruled in favor of the Appellant. The Court
held that Conversion to Christianity extinguishes SC status. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a Textualist Interpretation. The judge ruled that
the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, is a "Sovereign
Directive." The Court reasoned that the judiciary cannot "Add or
Subtract" religions from the Presidential list. The judge held that while
the social reality might be different, the "Legal Reality" is that a
convert loses the statutory protections reserved for SCs.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Exclusivity of the Presidential List (Article
341). It establishes that Religious Conversion results in the loss of
Caste-based Statutory protections, barring a constitutional amendment.

cases.title: Yogamaya M.G. v. Union of India, 2026 (Advocates Act & Article 19(1)(g) - Bar Council Elections)
cases.facts:
The Bar Council of India (BCI) introduced a rule prohibiting the office
bearers of local Bar Associations (Presidents/Secretaries) from
contesting elections to the State Bar Councils.
cases.issues:
- Can a statutory body (BCI) impose "Additional Disqualifications" on
candidates not found in the parent Advocates Act, 1961?
- Does the rule violate the Right to Form Associations under Article
19(1)(c)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
The Petitioner argued that the BCI is a "Delegate" and cannot legislate
new restrictions. They contended that being a leader of a local bar is a
"qualification," not a "disqualification." The rule was characterized as
"Protectionist."

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The BCI argued the "One Person, One Post" principle. They contended that
allowing local bar leaders to sit on State Councils leads to a "Conflict
of Interest" and "Administrative Paralysis."
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court (April 2026) directed the BCI to "Reconsider and
Withdraw" the rule. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment on Professional Democracy. The judge
ruled that the BCI's power is "Regulatory," not "Sovereign." The judge
held that the rule was "Manifestly Arbitrary" under Article 14 as it
penalized successful professional leadership without a rational nexus to
the parent Act.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Limits of Delegated Legislation. It
establishes that Statutory Bodies cannot impose "Invisible Bars" on the
democratic rights of their members.
